World.title: Thousands protest in Croatia to demand government clean up toxic waste
World.content:
Tens of thousands of protesters have marched through the Croatian capital demanding the government urgently clear a vast illegal dump of hazardous waste that residents say is poisoning a once-pristine mountain region.

Saturday’s demonstration in Zagreb was one of the largest protests Croatia has seen in years, driven by growing frustration that authorities have spent months failing to remove more than 30,000 tonnes of waste, including medical and industrial material, buried near the town of Gospic in the mountainous Lika region.

The anger has widened into a broader challenge to Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic’s conservative government, which opponents accuse of corruption and of covering up the pollution’s true scale.

Police and Europol, the European Union’s law enforcement agency, arrested 13 people in February over the illegal importing and dumping of the waste, brought in from elsewhere in the bloc since 2023.

Investigators said the scheme earned suspects more than $4m before it was uncovered at an abandoned industrial site outside Gospic.

Plenkovic visited the site last week and said his government had chosen a contractor to begin removing the waste, the first phase of a promised cleanup.

Croatian officials have also said soil and water tests around Gospic have not shown contamination, a claim that clashes with an assessment published last month by Croatia’s anticorruption agency, which found elevated metal levels in the soil and detected PFAS chemicals, known as “forever chemicals” for how long they persist, in nearby groundwater.

‘Not a tragedy, a crime’

That gap between the government’s assurances and the pollution findings is what brought crowds into Zagreb’s main square on Saturday, where organisers demanded a complete cleanup plan with binding deadlines within 20 days and the removal of all buried waste within three months.



Many protesters said they no longer trusted official explanations for how so much waste had gone unnoticed for so long.

“This is not a tragedy, this is a crime,” demonstrator Ivan Rittinger told The Associated Press news agency, arguing that someone had profited while officials looked away.

Vjekoslav Busic, who leads the Gospic Is Our Home community group that organised the march, told the crowd the failure went beyond any single official, asking who had built the institutions and appointed the people that let the pollution continue for years.

The rally drew lawmakers from across the political spectrum, including the centre-left Social Democratic Party and Most, a smaller anticorruption party whose name means “bridge”, alongside the well-known Croatian actor Rade Serbedzija, a sign of how far the anger has spread beyond any one faction.

Environmental experts say the damage has stayed local so far, but warn the region’s porous terrain and rivers could eventually carry pollutants towards the Adriatic Sea, a coastline the region’s tourism depends on.

Plenkovic has dismissed the criticism as an attempt by rivals to exploit the scandal, even as prosecutors continue investigating a Croatian company accused of burying toxic waste at several sites beyond Gospic.

World.title: Russia’s Putin meets US envoys to discuss Trump proposal to end Ukraine war
World.content:
Both Russia and Ukraine vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during talks in Moscow and Kyiv.

Share Russia’s Putin meets US envoys to discuss Trump proposal to end Ukraine war on social media

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has begun talks with envoys from the United States on ending more than four years of war in Ukraine, ahead of their expected visit to Kyiv on Sunday.

Putin met Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin on Saturday.

“Dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to Moscow. The situation is, of course, not simple,” Putin told the envoys in a ceremony aired on Russian TV.

Both Russia and Ukraine vowed not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during the negotiations, as Washington tries to revive US-led talks to end Europe’s worst conflict since the Second World War.

Earlier, Trump said son-in-law Kushner and Witkoff, his special envoy and business ally, were bringing “a proposal to end the war”.

In Putin’s address to them, he said: “I would like to ask everyone to convey their best wishes and words of gratitude to US President Mr Trump”.

Witkoff said Trump had sent his best wishes to Putin and ⁠⁠thanked him for ⁠⁠the limited ceasefire during the delegation’s visit. Putin said ⁠⁠Russia would do its ⁠⁠utmost to ensure ⁠⁠the safety of the mediators.

‘Refrain from strikes’

The talks come as the grinding war – which began with the Russian invasion in 2022 – has seen increasing civilian deaths and attacks this summer.

Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.

Russian strikes on Ukraine on Saturday killed at least seven people, including in the Kyiv suburbs, Ukrainian officials said.

The Kremlin said it would not strike Kyiv from midnight on Saturday, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would halt strikes on Moscow “from now” until Monday.



“The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight tonight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

Zelenskyy – who had offered a truce during the US visits – later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.

“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” Zelenskyy said on social media.

The Ukrainian leader said he had spoken to the US officials and that he expected them in Kyiv on Sunday.

It will be Witkoff and Kushner’s first visit to Kyiv since Trump returned to office last year with a pledge to resolve the conflict.

World.title: India crush Pakistan at T20 Asia Cup with record-breaking bowling display
World.content:
India claim seven-wicket win after Pakistan lose 10 wickets for just 28 runs as they are bowled out for 55.

India produced a dominant display to defeat Pakistan by seven wickets in the Women’s T20 Asia Cup in Dubai, bowling their rivals out for their lowest total in the format before rattling off their target inside nine overs.

Pakistan, having won the toss and elected to bat at the Dubai International Stadium on Saturday, made a promising start but collapsed spectacularly after an opening partnership of 27.

India eventually dismissed them for just 55 in 18.1 overs, with their spinners responsible for much of the damage.

Shree Charani and Prema Rawat were the stars of the bowling attack, taking three wickets apiece. Charani finished with remarkable figures of 3 for 7 from four overs, while Rawat returned 3 for 9. Deepti Sharma added two wickets for only five runs.

Pakistan’s innings initially appeared under control. Muneeba Ali made 13, and Shawaal Zulfiqar scored 14 for the first wicket.

But Shafali Verma broke the partnership by bowling Muneeba, and Charani then struck twice in the sixth over. She dismissed Gull Feroza for a duck before removing Zulfiqar, leaving Pakistan 29 for three.

The collapse continued almost immediately as Pakistan slipped to 32 for four in the eighth over before Rawat and Deepti Sharma intensified the pressure. By the 13th over, Pakistan were 45 for seven, and there was no prospect of recovering to a competitive total.

The final three wickets eventually fell with Pakistan on 55, giving India an exceptionally modest target. The total was Pakistan’s lowest in women’s T20I cricket, surpassing their previous low of 63 against India in the 2012 Women’s Twenty20 Asia Cup.



India survive brief wobble

Despite requiring only 56, India did not have everything their own way at the start of the chase.

Pakistan’s bowlers claimed three wickets, giving their opponents a brief glimpse of an unlikely route back into the contest. Fatima Sana was Pakistan’s most successful bowler, finishing with 3 for 17.

The target, however, was simply too small. India reached 57 for three in 8.4 overs, completing a seven-wicket victory with Harmanpreet Kaur unbeaten on 18. The Indian captain ensured there was no late drama and guided her side across the line with plenty of deliveries to spare.

The victory maintained India’s perfect start to the tournament. They now have six points from three matches and have already secured their place in the semifinals.

For Pakistan, meanwhile, the defeat leaves their qualification hopes dependent on their final group match against Hong Kong. They remain on two points and need a victory to give themselves a chance of progressing.

World.title: Germany’s far-right AfD eyes historic first in state election
World.content:
NewsFeed Germany’s far-right AfD eyes historic first in state election

Germany’s far-right AfD is projected to take power in one of the country’s 16 states for the first time. A win in the Saxony-Anhalt election would be the first time a far-right party has taken control of a regional parliament since the Second World War.

World.title: Norway Seizes Russian Ship, Testing Moscow in the High Arctic
World.content:
For the past several days, Norwegian security services had been tracking a Russian research ship.

It was cruising around Svalbard, an icy archipelago high in the Arctic near the North Pole that Norway controls but is governed by a one-of-a-kind treaty that gives the Russians access.

On Wednesday, the Norwegians pounced.

Armed with a court order that is part of a global effort to recover Russian assets, Norwegian police officers boarded the ship while it was docked in Barentsburg, a tiny Russian outpost in Svalbard. The officers confronted the captain of the ship, a somewhat clunky, 200-foot-long oceanographic vessel, and announced that they were “arresting” it.

The seized ship was part of a broader effort to enforce an international court judgment ordering Russia to pay a Ukrainian energy company, Naftogaz, more than $4 billion for expropriating that company’s assets in Crimea. The ship, owned by the Russian government and called Professor Molchanov, after a famous Russian scientist, is now prohibited from leaving Barentsburg until Norwegian courts decide what to do next.

“We have only acted as a messenger,” said Lars Fause, the governor of Svalbard.

He added that it was the first time Norway had taken action like this in Svalbard. The Russians quickly denounced it, with the foreign ministry spokeswoman calling it “piracy.” But the bold move fits neatly with the shifting geopolitics in this part of the Arctic and Norway’s increasingly aggressive stance.

World.title: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's top negotiators are meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.

Footage released by the Kremlin showed Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner being greeted by Putin, who said the current situation "is not so easy". He added Russia would explain "how we see the situation".

Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing with Ukraine to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days. On Sunday the envoys will travel to Kyiv for more talks.

On Friday, Trump said Witkoff and Kushner were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts from the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed.

At Saturday's talks in the Kremlin, Putin also said that "in any case, whatever happens, such contacts are undoubtedly always useful". He also thanked Trump for his peacemaking efforts.

The talks in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital are continuing behind closed doors.

Zelensky said earlier on Saturday that he had spoken to the envoys, who have "already begun working with the Russian side today".

"The plan for tomorrow's diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the US team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation," he added.

"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv."

Russian state media reported that President Vladimir Putin had ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv for three days due to the US visit.

US news outlet Axios reported that the US envoys would separately meet both Putin and Zelensky.

Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but the talks on Sunday would be the first in Ukraine.

It is not clear how the US envoys will be travelling from Moscow to Kyiv.

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

World.title: US hits three Iranian oil tankers after saying its warships were targeted
World.content:
The US military says it has hit three Iran-linked oil tankers after Iran launched ballistic missiles towards two American Navy warships in the region.

US Central Command (Centcom) said on Saturday it had "permanently disabled" a tanker near Kharg Island and another near Jask in the Gulf of Oman, and "completely destroyed" a third in the Gulf of Oman.

"It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers," Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote on social media.

Iran's state media confirmed the attacks. A spokesperson for Iran's military warned that strikes on US military vessels would be expanded if they continued attacking Iranian ships, the state media reported.

Iranian state media outlet IRIB reported that there were no casualties in the attack on the tanker near Kharg Island, and that footage indicated the vessel's cooling system put out the fire within an hour.

Kharg Island is a small rocky outcrop just 15 nautical miles (24km) off the coast of Iran. Ninety percent of Iran's crude oil comes through a terminal on the island - transported through pipes from the mainland.

The crews aboard the two attacked tankers in the Gulf of Oman were taken to shore in lifeboats, IRIB reported. One of those tankers was empty and the other was carrying a load of oil, it added.

Centcom said it "successfully evaded" multiple attacks from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeting a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. No American troops were harmed, it said.

Admiral Brad Cooper, Centcom's commander, said in a statement on Saturday: "Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours."

"We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."

Centcom, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, claimed that the three Iranian oil tankers were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".

The strikes come nearly a week after renewed attacks between the US and Iran, which followed a period of relative calm between the warring sides.

The US resumed attacks last Sunday, when it said it had struck two rocket launchers to prevent them being used to lay naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy murder case, after jury deadlocks
World.content:
"There will be no decisions made today," Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said on Friday concerning what could happen next in the case.

He said he would meet the rest of their legal team to decide whether they would pursue a new trial.

"The facts are Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and the evidence suggested to us that she was in control of her actions when she committed those homicides," Cruz said.

Outside the court on Friday, Reddington said he believed 11 of the 12 jurors would have delivered a verdict that favoured Clancy had it not been for the one holdout.

But it remains unclear what position any member of the jury took or what occurred in the deliberation room.

For weeks, the case gripped the country and sparked debate over the topic of postpartum psychosis. Many followed along with livestreams of the trial, as family members and experts testified. Each day, more than 200 members of the media crowded the court and groups of supporters in varying sizes often gathered outside.

The widespread attention even spurred comments on Friday from US President Donald Trump, who called the case a "horrible tragedy".

"She did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse," he said. "I assume there's going to be another trial."

Trump added: "But you'll find out what the price to pay is. There'll be a price."

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external. www.befrienders.org.

A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

World.title: At least two dead in blast at Bolivia military barracks
World.content:
At least two people have been killed after an explosion at a military barracks in Bolivia - but authorities fear the toll could be higher.

Bolivian Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said at least 81 people had been injured when "pyrotechnic material" detonated at the barracks, where an artillery regiment was stationed, about 14:30 local time (18:30 GMT) on Friday. Fourteen others remain missing.

Health official Rita Nebraska told local television between 10 and 15 people were believed to have died in the incident in Viacha, about 30km (19 miles) from La Paz, according to Reuters.

Police said dozens of homes had been damaged by the blast and that emergency workers were searching the rubble.

Nebraska said there was a risk of a further explosion and urged people to stay at least 150m from the military base.

Base commander Colonel Antonio Amaru told reporters on Saturday that a sergeant and 13 conscripted soldiers aged between 18 and 19-years-old were among the missing.

Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz expressed his "deepest solidarity" with the families of those who had died and had been injured.

He wrote on social media that a "thorough, technical and transparent investigation" would take place into what happened.

Police spokesman Roger Roca told news agency AFP that fireworks had been stored at the barracks and the cause of the blast remained under investigation.

Viacha's authorities have declared three days of mourning.

World.title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
World.content:
The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.

Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University College London explained.

"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."

To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.

His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.

The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.

More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.

But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.

For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.

"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

World.title: Trump signs order to remove endangered species protection for grey wolves
World.content:
Donald Trump has signed an executive order to remove endangered species protection for the grey wolf and a subspecies, the Mexican wolf.

The US president's decision could pave the way for pastoral farmers to kill the canines to protect their livestock. His order said ranchers played a "vital role" in the food supply chain and American cultural heritage.

But conservation groups have criticised the move, saying it could derail long-term efforts to recover the endangered wolf populations.

There were 319 Mexican wolves in the wild in the US in 2025, up from just four when they were reintroduced in 1998, US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) figures show.

Meanwhile, there are roughly 18,000 grey wolves across the US, though they are still considered endangered as most of their habitat has been destroyed by humans.

An attempt to de-list them at a federal level in 2022 became tied up in litigation, and some campaigners have indicated they intend to do the same of the US Department of Interior acts on Trump's order.

The executive order does not give ranchers immediate license to shoot wolves preying on livestock, but instead gives Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to determine whether the grey and Mexican wolf populations had recovered enough to warrant being taken off the endangered species list.

Noting that US livestock herds were at a 75-year low while demand for beef had risen by 10% in the past decade, the order added: "More can and should be done to support this critical industry."

However, environmental groups pointed to studies that suggested wolf attacks on livestock were rare and had little impact on ranchers' income.

"This is a huge distraction to placate a handful of ranchers and make them believe that wolves are a greater threat than President Trump's own policies," said Greta Anderson, deputy director of Western Watersheds Project, which works to conserve wildlife in western US states.

The Wolf Conservation Center noted that ranchers were entitled to up to 100% compensation for any livestock losses caused by wolves under the current system, with individual states providing funding for programmes to deter attacks.

"The Mexican grey wolf is not recovered simply because the population has grown," said Claire Musser, executive director of the Grand Canyon Wolf Recovery Project. "Weakening federal protections now would put decades of recovery work at risk."

The executive order comes as the Trump administration is seeking to lower record-high beef prices for consumers, driven by drought and an outbreak of parasites in US beef stocks.

Ranchers have been frustrated by Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on beef imports to address price rises, putting pressure on their already tight margins.

The US government launched a campaign to systematically exterminate wolves towards the end of the 19th Century. This, along with farmers and landowners trapping and killing wolves, pushed them to the brink of eradication.

Ranchers still view them as a nuisance, which tackling lethally constitutes a federal crime.

World.title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect
World.content:
As summer temperatures in Europe smashed records and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.

Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.

This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.

A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".

Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".

But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.

Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.

Poland's interior minister is clear.

"There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin KierwiÅski said, warning people to be on their guard.

World.title: Nepal rescuers try to reach dozens trapped in tunnel after two found alive
World.content:
The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.

In Nepal, however, rescue operations are taking place at seven hydropower tunnels in which more than 150 people are feared trapped - as well as in 19 other areas.

In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices at the Trishuli 3A hydropower site.

According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".

Crews clambered in to find Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan - both had injuries on their hands and legs, "possibly" from crawling through the tunnel. Both were airlifted to the Army Hospital in the capital, Kathmandu.

Maharjan, who was rescued second, is in a critical condition, the prime minister's office said. Shah was also undergoing medical tests.

The body of a third person was found in the same tunnel later. A local official said it was swollen and could not be immediately identified.

Officials believe another 39 people are in the Trishuli 3A tunnel, although it is not clear if all are alive.

World.title: Boss Mustapha at 70: The measure of a life of service, By Umaru J Abu
World.content:
My prayer for my mentor, leader and friend is that the God whom he has served so faithfully will grant him many more years in good health and strength; that the wisdom accumulated over seven decades will continue to benefit our country and coming generations; and that the seeds he has planted — in public institutions, in the Church, in education and in people — will continue to bear fruit long after the stories of our present politics have faded.

It was already past 11 o’clock that night when I finally got home.

We had spent much of the day poring over data on the performance of ministers, interrogating numbers, testing conclusions and considering what they meant for the work of government. It had been a long day, even by the standards of an office where long days were quite normal. I took my bath and was preparing to retire for the night when my telephone rang.

It was Boss Mustapha.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

There was something important that needed to be resolved. A decision had to be reached, and the resulting document needed to get to President Muhammadu Buhari the following morning. He apologised for calling so late and asked if I could return to the office.

So, back to the office I went.

We worked into the early hours of the morning, going over the issues until he was satisfied that what would reach the president was clear, considered and fit for purpose.

For me, that night captures something essential about the man whose 70th birthday we celebrate today.

For the better part of the nearly six years that Boss Mustapha (CFR) served as Secretary to the Government of the Federation, I had the privilege of working closely with him, providing technical support through the UK Government’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and its Partnership to Engage, Reform and Learn (PERL) programme. That vantage point afforded me something more valuable than a knowledge of the public record. It allowed me to observe the man behind the office.

And what I saw was an extraordinary devotion to duty.

Boss, as many of us simply call him, was a workaholic in the truest sense of the word. Midnight was not an unusual closing time. Files were read. Briefs were interrogated. Assumptions were challenged. Decisions were rarely taken casually. The demands of the office were enormous, but his appetite for work seemed even greater.

Yet, hard work alone does not explain Boss Mustapha.

The office of Secretary to the Government of the Federation occupies a peculiar place in Nigeria’s governance architecture. Its occupant must understand administration without being imprisoned by bureaucracy; politics without becoming consumed by partisanship; policy without losing sight of implementation; and power without forgetting that public office is ultimately a trust.

Boss understood these balances remarkably well.

He was a politician who understood the language of the public service and a public servant who understood the realities of politics. He could navigate both worlds without confusing their respective purposes. He understood when consensus was necessary, when bureaucracy needed to be pushed, when political judgement was required and, importantly, when the evidence simply had to speak.

That capacity became particularly important as we worked to strengthen performance management at the centre of government.

With the support of the FCDO through the PERL Governance Programme, we worked with his office to develop what became the first structured centre-of-government performance management system of that administration. It was demanding work. Building systems at the centre of government is rarely glamorous. It requires painstaking negotiations across ministries and agencies, agreement on what should be measured, the discipline to distinguish activity from results and, perhaps most difficult of all, the willingness to confront evidence when it is uncomfortable.

Boss provided the leadership space for that work to take root.

For someone like me, working alongside him was an education that no classroom could have provided. Through his mentorship, I gained a deeper appreciation of the inner workings of governance and public service at the highest levels: how decisions are shaped before they become announcements; how competing institutional interests are reconciled; how seemingly straightforward policy choices become complicated when confronted by political, administrative and fiscal realities; and how consequential decisions often rest upon hours of work that the public will never see.

Some mentors teach by instruction. Others teach by example.

Boss Mustapha did both.

I learnt from his discipline. I learnt from his attention to detail. I learnt from watching him manage difficult personalities and competing interests. I learnt that proximity to power should increase one’s sense of responsibility rather than one’s sense of importance. And I learnt that, at the highest levels of government, competence without character can only take a person so far.

Perhaps this is why it is impossible to understand Boss Mustapha fully without understanding his faith.

His Christianity is not an accessory to his public identity. It is central to the man himself. He is not merely a Christian by profession; he is a preacher and a man who has consistently committed his time, influence and resources to the service of God.

There is something instructive about a man who has occupied one of the most powerful offices in the country still finding fulfilment in building for God and for generations he may never meet.

His support for the Lutheran University of Nigeria in Demsa, Adamawa State, is an example. Through the mobilisation of resources, a major complex comprising a Senate building, administrative block and library was developed and donated to the university. Appropriately named the Wesley Mustapha Complex, the facility is more than brick and mortar. It represents an investment in knowledge, faith, human development and posterity.

That, too, tells a story about Boss.

Public office eventually ends. Convoys disappear. Titles change. Doors that once opened automatically begin to require appointments. What remains is the question every person who has been entrusted with responsibility must eventually answer: What did you do with the opportunity you were given?

Boss Mustapha has much with which to answer that question.

His years as SGF coincided with some of the most difficult moments in Nigeria’s recent history. He worked at the heart of government through economic challenges, complex political transitions and, most notably, the COVID-19 pandemic, during which he was called upon to lead the Presidential Task Force coordinating Nigeria’s response. These were assignments in which decisions had real consequences for millions of people.

Through it all, the characteristics I witnessed remained remarkably consistent: discipline, stamina, dependability and an abiding sense of duty.

But on this occasion of his 70th birthday, I find myself thinking less about the titles he has held and more about the lessons of the man.

Seventy years is a significant milestone. It provides an opportunity not merely to count years, but to examine what has been poured into those years.

In Boss Mustapha’s case, there has been service to country, to community, and to God. There has been a distinguished professional career, political engagement, stewardship at the highest level of government, investment in institutions and, perhaps less visible to the public, the mentoring of people who had the privilege of coming within his orbit.

I count myself fortunate to be one of them.

There are things I understand about government today because Boss allowed me to see government beyond textbooks and organograms. There are lessons about leadership I carry because I watched him work when there were no cameras present and no applause to be earned. And there are standards of professional commitment that remain etched in my mind because I witnessed a man, already occupying one of the highest offices in the land, still willing to sit over a document into the early hours because it mattered that the president received the best possible advice the next morning.

That late-night telephone call many years ago therefore remains with me.

Not because returning to the office at that hour was particularly remarkable. Many people in public service have similar stories. It stays with me because of what it revealed: that for Boss Mustapha, responsibility did not observe office hours.

When something needed to be done, it had to be done.

Today, the files are different. The office has changed hands. The relentless rhythm of his years as SGF has given way to another phase of life. But the values that sustained him through those years remain.

At 70, Boss Mustapha can look back upon a life of consequence. But knowing him, I suspect he will be more interested in what remains to be done than in what has already been accomplished.

And perhaps that is fitting.

For a man whose life has been defined by service, seventy should not simply be a celebration of arrival. It should be thanksgiving for the journey and a commissioning for the road ahead.

My prayer for my mentor, leader and friend is that the God whom he has served so faithfully will grant him many more years in good health and strength; that the wisdom accumulated over seven decades will continue to benefit our country and coming generations; and that the seeds he has planted — in public institutions, in the Church, in education and in people — will continue to bear fruit long after the stories of our present politics have faded.

Happy 70th birthday, Boss.

Thank you for the privilege of learning at close quarters.

Thank you for showing that professionalism and politics need not be enemies, that public power can coexist with humility, that faith can find expression in service, and that leadership, at its best, is ultimately about the responsibility one accepts for others.

At seventy, the offices Boss Mustapha has occupied are part of his biography. The lives and institutions he has helped to shape are his legacy.

Umaru J Abu can be reached through [email protected]

World.title: What kind of ancestor will you become?, By Martin Kalungu-Banda
World.content:
Ajadi ends where he began, facing forward. “Afrilition”, he writes, is the light towards a twenty first century African civilisation, a platform for intergenerational awakening. That the African world is ready to express itself fully and to define tomorrow in its own likeness. That the wealth that posterity builds will be measured by the capacity and the practices it leaves for the people who come after. His closing note is both hopeful and demanding, and he knows it. Struggle will come, but dignity, imagination and solidarity are renewable resources, and they renew exactly to the extent that we allow them to.

I. A book that begins with a question, not an argument

Most manifestos begin by telling you what is wrong. Afrilition begins by asking its author something uncomfortable: what kind of ancestor will I become?

That question is the hinge on which the whole book turns, and it is worth sitting with before reading a single page further. It quietly reverses the direction in which most of us think about Africa. We are used to looking backwards, to empire, to the trans-Atlantic trade, to colonial borders and colonial schooling, and measuring ourselves against that wound. Ajadi turns the reader around to face the other way. The people who will judge us are not behind us. They are ahead of us, and they are not yet born.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This is why the book takes the form it does. Ajadi writes as a grandfather addressing his grandchildren, though he is plainly writing to anyone still searching. He calls them the eyes of tomorrow, and hopes they will not be too infected by a reality that has been framed for them as the normal way of seeing. The letter form is not decoration. A letter to a child cannot hide behind jargon, cannot posture for peer review, and cannot afford cynicism, because you do not hand cynicism to a child as an inheritance. The genre disciplines the content. It forces the book to be both tender and useful.

II. The Word Itself

The title is a coinage, and the coinage is an argument. Afrilition fuses Africa with ebullition, the bubbling, the effervescence, the state of a thing coming to the boil. Not Africa restored. Not Africa developed. Africa emerging, under its own heat, into a form it has not yet occupied.

Ajadi extends the same care to the name of the continent. He makes a deliberate choice to trace Africa to an Egyptian root meaning ‘motherland’ or ‘birthplace,’ and says plainly that this is his preferred source. The honesty of that framing is characteristic of the book. He is not claiming settled etymology, he is claiming the right to choose which story he stands in. Naming, in Afrilition, is an act of self-authorship rather than an act of record keeping.

That posture is announced early and held throughout. He states that there is nothing inherently wrong with being described as black, even where the description bears little relation to actual skin tone. The problem he identifies is a different one, that pigmentation, rather than culture or choice, has been allowed to define a people. We received a caste classification from oppressors and colonisers, he writes, and then accepted it as identity. He engages Malcolm X and others who wrestled with the same inheritance, and he does so respectfully, but refuses to end where they ended.

His formulation of the alternative is the sentence I would put on the cover: we must move beyond reaction to intention.

III. Why the Strength of this Book is its Refusal to Be a Grievance

There is an easy version of this book that Ajadi did not write. It would catalogue the crimes, name the perpetrators, and generate heat. He says explicitly that Afrilition is not about heroes and villains, or good and bad, but about what must be done so that the African world can play its part in renewing humanity towards a sustainable future. That single decision is what makes the book generative, rather than merely correct.

He is unsparing about the damage. He describes what centuries of European dominance have cost: a continent defined by its worst, whether imagined or actual; a Europe left with the false impression of being best at everything; and a world brainwashed into treating European choices as the standard for all civilisation. He names the genocidal colonial experience and the overbearing trauma of enslavement, without softening either.

And then he declines to make them the destination. Afrilition, as he defines it, is a determination to heal, to leave the wounds behind, and to move with purpose towards confidence and emergence. He points to the two decades of this century as evidence that something is shifting, citing the recalibration of French influence across Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Guinea as markers of a continent moving into greater independence and self-actualisation.

What keeps this from collapsing into triumphalism is his insistence that the goal is not to win. He argues that the world does not need another battle of hierarchy or a struggle for the dominance of any one geography or people. It needs many alternative solutions to common problems. Africa, in his reading, is well placed to emerge in its distinction, offering a defined contribution to the human condition, rather than competing for someone else’s space. Human evolution, he writes, needs variety, vitality and volition.

The most beautiful line in the book carries this whole ethic: there is enough space in the sky for all the birds to fly.

Ajadi’s name for African youth is a demanding one, warriors of posterity’s illumination. Read alongside his description of the warrior of light, seeking depth, standing aloof from false dawns, revealing the light in others so that your own does not distract from their direction, in service to those who follow, it becomes clear that he is not offering the young a compliment. He is offering them a job description.

IV. The Numbers, and What He Does With Them

Afrilition is not sentimental about its optimism. Ajadi grounds the case in demography and materials, and the figures do a great deal of work.

On people: Africa is projected to hold roughly a third of humanity, with the youngest population on the planet at a median age of about 19.7 years, and to supply no less than a quarter of the global workforce by 2050. By 2030 young Africans are expected to make up 42 per cent of the world’s youth. By 2035, more young Africans will enter the workforce each year than in the rest of the world combined. That last statistic is not a forecast about Africa. It is a forecast about the global workplace, and Ajadi says so. The way work is inspired, sustained and delivered across every industry will be defined by this cohort.

On materials: the continent produces at least 90 per cent of the world’s platinum, leads by a distance on gold, and supplies over 70 per cent of cobalt, largely from Congo. In agriculture, 94 per cent of the world’s yams, 70 per cent of global cocoa from West Africa, and 63 per cent of global cassava, before counting the Caribbean and countries such as Brazil with large African populations of the diaspora.

Here is where the book earns its keep. Ajadi does not present these as reasons for pride. He presents them as a warning about position. A continent that supplies the world’s minerals and food, while importing the world’s definitions of value, has arranged itself as an input. His chapter on the shift from raw material producer to value adding society is the practical spine of the manifesto, and it connects directly to his fear about the youth, that the demographic dividend will be squandered if young Africans measure themselves by borrowed milestones and seek validation from those who assume their inferiority.

V. Women, and the Honesty of the Ledger

The section on women is among the book’s strongest, partly because it resists the two usual failures – pity and flattery – and simply reports.

African women, despite everything stacked against them, lead the world in business startups and entrepreneurship at roughly 26 per cent, against about 5.7 per cent for their European counterparts. They make up 58 per cent of the self-employed population. Ajadi’s point is not that they are coping admirably. It is that they are already outperforming, and that the continent’s returns on girl child education and on advancing women’s equality are enormous, with as much as 10 per cent added to annual GDP on the table.

He celebrates Namibia’s example of a woman president, Netumbo Nandi Ndaitwah, alongside Vice President Lucia Witbooi and a cabinet that is half women, and he asks that this be built upon rather than admired. He also makes a historical argument that deserves wider circulation, that the agency of women was considerably stronger in many precolonial African settings than it is now. This reframes gender equity as recovery rather than importation, and as enlightened self interest rather than charity.

VI. Warriors of Posterity’s Illumination

Ajadi’s name for African youth is a demanding one, warriors of posterity’s illumination. Read alongside his description of the warrior of light, seeking depth, standing aloof from false dawns, revealing the light in others so that your own does not distract from their direction, in service to those who follow, it becomes clear that he is not offering the young a compliment. He is offering them a job description.

And he attaches to it the sharpest warning in the book. Without a genuine transformation of values, he writes, what emerges from a youth bulge may resemble a swarm of locusts, devouring everything in its path because everything in its path looks like a threat to survival. Numbers alone do not produce a future. Numbers without values produce appetite.

He is equally clear that the cohort currently prepared for a multipolar, digital order in which African choices count as much as anyone’s is small. So the call is to design, to build systems of engagement and inspiration that are fit for purpose before the demographic shift arrives, not after. His instruction to the young is characteristically blunt. Engage these values, adapt them, translate them into living African wisdom. Do not brand secondhand thinking as new.

His evidence that this is possible is drawn from listening. He cites a survey of young people conducted across seven West African countries through King’s College London’s conflict and security research group in 2006, and notes what struck him. Young people expressing themselves with unapologetic clarity, questioning their elites boldly, challenging the norms of their societies in the open. They were, in other words, already doing it.

VII. Validation, Education, and the Economics of Abundance

Three linked chapters form the diagnostic core, and they are the passages most likely to make an African reader wince.

On validation. Ajadi names the hunger for external approval as one of the most insidious barriers to African excellence, born of colonialism, fed by the indoctrination of enslavement, and matured into a craving for the blessing of neocolonial structural power. He is willing to follow the thought to its most uncomfortable end, that Africans are among the most effective individual champions of white supremacy, not only in its political form but in the daily forms of self-neglect, toxicity towards one another, and enmity between kin. His answer is not to react to racism, which would keep the racist as the reference point, but to locate validation internally.

Read this book if you are tired of two exhausted genres: the literature of African grievance, which is accurate and immobilising, and the literature of Africa rising, which is cheerful and hollow. Afrilition belongs to neither. It takes the wound seriously enough to name it and then refuses to build a house there… Read it slowly, because it is written as a letter and letters reward slowness. Read it with young people, because they are its intended addressees and its subject.

On education. He draws the line most of us avoid drawing, that an education system which preserves colonial development and colonial thinking is not neutral; it is a functional system of white supremacy. He separates education from indoctrination and asks the reader to work out honestly which one they received. He also names the assumption smuggled inside the word ‘development,’ that to modernise you must Westernise, and that proximity to Western culture and process is the measure of how civilised you have become.

On economics. Ajadi rejects the-winner-takes-all as the natural order and calls his own generation’s veneration of it a nightmare mistaken for maturity. His critique is precise rather than merely disapproving. The system confuses money and similar symbols, which are artificially or naturally scarce, with value itself, and it constructs hierarchy out of manufactured scarcity, so that your worth requires everyone else’s diminishment. In one of the book’s most quotable images, he observes that we are only tall while standing on the kneeling of others.

The alternative he sketches is plural rather than utopian. Wealth already has many forms in African societies: money, property, title, power, celebrity, popularity, trade, artisanal skill, and specialised or broad knowledge. A society that can count in all of these currencies has more ways to make people whole than a society that can count in only one. An economy resting on the prosperity of a few and the exploitation of the many, he argues, is doomed in the home of humanity.

VIII. What He Asks You to Do

The final chapter converts the manifesto into practice, and the three drivers he names are worth learning by heart.

First, leverage diversity and connect our common humanity, designing deliberately for our best natures, while managing the worst that will inevitably surface.

Second, establish processes that sustain commitment and discipline, evolving practices that deliver the kind of continuous progress that carries across generations.

Third, build structures that adapt, because context in the African world will keep changing and rigidity is a slow form of failure.

Notice what these are not. They are not policies to be lobbied for, and they are not demands addressed to anyone else. They are capacities to be built by the reader, in the reader’s institution, family, firm, school, congregation and community. This is why Afrilition deserves study rather than agreement, and practice rather than study.

Ajadi ends where he began, facing forward. Afrilition, he writes, is the light towards a twenty first century African civilisation, a platform for intergenerational awakening. That the African world is ready to express itself fully and to define tomorrow in its own likeness. That the wealth that posterity builds will be measured by the capacity and the practices it leaves for the people who come after. His closing note is both hopeful and demanding, and he knows it. Struggle will come, but dignity, imagination and solidarity are renewable resources, and they renew exactly to the extent that we allow them to.

IX. The Invitation

Read this book if you are tired of two exhausted genres: the literature of African grievance, which is accurate and immobilising, and the literature of Africa rising, which is cheerful and hollow. Afrilition belongs to neither. It takes the wound seriously enough to name it and then refuses to build a house there.

Read it slowly, because it is written as a letter and letters reward slowness. Read it with young people, because they are its intended addressees and its subject. Read it with a pen, because roughly every third page contains a sentence you will want to argue with, and Ajadi has clearly written a book that expects to be argued with, rather than admired.

Then do the harder thing, which is to answer his question in your own name. Not what Africa should become. What kind of ancestor you will become.

Eight Questions for Adewale Ajadi

Framed to open the author’s thinking rather than to test it, and sequenced to move an audience from the personal, through the diagnostic, into the practical.

You open with a question rather than a thesis: what kind of ancestor will I become? Take us to the moment that question first arrived. What were you doing, and what had to be true in your life for that question to become unavoidable?

This opens the book at its emotional source and lets the audience meet the man before the manifesto.

You built a word to carry this book, Afrilition, Africa brought to the boil. Why did the existing vocabulary fail you? What can this word say that renaissance, development and rising cannot?

This invites him to explain his own coinage, and to show the audience how much political work ordinary words are quietly doing.

You say the shift we need is from reaction to intention. In practice, how does an African leader, teacher or parent tell the difference in real time? What does a reactive decision look like on a Tuesday morning, and what would the intentional version of that same decision have been?

This forces the book’s central abstraction into a form listeners can apply the same day.

You write that Africans are among the greatest individual champions of white supremacy, including in how we treat one another. That is a heavy sentence. Who did you have in mind when you wrote it, and what does it cost a person to stop?

This gives him room to defend the book’s most confronting claim in his own words, and to speak about repair rather than blame.

Your generation, you say, venerated a capitalist nightmare as the natural order. What did that veneration cost you personally, and what would you undo if you could?

This turns the economic critique into testimony. Audiences trust a critic who first indicts himself.

You warn that a youth bulge without a values transformation could behave like a swarm of locusts. That warning is aimed at the same young people you call warriors of posterity’s illumination. What do you actually need adults to build in the next ten years so that the second outcome wins?

This puts the responsibility back on the older listeners in the room, which is where the book puts it.

Africa supplies most of the world’s platinum, cobalt, yams and cocoa, and still imports the world’s definition of value. If a young African entrepreneur told you tomorrow that she wants to add value at home, instead of exporting raw, what would you tell her to expect, and what would you tell her to refuse?

This converts the value adding chapter into concrete counsel, with an explicit ask for what to say no to.

You address this book to your grandchildren. Suppose they read it in 2075. What is the one practice, not the one idea, that you would most want them to find still alive in their families and communities, and how would they know we had failed?

This closes by asking him to define success and failure himself, and leaves the audience holding a practice rather than a summary.

Martin Kalungu-Banda, a senior faculty at Presencing Institute, MIT, USA, co-faculty at Ubuntu.Lab Institute, and visiting fellow at Said Business School, writes from Oxford England.

World.title: Sunbeth Global Concepts redeems ₦25.1bn CP, demonstrating strong liquidity, investor confidence
World.content:
Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited, a leading agro-commodities sourcing and trading company, has announced the successful and timely redemption of its ₦25.1 billion Series 1 Commercial Paper (CP) issued under its ₦200 billion Commercial Paper Programme.

The redemption, completed on the notes’ maturity date of 4 September 2026, underscores the Company’s financial discipline, liquidity position and commitment to meeting its obligations to investors.

Sunbeth, one of Nigeria’s leading cocoa exporters and a significant contributor to the country’s non-oil export sector, secured regulatory approval in March 2026 to establish a ₦200 billion Commercial Paper Programme to support the continued growth of its agricultural export operations. Under the programme, the Company completed its Series 1, Series 2 and Series 3 issuances in March 2026, attracting total subscriptions of ₦165.73 billion against an initial target of ₦100 billion. Of this amount, Sunbeth accepted ₦150.4 billion across the three series, reflecting strong investor demand for the issuance Commenting on the redemption, Olasunkanmi Owoyemi, Chief Executive Officer, Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited, said:

“Meeting our Series 1 obligation in full and on schedule reflects the strength of our business fundamentals, prudent financial management and the confidence investors have placed in Sunbeth.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Credibility is earned through consistent performance, transparency and honouring our commitments. As we continue to scale our participation across the agricultural value chain, maintaining that discipline remains central to how we grow.”

Adeyemi Aduwo, Chief Financial Officer of Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited, added:

“The successful redemption of the Series 1 notes reflects the disciplined approach we take to capital and liquidity management. Our focus remains on deploying capital efficiently, maintaining strong financial controls and ensuring that our growth is supported by a funding structure that enables us to meet our obligations as they fall due.”

In under ten years of operations, Sunbeth has grown into a significant player in Nigeria’s agricultural export ecosystem. The Company has exported more than 200,000 metric tonnes of cocoa beans and 60,000 metric tonnes of cashew nuts to international markets, positioning it among the country’s leading commodity exporters.

The Company works directly with more than 30,000 farmers and collaborates with over 250 local buying agents nationwide. Its global strategic partners include multinational commodity and financial institutions such as Cargill, GCB Group, JB Cocoa, Touton, Macquarie and StoneX.

PublicSunbeth currently holds investment-grade ratings across both short- and long-term categories from DataPro, GCR, Agusto & Co. and Intelligence Africa. The Company is rated A2 on the short-term scale by all four agencies, with long-term ratings of A by DataPro, BBB+ by GCR, BBB by Agusto & Co. and BBB+ by Intelligence Africa, the latter with a stable outlook.

Its Commercial Paper Programme is also subject to FMDQ Securities Exchange’s disclosure and reporting requirements, providing noteholders and the broader market with ongoing visibility into the Company’s financial position and performance.

The Company continues to deepen its procurement capacity, strengthen international partnerships and expand its participation across higher-value segments of the agricultural value chain in Nigeria and across sub-Saharan Africa, where it continues to build a growing operational footprint.

About Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited

Sunbeth Global Concepts is a global agro-commodities sourcing and trading company committed to empowering farmers and driving socio-economic impact through strategic partnerships, innovation and industry expertise.

Since its establishment in 2017, the Company has built strong roots in the cocoa industry and continues to expand its presence across the broader agricultural value chain, delivering sustainable growth and trusted solutions to partners worldwide.

World.title: How my wife developed frequent headaches after switching to fresh orange juice — Yemi Osinbajo
World.content:
Former Vice-President Yemi Osinbajo has recounted how his wife, Dolapo, began experiencing frequent headaches while maintaining a daily habit of drinking freshly squeezed orange juice.

Mr Osinbajo shared the experience while speaking about food preservation and the use of chemicals by some farmers and traders to preserve or artificially ripen fruits and vegetables.

He spoke at the Open Day for Gardeners’ Seminar in Lagos on 28 August. The seminar, themed “Leaving the Earth Better Than We Found It”, formed part of the fifth edition of the Open Day for Gardeners, held at the Ecobank Pan African Centre in Victoria Island, Lagos.

A video of his remarks was subsequently uploaded to his YouTube channel on Wednesday.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to Mr Osinbajo, his wife had stopped drinking Coke, Fanta and other carbonated drinks many years earlier and had developed a habit of drinking a glass of freshly squeezed orange juice daily.

“Dolly, my dear wife, likes to have a full glass of freshly squeezed orange juice every day. A very healthy habit, by the way. And, you know, especially because she stopped drinking Coke, Fanta, or any of those carbonated drinks. She just stopped completely many years ago. And she would look at my own Coke-drinking habits, you know, with a lot of disapproval.

“I mean, look, you should be doing something healthy. But then, after a while, she started having some strange headaches, drinking her fresh juice every day. Very strange headaches,” he said.

The former vice-president said they initially did not suspect the orange juice because they considered it a healthy drink.

“Then she checked everything she was eating or drinking. We were wondering what could be the cause of this. Of course, it couldn’t possibly be the healthy orange juice.

“It must have been something else. But after nothing showed up, she sent one of her freshly squeezed orange juice batches to a lab for testing.

“The results came back. It showed that the orange juice, freshly squeezed, was not fit for human consumption. This is freshly squeezed orange juice. Not fit for human consumption,” he said.

Mr Osinbajo did not disclose what the laboratory found in the orange juice.

Studies

Mr Osinbajo also raised concerns about substances some farmers and produce sellers use to treat fruits and vegetables.

He said some farmers use dangerous pesticides on fruits and vegetables, while some sellers use chemicals to ripen or preserve produce.

“Apparently, farmers use dangerous pesticides for fruit and vegetables, you know, and sellers, fruit sellers, vegetable sellers, use very dangerous chemicals, sometimes to ripen or preserve fruits and vegetables,” he said.

Mr Osinbajo specifically cited calcium carbide, which he said was frequently used to force fruits to change colour and appear ripe quickly.

“Calcium carbide is used very frequently to force fruits, such as bananas, mangoes, pawpaws and tomatoes, to change colour very quickly, to look ripe very quickly,” he said.

The former vice-president also cited studies which he said examined the use of chemicals by fruit and vegetable sellers in different parts of Nigeria.

“There was a study in 2024 in Ado-Ekiti. They found that half of the 20 fruit sellers interviewed, small study, admitted using calcium carbide,” he said.

“Another study in Uyo found that 25 per cent of fruit sellers used calcium carbide. These were the ones, of course, who said, who agreed that, yes, we do, 25 per cent.”

Mr Osinbajo also cited a 2023 Lagos survey involving 50 fruit and vegetable retailers.

“In Lagos here, there was a survey done in 2023. Fifty fruit and vegetable retailers in Lagos were surveyed.

“They just picked 50 of, you know, those who were selling fruit and vegetables. Twenty-two of them admitted to using chemicals to preserve the produce,” he said.

He went on to list substances he said were being used to preserve or ripen produce, including calcium carbide, Sniper, DDT and brodifacoum.

Mr Osinbajo warned consumers against assuming that produce was safe simply because it appeared fresh.

“The fact that fruit looks fresh doesn’t mean that it is safe, and the fact that a drink is natural doesn’t mean that something dangerous has not been added to it along the way, especially along the journey from the farm to the table,” he said.

Calls for regulation

The former vice-president called for stronger regulation and enforcement, as well as greater public awareness about food safety.

He said farmers and traders should be educated about safer alternatives, while consumers should pay greater attention to the produce they buy.

“Consumers must learn to ask questions, wash produce properly, and report suspicious practices,” he said.

“One of the things I think we have to bear in mind all the time is that it is you and I, people like you and I, who take on these causes and campaign in our local communities and ensure that things change.”

Mr Osinbajo said government regulation needed to be enforced but argued that individuals also had a role to play in addressing unsafe practices.

“Government regulation needs to be enforced, but in a country this size, we have to be active ourselves.

“Individuals have to be active in our own communities to ensure that these things are reported, suspicious things like this are reported, and that change is made,” he said.

World.title: APM tackles defence minister over claim on insecurity, says terrorism not defeated
World.content:
The Allied Peoples Movement (APM) has criticised the Minister of Defence, Christopher Musa, over his claim that Nigeria has defeated terrorists and that insecurity has improved under President Bola Tinubu.

The party said the minister’s assertion was a distortion of the security situation in the country, arguing that Nigerians continue to face killings, abductions, displacement and other forms of violence.

Mr Musa, while speaking earlier on Channels Television’s Politics Today, said terrorist attacks were no longer as rampant or brazen as they had been in the past, adding that kidnapping had become more prevalent.

Asked whether Nigeria had defeated terrorists or merely displaced them, the minister said, “Frankly speaking, we have defeated terrorists because now, like I said, the attacks are not as rampant and it is now.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Musa also described kidnapping as a “social ill,” noting that there were cases of wives kidnapping their husbands and husbands kidnapping their children.

He maintained that security had improved under Mr Tinubu and that reports of terrorist attacks were no longer as frequent as they were previously.

However, in a statement on Saturday signed by its National Publicity Secretary, Abubakar Yusuf, the APM condemned the minister’s position, describing it as an attempt by the administration to downplay the country’s worsening insecurity.

The party cited the 2026 Global Terrorism Index (GTI), claiming that Nigeria had risen from sixth place in the 2025 index to fourth place among the world’s most terrorism-affected countries.

The APM said it was “deeply disappointing” that a minister of the federal republic would make such claims while Nigerians continued to suffer killings, kidnappings and displacement.

The party alleged that the situation had exposed what it described as the Tinubu administration’s “insensitivity” to the plight of Nigerians facing killings, rape, abductions for ransom and captivity by armed groups.

It further claimed that more than 600,000 Nigerians had been killed and at least 2.2 million others abducted during the three years of Mr Tinubu’s presidency.

The APM also referred to the reported abduction of hundreds of people in Niger State, saying about 600 Nigerians, mostly women, children and elderly people, were abducted from Dekera, Gidan-Zana and Sabon Gida communities and remained in captivity.

The party cited data from SBM Intelligence, which it said showed that kidnapping for ransom had become a highly monetised industry, with more than ₦7.78 billion paid as ransom between July 2025 and June 2026.

The APM accused the administration of being either “dangerously disconnected from reality” or deliberately attempting to manipulate public perception by denying the scale of insecurity in the country.

It particularly faulted the minister’s description of some kidnapping cases as a “family affair,” saying abduction remained a serious security threat to Nigerians.

“If the security situation has truly improved as the administration claims, the APM challenges the President, the Minister of Defence, and other senior officials of the Tinubu Presidency to travel by road without armed security details as other Nigerians must do,” the statement said.

The party further accused Mr Tinubu of lacking the capacity to develop and implement a blueprint capable of tackling insecurity, saying Nigeria could not survive another four years under what it described as a “hopeless and incompetent administration.”

The APM, however, urged Nigerians not to despair and called on them to support its presidential candidate, Seyi Makinde, in the 2027 election.

It said Mr Makinde had a blueprint to address insecurity and other challenges confronting the country.

Mr Tinubu is seeking re-election in 2027, while the APM said its candidate would offer an alternative to the incumbent administration.

World.title: D’Tigress suffer second straight World Cup defeat against Hungary
World.content:
Nigeria’s D’Tigress suffered their second consecutive defeat at the 2026 FIBA Women’s World Cup after losing 67-71 to Hungary in Berlin on Saturday.

D’Tigress, who were seeking their first victory of the tournament following their 81-99 defeat to South Korea, struggled to recover from a slow start as Hungary established an early advantage.

Hungary led 21-13 at the end of the opening quarter and maintained control in the second period to take a 36-26 lead into half-time.

Nigeria remained 10 points behind at the end of the third quarter, with Hungary holding a 52-42 advantage heading into the final period.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

D’Tigress, however, produced a determined response in the fourth quarter, outscoring Hungary 25-19.

The late rally brought Nigeria back into contention, but it was not enough to overturn the deficit as Hungary held on for a four-point victory.

Amy Okonkwo led Nigeria’s scoring with 17 points, six rebounds and two assists in 29:46 minutes, while Ezinne Kalu contributed 11 points, three rebounds and a game-high nine assists in 35:51 minutes.

Efe Balogun added 13 points, four rebounds and three assists, while Victoria Macaulay provided 11 points in just 17:04 minutes off the bench.

Murjanatu Musa scored 10 points, grabbed four rebounds and provided one assist in 29:29 minutes.

The defeat leaves D’Tigress still searching for their first win of the tournament after two games.

Nigeria’s second loss comes after they were beaten 81-99 by South Korea in their opening game despite a strong showing from Okonkwo, who scored 22 points, grabbed seven rebounds and provided three assists.

Against South Korea, Nigeria stayed competitive for long periods but eventually struggled to contain their opponents’ offensive firepower.

The loss to Hungary was a much closer contest, with D’Tigress showing greater resistance after falling behind early.

Nigeria will now have to regroup for their remaining World Cup assignment, having been unable to convert their fourth-quarter comeback into victory against Hungary.

World.title: PT Health Watch: Common cancer risk factors that should not be ignored
World.content:
Cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide, but health experts say many cancer cases are linked to preventable risk factors.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) estimates that cancer caused nearly 10 million deaths globally in 2024, accounting for almost one in six deaths worldwide. It says about 38 per cent of cancers can currently be prevented by avoiding known risk factors and implementing evidence-based prevention strategies.

Cancer continues to affect thousands of families in Nigeria every year. According to WHO, an estimated 130,000 new cancer cases were diagnosed in 2022, with 80,000 deaths.

While cancer can result from several factors, including genetic changes, age and environmental exposures, some established risks are linked to infections, substances and behaviours that can be prevented.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In a recent health awareness video, Nigerian physician and health communicator, Chinonso Egemba, popularly known as Aproko Doctor, highlighted some of these risks, including hepatitis B, aflatoxin, tobacco, alcohol and human papillomavirus (HPV).

Hepatitis B

According to Aproko Doctor, hepatitis B is particularly dangerous because it can remain in the body without obvious symptoms while damaging the liver.

“When it goes untreated and untested, it’s a virus that starts attacking your liver. Many Nigerians currently are living with it right now, and many of them don’t know because it can sit quietly inside your body for years without a single symptom,” he said.

His warning is supported by WHO, which says chronic hepatitis B infection can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer.

WHO estimates that 240 million people were living with chronic hepatitis B globally in 2024, with the infection contributing to about 1.1 million deaths, mainly from cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common type of primary liver cancer.

Hepatitis B is preventable through vaccination. WHO recommends hepatitis B vaccination as an important measure for preventing infection and its long-term complications.

Aflatoxin in food

Aproko Doctor warned that the cancer risk can begin with improperly stored food.

“Aflatoxin is basically a poison produced by fungus,” he explained, noting that it can contaminate foods such as grains and groundnuts when they are poorly stored.

According to WHO, Aflatoxins are a group of poisonous mycotoxins produced by certain moulds (Aspergillus species) that contaminate food crops and pose severe health risks like liver cancer. They are toxins produced by certain moulds and can contaminate crops including maize, sorghum, rice and groundnuts. Exposure to aflatoxins can cause liver cancer.

WHO advises discarding food that appears mouldy, discoloured, or shrivelled because mycotoxins can penetrate beyond the visibly affected part.

Aflatoxin exposure can also be particularly dangerous in people infected with hepatitis B. The WHO/FAO Joint Expert Committee on Food Additives says hepatitis B infection is an important contributor to the ability of aflatoxins to cause liver cancer.

This means food storage and handling can also form part of cancer prevention, particularly in communities where grains and other foods are stored for long periods in warm or damp conditions.

Tobacco smoking

Tobacco remains one of the most established cancer risks.

“Smoking generally, as long as you light it with fire and put it on your body, increases the risk of cancer, especially tobacco smoke,” Aproko Doctor said.

He added that the danger was not limited to lung cancer because tobacco smoke contains cancer-causing chemicals that can damage cells throughout the body.

WHO says tobacco smoke contains more than 7,000 chemicals, at least 69 of which are known to cause cancer. Tobacco use is the world’s single greatest avoidable risk factor for cancer mortality.

Smoking can cause cancers of the lung, mouth and throat, oesophagus, bladder, kidney, liver, pancreas, stomach, colon and rectum, cervix and blood, among others.

Alcohol

Alcohol is another established cancer risk. WHO confirms that alcohol consumption increases the risk of several cancers, including cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, colorectum and breast.

WHO also says no level of alcohol consumption can be considered risk-free in relation to cancer.

“The more alcohol you drink, the higher the risk. However, how much and how fast the risk from drinking alcohol increases differs by cancer type,” it noted.

The global body explained that alcohol increases the likelihood of developing certain cancers, with the risk influenced by the amount consumed and other factors.

Human papillomavirus

According to Aproko Doctor, the virus is common, and some types can cause cancer, particularly cervical cancer.

“In women, this particular HPV is responsible for cervical cancer,” he noted.

According to the WHO, persistent infection with high-risk HPV types causes nearly 99 per cent of all cervical cancer cases. HPV is also associated with cancers of the vulva, vagina, anus, penis and mouth and throat.

Although HPV infection is very common, not everyone infected with the virus will develop cancer. WHO says about 90 per cent of HPV infections are controlled naturally by the body, while persistent infection with high-risk types can lead to cancer.

WHO recommends a complete three-step strategy to stop cervical cancer through vaccination, screening, and treatment.

READ ALSO: WHO restricts Ervebo use in Bundibugyo outbreak

Preventing Cancer

A 2026 global analysis by WHO and its International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) estimated that 37 per cent of all new cancer cases diagnosed globally in 2022, about 7.1 million cases, were linked to preventable causes.

Tobacco was the leading preventable cause, accounting for 15 per cent of all new cancer cases, followed by cancer-causing infections at 10 per cent and alcohol at three per cent.

WHO recommends avoiding tobacco, reducing or avoiding alcohol, maintaining a healthy weight, eating a healthy diet, engaging in regular physical activity and receiving recommended vaccinations against cancer-causing infections such as hepatitis B and HPV.

As Aproko Doctor noted, understanding the risks is an important first step.“Don’t let anybody deceive you. Say no to smoking in any form,” he said.
