The Democrat — who was quick to raise his childhood memories of watching Hockey Night in Canada and his love of lacrosse, Canada's other national sport — isn't ruling out all tariffs.

He cited duties on windmill parts or solar rigs as an example of tariffs he would keep if it would help build up his state's renewable energy industry.

"But it's because you're being very particular about exactly what kind of industries you're trying to protect. This is just across the board, ridiculousness, for no particular reason," El-Sayed said.

"So I can't quite explain it. Except for that everything Donald Trump does is ham-fisted, chaotic and self-serving."

His Republican rival has largely stayed away from talking about Trump's tariffs on the campaign.

Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers speaks during a campaign event on Aug. 20 in Detroit. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

Mike Rogers's camp didn't respond to CBC's request for an interview, but was recently asked by Fox News if he supports Trump's handing of the trade deal with Canada and backed the president's objectives.

"The Canadians have not been good partners on this," Rogers said in an interview on Fox & Friends on Monday. "I think they think that the Republicans are going to lose in the midterms, and then that the Democrats are going to open up the borders again and absolutely undercut the people who build cars and car parts right here in Michigan."

Voters mixed on if tariffs play into their vote

Residents in Genesee County were mixed on whether the tariffs will impact their votes.

Carl Olson, teammates with Holmes and Hunt, offered a quick "no."

"I think eventually everything will level out and everything will go back to normal," he said.

Carl Olson, who doesn't see tariffs affecting his vote in the midterms, gets ready to bowl in Flint. (Gian Paolo Mendoza/CBC)

"If anything, it made it stronger that I will never vote Republican," said Joan Castor, when stopped in the Flint downtown core.

Down the street, Matt Zastrow said work and housing are his main concerns. If he votes, it will be for the Republican candidate.

"I think Trump's doing a good enough job right now. I'm not sure where we would be if we had somebody else in there," he said.

Glenn Stevens Jr., executive director of MichAuto at the Detroit Regional Chamber, stands in front of a view of the Michigan side of the Gordie Howe International Bridge. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)

So far, industry in the region is largely staying out of politics. Businesses CBC contacted didn't want to speak on the record, citing the atmosphere.

Glenn Stevens Jr., executive director of MichAuto at the Detroit Regional Chamber, said businesses he speaks to want to see the cloud of uncertainty this trade war has brought cleared.

"Politics is not what this is about," Stevens Jr. said. "This is about making cars, in our perspective, moving lumber, moving energy, moving agriculture to the market and employing people.

"So the politics and the rhetoric are one thing, and that's at a crescendo right now, but the economics really are what speaks."

World.title: B.C. man who went missing in mountains for several days found alive
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Squamish man who was missing in the mountains for several days has been found alive.

Stanislav Volo went for a hike on Sunday above the Sea-to-Sky Gondola and did not return home.

Speaking to CBC News from Squamish General Hospital after he was found, Volo said his phone died when he got to the top of a hike, and he was "going in circles and circles trying to find a way down," having to stay near a creek to get fresh water.

"I was crying from happiness," he said of his reaction to seeing people again on Friday, calling it a miracle.

He said when he eventually saw people searching for him on a road, they were crying too — reflecting how much they had hoped to find him.

Security cameras capture Stanislav Volo exiting the Sea-to-Sky Gondola around 11:30 a.m. PT on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Squamish RCMP)

Volo said he got injured while on the hike, and had to wait a few cold nights for his foot to heal.

He said he learned a lot about survival in the wilderness, and was determined to not spend the rest of his time on the mountain.

Volo survived by eating twigs and wildflowers.

"When you still have some sort of stamina, some energy, and you can actually do something and that's why ... I decided to, like, keep going," he said.

Stanislav Volo is seen in this handout image from authorities. (Yana Geng, Squamish RCMP)

His sister Ola Volo confirmed her brother was found earlier Friday.

"We found him," she said. "He walked out on the road on his two feet."

She eventually went to see her brother in hospital, where she connected him with CBC News.

He celebrated by eating pizza, calling it "very tasty."

'Remarkable that he survived'

Squamish Search and Rescue also confirmed that Volo had been found alive.

"It's absolutely remarkable that he survived," said search manager Tyler Duncan.

Volo managed to walk out onto the Indian Arm Forest Service Road where search and rescue had been flying a drone to look for him.

"He walked out of the forest onto the road and [we] were able to meet him and get in contact with him and provide him with some very basic first aid," Duncan said.

Volo was tired, hungry, cold and wet but overall he was doing well and wasn't injured, Duncan said.

The road he was walking on is on the backside of Mount Habrich Loop and he would have gone through difficult and technical terrain to reach the road.

"I would absolutely love to sit down with Stas and have a good conversation about what he has been up to for the last six days," Duncan said. "It's got to be a remarkable story."

WATCH | Search teams looking for missing hiker in Sea-to-Sky region: Search teams looking for missing hiker in Sea-to-Sky region | Duration 2:08

Duncan said it was one of the most "involved" searches he had been a part of in his 15 years in search and rescue.

"He was out in that storm. It must have been an absolutely horrendous experience for him," Duncan said.

Went hiking above the Sea-to-Sky Gondola

Volo planned to hike the Mount Habrich Loop and surveillance footage showed him getting off at the top of the Sea-to-Sky Gondola in Squamish around 11:30 a.m. PT on Sunday.

Drones, helicopters and police dogs joined in the search along with many volunteers from multiple search-and-rescue agencies.

The search for the missing Squamish man focused around Mount Habrich Loop. (Squamish Search and Rescue)

On Tuesday, Volo made a call to 911 saying he was stuck on the mountain.

RCMP Sgt. Katrina Boehmer said Volo was transported to hospital and is being treated for what is believed to be minor injuries.

World.title: How public institutions — like schools and transit — are handling Quebec's new secularism law
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

From university halls to garages in Montreal's Metro network, public institutions across Quebec are quietly locking prayer rooms and rewriting employee guidelines as the province’s expanded secularism law takes full effect.

Law 9 significantly broadens the reach of Bill 21 and extends restrictions.

The religious symbols ban passed into law in 2019 now applies to daycare staff and prayer spaces are now forbidden in places like university campuses, or the facilities of a transit agency like Montreal's Société de transport de Montréal.

But as institutions rush to comply with the changes, administrators and legal experts warn that the government has left them navigating a complex legal grey zone with few clear guidelines on how to actually enforce the rules.

Law 9 took effect on Sept. 1.

Prayer rooms closed, chapels can stay

Concordia University — which had a large prayer room, according to the Muslim Student Association — says it no longer has any places set aside for prayer.

McGill University says it intends to comply with its legal obligations as well. Dawson College declined to comment.

“All the signs have been taken down,” said Ezekiel Montoya Desjardins, the vice-president of external affairs at the Dawson Student Union, who managed the prayer rooms there.

Signage and some furnishings, like carpeting, have been removed and the rooms are empty now. Montoya Desjardins said he understands the government’s position, but secularism doesn’t need to be defined as no religious activity.

“I think that it means there is neutrality in all religions at school,” he said, noting that the prayer rooms were mostly used by the Muslim community, but were open to everyone.

Law 9, adopted by the Quebec government in the spring, puts limits on praying in public. (Radio-Canada)

As for Vanier College, Benoit Morin, the school’s director general, said the small prayer room has been locked since the start of August. A notice on the door says Muslim students can head across the street to a mosque to pray.

While prayer rooms like that one close, religious practice in chapels, like the one at Université Laval, Concordia, McGill and Bishop’s University, is allowed.

Vanier catching up with the law

Morin said the school is still working on two important steps included in the law. The first is establishing a process whereby religious accommodations can be requested and determined by management, and initiating a complaints process as well.

Before, students would ask professors for religious accommodations. Now that request will go up to Morin's office, for him or someone he delegates to decide.

And when it comes to complaints about someone not operating in line with the multiple existing secularism laws, there needs to be a new, separate registry for Law 9 complaints that can be audited by the ministry, he said.

The school also created new training for security guards to teach them about Law 9 and give warnings to people if they see something that isn't in line with the law, he said.

LISTEN | Exploring some of the effects of Quebec's expanded secularism law: Let's Go 10:08 Secularism law expansion goes into effect for STM, daycare workers New rules are going into effect as of today as part of Law 9, the latest expansion of Quebec's secularism laws. We'll go over what changes concretely for places like schools, daycares, and even the STM. Let's Go researcher Sarah Jesmer breaks it down.

Morin said the new measures are affecting Vanier's ability to teach students the importance of living peacefully together.

“It was and still is fairly complex to determine the fine print as to how it should live within the walls of Vanier,” he said. “And we've been working hard throughout the summer to make sure that we can be compliant.”

The hope is schools like Vanier will be consulted more before such laws are adopted in the future as “it has a deep impact on communities that have been built over several years,” he said.

Daycare union keeping close eye on enforcement

The law also bars workers in subsidized daycares and private schools from wearing religious symbols. Those already in their positions are exempt.

A spokesperson for the federation representing health and social service workers is looking into the impact on its 13,000 daycare workers across 400 subsidized daycares.

In a statement, Lucie Longchamp, the spokesperson for the Fédération de la santé et des services sociaux-CSN, said it has asked its member daycares to identify Law 9's impacts and the federation “will closely monitor developments in the coming weeks.”

Lucie Longchamp is the spokesperson for the Fédération de la santé et des services sociaux-CSN. (Radio-Canada)

She said the federation expects to hear about a breakdown of services, departures and hiring difficulties. From there, the federation will have more to say on the matter.

The spokesperson also said the FSSS-CSN will continue to “advocate for an open, pluralistic model of secularism that does not further jeopardize the provision of non-profit educational services.”

STM closes prayer space, adjusts policies

Montreal's public transit agency is telling employees they can no longer pray on workplace property.

The Société de transport de Montréal (STM) says it has four rooms that employees can use for silent activities such as meditation and yoga but can no longer be used for prayer.

The agency says signs have been posted outside the rooms to remind people of the ban, and said supervisors who witness religious practices should address the matter with the employee.

The STM union representing maintenance workers declined to comment.

Inside the transit network, musicians can still sing about their beliefs and wear whatever they want, but they can't "manifest any religious practice" or lead a worship service with music in the Metro.

STM spokesperson Amélie Régis said the agency’s special constables, with new training, will be intervening if any Metro performers are praying or evangelizing.

The union representing professionals like engineers and architects said there are resource rooms used for prayer at STM garages. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

Groups like Jehovah's Witnesses will still be allowed to operate, even talking to people about their beliefs. Since they aren’t forcing their beliefs on people, but instead waiting to be engaged by passersby, the STM isn’t going to prohibit the practice.

“It is our understanding that discussing a belief is not a religious practice,” she said.

Régis said constables will intervene by "prioritizing an awareness-raising approach," so warnings will be given to those who don’t follow the rules.

Lawyer says there’s a ‘grey zone’

The penalties laid out in Law 9 are fines that, in general, range between $125 and $1,125.

The law outlines how the province is going to enforce the law, with inspectors who can go into an institution, take photos and report back.

However, the onus is still on employers to ensure compliance.

Constitutional lawyer Frédéric Bérard said Law 9 represents a significant expansion of both where government oversight applies and what measures are enforced.

"You can say that it goes, you know, way beyond Bill 21," Bérard said. "One should ask the following question: What was the objective behind that?"

He argued the government cannot point to concrete examples of public prayer in places in the Metro causing disruptions, calling the legislation political pandering rather than a response to real needs.

While Bill 21 targeted authority figures like teachers and police to prevent state influence, Bérard said extending restrictions to cafeteria workers, janitors and transit employees reveals a shift toward removing visible religious presence entirely.

"So what's the next step, actually?" he asked. "Are we going to ban Muslim women from wearing veils in public, on the street? Are we going to go that far?"

Bérard added that public institutions are left navigating a legal grey zone without clear rules on enforcement or handling non-compliant employees.

It offers no guidance on what to do if an employee refuses to comply.

"What do we do with people who keep wearing their religious symbols? Do we fire them? How do we do that?" Bérard said. "Those institutions are not quite clear about what they have to do in order to respect the new bill."

CBC News reached out to the office of the minister responsible for secularism and was told they would respond soon. The story will be updated.

World.title: Conrad Black: Mark Carney puts it all on the line
World.content:
Article content

If the prime minister is not successfully contradicted, as I wrote here last week, it will be a challenging time but a great opportunity to strengthen the Canadian nationality. If we really have been provoked into a commercial war, it will be time for Canada to shed the somewhat hackneyed image of the upright, red-coated Mountie portrayed by Nelson Eddy in the famous 1954 film Rosemarie, (where someone purporting to be Québec Premier Maurice Duplessis makes a cameo appearance), and resort to further unsportsmanlike measures. We should make cooperative arrangements with some of the Commonwealth Caribbean countries and actively entice winter migrants from Florida and other temperate U.S. states. More piquant and an undoubted public service to the United States would be to provide heavy funding for authentic American legal aid charities and clog American courts and reduce the obscene 98 per cent conviction rates in American criminal courts, 95 per cent of those without a trial. The United States today has four percent of the world’s population and about 25 per cent of its incarcerated people; many Americans would thank us for helping to relieve “the sweet land of liberty” of this shame and hypocrisy. These are areas where it would be hard for the United States to retaliate-both sides can keep raising tariffs if they want but it is unlikely to achieve very much, although we could eventually manufacture much more for ourselves and take over the U.S. part of our automobile industry.
