World.title: Public officials among those abusing Jetten online, AD finds
World.content:
A council official, a police employee and a member of the Dutch air force are among thousands of people posting homophobic abuse under prime minister Rob Jetten’s social media messages on X, an investigation by the Algemeen Dagblad (AD) has found.

The paper analysed 45,860 replies to 323 posts sent from the prime minister’s official account during his first six months in office. One in 20 – 2,293 replies – was homophobic, it said.

The abuse appeared under routine posts, from a congratulatory message for Queen Máxima to a post about Amsterdam Pride, and did not depend on the topics Jetten was writing about.

AD identified two recurring forms of abuse. The first was crude slurs and the second, far more common, was a single insinuating question posted in Dutch hundreds of times: “Did you tell them you’re gay?”

Hard to prosecute

Most of the accounts did not belong to anonymous trolls, AD said. The large majority left a single homophobic reply and never returned, and the 10 most persistent accounts together produced less than 6% of the total.

Only a handful of repeat posters could be traced, among them the council, police and air force employees. Marloes van Noorloos, a professor of criminal law at Leiden University, told the paper that the insinuating questions were hard to prosecute as hate speech or criminal insult, because it depends largely on wording and context.

Civil servants, she said, could face disciplinary action under the rules governing public employees.

Jetten’s response

Jetten is the Netherlands’ first openly gay prime minister, and has said he files a police report every week over the abuse he receives about his sexuality. At the WorldPride conference last month he said big social media companies were “barely moderating content for hate speech”.

X’s own rules prohibit attacking users over their sexual orientation, but the company has taken little action, according to AD.

Dutch acceptance of homosexuality has stalled after years of progress. Jetten has said the Netherlands needs to get back on track and return to the top 10 countries for LGBTQI+ rights, from where it fell to number 13 after 2018.

World.title: Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short
World.content:
Dutch farmers are still facing a compulsory cut in the number of animals they can keep as livestock, after the government’s environmental assessment agency found the cabinet’s nitrogen plan would fall just short of its own 2035 target.

The agency, PBL, assessed the €20 billion nitrogen plan at the cabinet’s request and called it an important step that could bring the farming emissions target within reach.

But it found the measures worked out so far leave a gap, and that an across-the-board cut of 5% to 10% in farmers’ livestock rights, the permits that cap how many animals a farm may hold, is still needed.

The coalition has always said that a blanket cut is a last resort, to be used only if the targets are missed in 2035. Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen called it an “emergency brake” on Friday and “a no-go for the cabinet.”

Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, against 2019 levels, under the package agreed in June. PBL expects the herd to shrink further regardless as farms adapt to those rules, with some businesses forced to close.

The agency was more positive about the plan’s benefits for the environment, but warned the nitrogen problem will not just disappear. On more than half the area of the most sensitive protected sites, deposition is still expected to breach the critical threshold in 2035.

Nature groups called the plans the minimum needed to start repairing decades of damage. The farmers’ party BBB and the farm lobby LTO said the extra cut was unacceptable, though LTO is staying at the table to negotiate the rest of the package.

World.title: Dutch soil scientist wins Ig Nobel for burying 1,000 underpants
World.content:
A Dutch scientist has won the Ig Nobel prize for conducting a study that involved burying around 1,000 pairs of underpants and digging them up two months later.

Marcel van der Heijden, a soil scientist at the University of Zurich, shared this year’s Ig Nobel for soil science with three colleagues. The annual prizes, a parody counterpart to the Nobels, reward research that “first makes people laugh and then makes them think.”

Volunteers buried identical cotton underpants across more than 25 countries, then dug them up after two months and recorded what was left. The more the fabric had rotted, the healthier and more biologically active the soil.

“Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” van der Heijden said in a statement, adding that healthy soil was crucial for fertility and for the wider ecosystem.

This year’s ceremony was held in Zurich, the first time it has taken place outside the US after more than three decades in the country.

Organisers said they could not in good conscience ask winners or visiting journalists to travel to the US this year, a decision widely assumed to be down to American immigration policy. Next year’s event will be in Antwerp.

Dutch researchers are Ig Nobel regulars. According to broadcaster NOS, they have won 22 times since the first ceremony in 1991, including last year’s award for showing that a drink can improve people’s foreign-language skills.

World.title: Dutch road traffic CO2 falls for first time since pandemic
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Emissions from road traffic in the Netherlands fell in 2025 for the first time since the Covid pandemic, according to figures from the national statistics agency CBS.

Vehicles produced 26.6 million tonnes of CO2 last year, 1.6% less than in 2024 and 2.2% below the level of a decade earlier.

Passenger cars account for almost 58% of the total. Their emissions fell 1.9% on the year even though the distance driven rose slightly. Fully electric cars produce no CO2 while being driven, and around 7.4% of cars on the road were fully electric in 2025.

The saving covers tailpipe emissions only, not the CO2 released to generate the electricity used to charge those cars.

Emissions from vans and lorries, which together make up 40% of the road total, also fell, mainly because commercial vehicles were driven fewer kilometres.

The longer-term picture is more mixed. While car emissions were 9.1% lower than in 2015, those from vans and lorries were higher, as the distance driven by commercial vehicles rose over the decade.

The Netherlands remains well short of its climate law target of a 55% cut in greenhouse gas emissions on 1990 levels by 2030.

World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb

Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains. World.title: Poland to begin using sewage water to cool power plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will begin using reclaimed sewage water to cool power plants from the start of next year. The measures are intended to reduce the use of fresh water and make the power system more resilient to increasingly frequent droughts. The change comes after some of Poland’s power plants were partially shut down this summer amid a series of heatwaves and lack of rain that led to record-low water levels in many rivers. 💧⚡ Otwieramy sektor energetyczny na wodę odzyskaną. Od 1 stycznia 2027 r. polskie elektrownie i elektrociepłownie będą mogły wykorzystywać wodę odzyskaną ze ścieków komunalnych w systemach chłodzenia. Nowe rozwiązania przedstawiliśmy dziś wspólnie z ministrem energii… pic.twitter.com/qRDOgjcDwb — Dariusz Klimczak (@DariuszKlimczak) September 3, 2026 “This may seem to many like a minor change, but it is of fundamental importance for many power-generating units in Poland,” said energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Thanks to this, we will be even more resilient and even better prepared for crises of all kinds.” The legislation was first proposed by a group of MPs from The Left (Lewica) and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), two members of the current ruling coalition, in May, and was then approved by parliament in July. Last week, President Karol Nawrocki signed it into law. The law, which will come into force at the start of 2027, introduces a definition of water recovered from municipal sewage, which, in turn, will allow its use in the cooling circuits of power stations and combined heat and power plants. Power stations require large amounts of water to help cool and condense steam, which drives the turbines, back into liquid form so that it can be reheated into steam once more. Orlen Termika, a subsidiary of state energy giant Orlen, has announced that it plans to invest more than 1 billion zloty (€230 million) over the next four years to maximise the benefits of the change by connecting sewage treatment plants with three of its power and heat plants around Warsaw. According to Andrzej Gajewski, the CEO of Orlen Termika, one of the plants, Żeran, will be able to save up to 80% of previous water use. Another, Siekierki, will save up to 20%. The company also plans to install heat pumps to extract heat from sewage, which can then be used to help supply heat to residents of Warsaw before the water is then used to cool down the plants. Sewage is relatively warm, typically between 10°C and 20°C, making it a good source of recoverable heat. “From the point of view of security of supply for Warsaw’s residents and from the point of view of efficiency – that is, the price of heating – this is the best and most advantageous solution,” emphasised Gajewski. Poland’s power grid operator has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid a heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced https://t.co/fIDR4SimgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Poland has experienced increasingly hot temperatures in recent years. This summer, the country broke its all-time record, as temperatures reached more than 40°C. That, along with low amounts of rainfall, has seen rivers reach record lows. As a result, Poland’s power grid operator has this summer been forced three times to invoke emergency measures to ensure supply. Previously, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. Last month, state power supplier Enea announced that it had reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants due to the low level of water in the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, just over 1% of Poland’s total, was taken offline. World.title: Prime minister’s “right-hand man” elected as Polish constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition. Critics argued that the nomination violated the government’s pledge to “depoliticise” the TK, including by banning recently active politicians from sitting on it. Berek served as a government minister from 2023, when Tusk came to power, until last month, when he stepped down in order to run for the TK. However, it is far from clear what will happen next. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has this year refused to swear in four TK judges chosen by parliament, and he has made clear that he also opposes Berek’s candidacy. ✅Sejm dokonał wyboru Macieja Berka na stanowisko sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. pic.twitter.com/ek0ak9C33v — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 4, 2026 In mid-August, Berek announced that he was leaving the government, where he had served as minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy. Shortly afterwards, Tusk confirmed that Berek would be nominated to fill an upcoming vacancy on the TK. The prime minister argued that, during his time in government, Berek had undertaken a technocratic role that was “apolitical and nonpartisan”. He said that Berek’s extensive experience in constitutional law and the legislative process made him an ideal candidate. However, some MPs from Tusk’s junior coalition partners publicly opposed the nomination. They noted that the government’s parliamentary majority had, in 2024, approved a law banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. The law never went into force as it was effectively blocked by a combination of then-President Andrzej Duda and the TK itself, which were both aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party from 2015 to 2023 and now the largest opposition group. Polish NGOs have urged Tusk's "right-hand man" to withdraw his Constitutional Tribunal candidacy, warning his political ties could undermine efforts to restore the court’s independence. The nomination has also exposed tensions within the ruling coalitionhttps://t.co/jQn0MyuS7G — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 Ahead of today’s vote in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, it remained unclear if Berek’s candidacy would be approved. In the end, he obtained the necessary majority, receiving the support of 226 MPs among the 437 who voted in the 460-seat chamber. Within the ruling coalition, only four MPs voted against Berek’s candidacy, including one from Tusk’s own centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Klaudia Jachira. Another opponent was Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of Tusk’s junior coalition partners, and the speaker of the Sejm. Eleven MPs from the ruling coalition did not take part in the vote. The entire right-wing and far-right opposition voted against Berek’s candidacy. Berek is now meant to join the TK after the next vacancy on its 15-person bench opens up on 18 September, when the nine-year term of an existing judge, Justyn Piskorski, ends. However, under Polish law, a new TK judge must first swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the ruling majority in the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. Nawrocki argued that there were legal doubts over the appointment of the quartet whose oaths he refused to receive. However, the government says that the president does not have the right to assess their candidacies and that the swearing-in is merely a formality. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The four judges instead organised their own swearing-in ceremony in the Sejm before a notary, after which they forwarded their oaths to the president and attempted to take their seats on the TK. However, the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, refused to allow them to serve, citing their failure to swear an oath before the president. Święczkowski previously served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government and is still seen as loyal to the party. In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim order requiring that the four judges be allowed to take up their positions. However, Święczkowski has ignored it, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 It appears likely that Nawrocki will refuse to swear in Berek. “I think the last thing the TK needs is another politician, especially a politician who is a close collaborator of Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” said Nawrocki on Thursday. On Friday morning, ahead of the Sejm vote, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, addressed the chamber to outline the president’s opposition to Berek’s candidacy. He said that, as well as Berek’s political association with the government, there are doubts over whether he even meets the formal requirements to sit on the tribunal, in particular the need to have practised the law for at least 10 years. Berek says he does meet that requirement. Adding to the confusion is the fact that Tusk’s government does not regard the current TK as legitimate because of the presence of judges, including Piskorski, who were unlawfully appointed when PiS and Duda were in office. It ignores all TK rulings. Tusk has emphasised that one of the reasons he wants to appoint Berek to the TK is to help “fix” the tribunal. Berek’s nomination means that there are now eight TK judges chosen by the ruling coalition, giving them a majority on the court. However, with Nawrocki and Święczkowski refusing to accept four of them, and likely to reject Berek too, some kind of drastic action would be required to allow them to begin to serve. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. President Karol Nawrocki has launched a programme allowing Polish companies looking to expand into international markets to apply to join his foreign visits. “Seats on the presidential plane will soon be available to Polish businesses,” Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, announced in a video published on X. “I want Polish companies, including small and medium-sized ones, to be able to establish new contacts, develop existing business relationships and successfully conquer foreign markets alongside the president.” Już niedługo miejsca w prezydenckim samolocie będą dostępne także dla polskiego biznesu. When deciding which businesses to invite on the trip, the presidential chancellery says it would seek “well-established companies with the potential to grow in the US market and seeking new partners and opportunities for collaboration” Those selected will be invited to travel on the presidential flight from Warsaw to New York and back, and will also receive local transportation. In recent years, a growing number of Polish companies have expanded abroad, helped by the country’s strong economic growth over the past three decades. Poland has summoned Russia’s ambassador in response to recent hostile actions against Germany. “[We] expressed our strong condemnation of state terrorism perpetrated by Russia – because what is a problem for one ally is a problem for the entire alliance,” said Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Putin’s Russia remains one of the most serious security threats – not just for Europe, but for the entire world order,” he added. “Its goal is to permanently destroy the European security architecture.” 💬 Nie ma zgody na podpalenia, ataki na kolej, morderstwa i inne prowokacje. Polska też wezwała ambasadora Rosji po to, aby wyrazić nasze stanowcze potępienie dla terroryzmu państwowego autorstwa Federacji Rosyjskiej. | wicepremier, minister spraw zagranicznych @sikorskiradek… pic.twitter.com/LChAjwsX8H — Ministerstwo Spraw Zagranicznych RP 🇵🇱 (@MSZ_RP) September 3, 2026 On Tuesday, the German government announced that it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. In response, it ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin. This week also saw attempts to sabotage Germany’s electricity network in two locations. While they are still being investigated, on Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested that they may also be part of “Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region”. On Thursday, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that Russia’s ambassador to Warsaw, Georgy Mikhno, had been summoned to the ministry. Wewiór said that Poland wanted to convey “our firm opposition to the escalation of Russia’s aggressive actions” as well as to show solidarity with Germany. A number of other European leaders have also this week expressed solidarity with Germany, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Poland has itself been a major target for Russia. Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland was the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage. It has also suffered cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, and “weaponised migration” on its eastern border. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates in the country, with Moscow responding by doing the same with Polish consulates operating on its territory. This week, after a fire broke out at a drone factory in Poland, Tusk said that there is “no doubt” it was caused deliberately and suggested it was also likely carried out on behalf of Russia. World.title: Poland moves to allow local communities to ban short-term rentals
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals – the type of privately owned accommodation offered through services such as Airbnb and Booking.com. Such services have boomed in Poland in recent years, like in other parts of the world. But that has prompted a backlash from many communities, which argue that short-term rentals can cause disruption, reduce the availability of housing, and drive up prices. However, the proposed measures have already caused divisions within the ruling coalition and must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. ❗ Rada Ministrów przyjęła autopoprawkę do projektu ustawy dotyczącego najmu krótkoterminowego. Nowe rozwiązania dadzą mieszkańcom i samorządom konkretne narzędzia do reagowania tam, gdzie najem krótkoterminowy powoduje problemy z bezpieczeństwem i porządkiem publicznym. ➡️… pic.twitter.com/7KvW2O4AKW — Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki (@SPORT_GOV_PL) September 2, 2026 Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that, following a “difficult process” of discussion, his coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, had agreed on the measures. They would grant “greater rights for residents, communities, housing cooperatives and local authorities regarding the situation in the short-term rental market”, said Tusk. “Wherever order, safety and basic comfort of life are threatened, decisions can be made to exclude these types of businesses.” The new rules would allow homeowner associations (wspólnoty mieszkaniowe) and housing cooperatives (spółdzielnie mieszkaniowe) to prohibit short-term rentals. If a majority of members voted to adopt such a ban, operators of short-term rental properties would have six months to end operations. Municipal councils (rady gmin), at the request of the mayor, would also be given the power to designate specific areas within their territory in which short-term rentals would be banned or restricted (for example, to a certain number of days a year). There would also be greater powers for residents and housing groups to initiate official inspections of properties if they believe there are violations of public safety and order rules. If a property violated such regulations three times within six months, it would be banned from operating for a year. Tusk noted that, if the bill becomes law, it would not fully go into force until 2028, in order to give enough time for businesses and communities to adapt to the new rules. If Poland does introduce the new measures, its cities could follow the example of many of their European counterparts, such as Barcelona, Paris and London, which have introduced various restrictions on short-term rentals. The European Union has also moved to more tightly regulate the sector. The Left celebrated the government’s decision to restore tougher elements of the bill, saying it would help avoid “situations where short-term rentals turn into a nightmare, stripping residents of their peace”. The leader of Poland 2050, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, declared that they had “scored another goal against the lobbyists” by toughening the legislation. World.title: NfP podcast: How small towns became a testing ground for Poland’s far right
World.content: In our new podcast, Notes from Poland’s editor-in-chief Daniel Tilles speaks with deputy editor-in-chief Alicja Ptak about her research into how four contentious issues – migration, women’s rights, Jewish heritage and LGBT+ rights – have played out in 19 smaller towns and cities in Poland. They discuss how national far-right talking points are being imported into smaller towns, how these issues are covered and contested at the local level, and what this all means ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. This conversation was based on a report produced as part of Notes from Poland’s new bespoke service offering our expertise to clients. There is now “no doubt” that a fire this week at a drone factory in Poland was caused deliberately, says Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who also suggested it was carried out on behalf of Russia. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Tusk noted that there had been “some very disturbing incidents and events in Poland and Germany over the past few [days]”. “This is a continuation of Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region,” he continued. “Unfortunately, these are not the first cases and, even worse, they certainly won’t be the last.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Najbliższe tygodnie i miesiące będą krytyczne nie tylko jeśli chodzi o zdarzenia na froncie i w ogóle całą wojnę rosyjsko-ukraińską, ale te tygodnie i miesiące będą także bardzo dużym wyzwaniem dla wszystkich państw w tej części Europy, ze względu na… pic.twitter.com/ZcjVMjhWc0 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 2, 2026 On Sunday, a fire broke out at a production facility in the Polish city of Lublin belonging to JFG Composites, a company that produces components for the aerospace industry, including for military helicopters. Then, in the early hours of Monday morning, another fire occurred at a plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna, south-central Poland, belonging to WB Electronics, a Polish firm that is the largest producer of drones in the European Union. It supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. By Monday afternoon, Polish prosecutors and the security services had confirmed that they were investigating the Skarżysko-Kamienna fire as a potential “crime of a terrorist nature” carried out with the involvement of “foreign intelligence”. On Tuesday, improvised explosive devices were found at one electricity substation in Germany near the border with Poland while another substation in the west of the country was attacked. World.title: Langdon Appears in Prague! Netflix Presents New Series Based on Dan Brown
World.content:
Netflix has begun filming its new series based on Dan Brown’s The Secret of Secrets, bringing Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon back to Prague.

The production officially started in the Czech capital this week, with Netflix releasing a first look at Morgan Spector as Langdon and Rebecca Hall as scientist Katherine Solomon. The series is currently untitled and does not yet have a release date.



Netflix has now added five more actors to the production. Mamoudou Athie will appear as Michael Harris, Ben Levi Ross as Alex Conan, Anamaria Marinca as Dr. Gessner, Richard Sammel as Karl Muller and Elena Saurel as Susan Housemore.

The series is being developed by Carlton Cuse, who co-created Lost and later worked on Jack Ryan, Locke & Key, Bates Motel and Five Days at Memorial. Cuse serves as co-creator, showrunner, writer and executive producer. Emma Forman is also an executive producer for Genre Arts, alongside Cuse and Brown.

Brown is involved in the project as a co-writer and executive producer.

The novel takes Langdon through several recognizable parts of Prague, including Charles Bridge and the Klementinum, as he searches for answers following Solomon’s disappearance. Netflix says the television adaptation will combine scientific ideas, historical mysteries and mystical elements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dan Brown (@authordanbrown)

The Secret of Secrets was published in September 2025 and became the latest installment in Brown’s Robert Langdon series. The book was released simultaneously in multiple countries, including the Czech Republic, and Prague is closely tied to its plot.

The Czech Republic is expected to play a significant role in the new television production. Prague has previously served as a filming location for a wide range of international productions, making the city a familiar setting for foreign film and television crews.

The arrival of the Netflix series could also have an impact beyond the production industry. Czech travel companies and Argo, the publisher of Brown’s books in Czech, have previously pointed to the potential for two waves of tourism connected with the project: first from readers discovering the novel and later from viewers of the television adaptation.

World.title: Prague Planetarium to Become a Concert Venue Under the Stars
World.content:
The Prague Planetarium in Stromovka will host a new series of chamber concerts combining live music with projections of the universe from September 2026.

Called Niche Nites, the series will feature 10 concerts between September 2026 and June 2027. Each performance will be accompanied by visuals projected across the planetarium’s 22-metre-wide dome, with the imagery responding to the music in real time.



The programme will take place on the final weekend of each month. Rather than staging repeated performances, each musician or group will appear at the planetarium only once, giving every concert its own programme and visual design.

The series will open on September 25 with cellist Terezie Kovalová, whose work combines classical music with pop, alternative and electronic influences.

Other performers confirmed for the programme include guitarist and composer Michal Pavlíček, who will appear with singer Bára Basiková, pianist and composer Beata Hlavenková, and singer-songwriter Lenka Dusilová. Further names will be announced by the organisers in the coming months.

Producer and dramaturg Michala Komrsková said the project is intended to present established Czech musicians in a more intimate setting than the large concert halls where they usually perform.

The planetarium’s technology will play a central role. Its dome is fitted with an LED system containing millions of diodes, allowing large-scale visual sequences to accompany the performances. The imagery will be prepared specifically for each concert rather than using a single projection throughout the series.

More recently, the planetarium was used during this year’s Spectaculare festival, which combined music by composer Rafael Anton Irisarri with visual work by Czech artists Dalibor Cée and Alex J. Jindrák.

World.title: Gipsy Kings by André Reyes to Perform in Prague This November
World.content:
The legendary Gipsy Kings by André Reyes will perform in Prague this November, bringing their distinctive mix of flamenco guitar, rumba and Latin rhythms to Lucerna Great Hall on November 29, 2026.

Led by founding member André Reyes, the group will perform some of the songs that made the Gipsy Kings famous around the world, including “Bamboleo,” “Djobi Djoba” and “Volare,” alongside newer material.



The concert is being presented by Gotobeat and will begin at 7 p.m. Tickets are online here.

From southern France to the world

The Gipsy Kings’ story began with the Reyes family and their musical roots in the south of France. André Reyes was one of the founding members of the group, which went on to combine traditional flamenco with rumba, Latin rhythms and pop influences.

Their energetic guitar playing and Spanish-language songs helped turn rumba flamenca into an international sound. Tracks such as “Bamboleo” and “Djobi Djoba” became global hits, while their version of “Volare” introduced the group to an even wider audience.

Music associated with the Gipsy Kings has sold more than 60 million records worldwide, making the group one of the most successful international acts to emerge from the flamenco-rumba tradition.

Their music has also appeared in popular culture, including their version of “Hotel California,” which featured in The Big Lebowski.

A new generation of the Reyes family

André Reyes continues the tradition today with Gipsy Kings by André Reyes, performing alongside younger members of the Reyes family.

The current show combines the group’s best-known classics with newer music, including material connected to Nací Gitano, the band’s latest project. The group is also touring internationally in 2026 as part of its Viva el Arte Tour.

For audiences, the concert offers a mix of familiar songs and new material, with the performance centred on the fast-paced guitar playing, percussion and vocals that have defined the Gipsy Kings sound for decades.

Date: Sunday, November 29, 2026

Time: 7 p.m.

Venue: Lucerna Great Hall, Štěpánská 61, Prague 1

Promoter: Gotobeat

World.title: No Tickets Needed: Six Free Events in Prague This September
World.content:
Prague is offering a packed lineup of free events this September, from an air show and science festivals to a rare public viewing of the Czech Crown Jewels and a celebration marking a local brewery’s 15th anniversary.

Here are some of the best events taking place across the Czech capital this month.



Free Sightseeing at Historic Sites

The National Heritage Institute will open selected state-owned castles, chateaux, monasteries and other historic sites to visitors for free on Sunday, September 27.

Most of the properties managed by the institute will take part, although the tours and routes available will vary by location. Free admission will cover standard tours and selected additional routes. Capacity is limited, so visitors must book a free ticket online in advance for a specific time.

The Prague 10 Science Festival returns to Gutovka on Saturday, September 12.

From 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., 25 stations will offer visitors the chance to take part in chemistry experiments, explore LEGO robotics, play math games and learn more about nature, technology and the human body.

The program will also include workshops, a competition, a toy and plant swap, and a science show by Michael Londesborough. DJ SÂN will perform from 6 p.m., with the festival continuing until 8 p.m.

Dokola Festival

The Dokola Festival will take place on September 10 and 11, focusing on creative ways to reuse items rather than throw them away.

Visitors can repair broken electronics, make furniture from leftover wood, upcycle old clothes or try making kimchi. The program will also feature talks, a clothes swap, an upcycled fashion show and stand-up comedy. Most of the program is free, although some workshops charge a nominal fee.

Břevnov Brewery Celebrates 15 Years

Břevnov Brewery will mark its 15th anniversary on Saturday, September 12, with a day of beer, live music and family activities.

From 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., the meadow beside Břevnov Monastery will feature beer from the local brewery, along with special brews from other monastic breweries from across the Czech Republic.

Live performances by HUGO, Funk Corporation and JAKSI TAKSI will accompany guided brewery tours, barrel-throwing and timed barrel-rolling competitions, as well as activities for children.

There will also be a workshop for visitors interested in learning how to brew beer at home.

Czech Crown Jewels on Display

One of Prague’s most prestigious treasures will go on public display this month, when the Czech Crown Jewels are exhibited in Vladislav Hall at Prague Castle from September 19 to 28. Admission is free.

The exhibition marks 500 years since Ferdinand I of Habsburg became King of Bohemia. Alongside the famous St. Wenceslas Crown, the display will feature the royal sceptre and orb, a coronation robe dating from 1653 and historic keys once used by guardians of the Crown Archive.

Visitors will enter through the South Gardens and Bull Staircase from Hradčanské Square. Everyone must pass through a security check, and organizers advise against bringing prams.

Letňany Airport Day

After a two-year break, Letňany Airport will once again open its doors to the public on Saturday, September 5.

This year’s event will focus on legendary training aircraft and pilot training during World War II and the postwar years.

The program will feature historic aircraft from the Czech Republic and abroad, demonstrations by the Czech Army and police, model aircraft and a chance to see the airport’s current operations.

Events will take place in half-hour blocks between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m.

World.title: Fire During C-Section at Bulovka Hospital Leaves Woman Seriously Burned
World.content:
A woman suffered serious burns during an emergency cesarean section at Prague’s Bulovka Hospital on Aug. 25, hospital spokeswoman Eva Stolejda Libigerová said.

The cesarean was performed because of an acute obstetric complication. The woman’s condition is now stable and she does not require intensive care, the hospital said. She is recovering in a standard ward with her newborn.



The hospital is investigating the incident as part of its internal procedures for reviewing patient safety and the quality of medical care. It said it would take appropriate measures once the investigation is complete.

Fire broke out during surgery

According to information obtained about the incident, medical staff were attempting to control bleeding toward the end of the operation when a fire broke out involving a surgical device.

The device was reportedly being used shortly after the patient’s skin had been treated with a disinfectant.

The woman suffered second- and third-degree burns to her inner thighs, sides, lower abdomen and genital area, according to the available information.

Two days after the operation, she was transferred to the Burns Medicine Clinic at University Hospital Královské Vinohrady for treatment. She was later returned to Bulovka Hospital’s postpartum ward.

The circumstances surrounding the fire, including how it started and whether established safety procedures were followed, are being examined by the hospital.

Previous incident at Bulovka maternity clinic

The hospital’s gynecology and obstetrics clinic was also the site of a serious medical error in March 2024.

In that case, staff mistakenly identified two patients of Asian origin. A pregnant woman who had arrived for a routine examination was incorrectly subjected to a curettage procedure, resulting in the loss of her pregnancy.

An internal investigation concluded that two employees had violated established procedures and internal rules. The hospital subsequently ended its cooperation with one of them.

Police also investigated the case on suspicion of negligent bodily harm but ultimately brought no charges.

The woman later reached a settlement with the hospital worth 2.3 million Czech crowns. One of the employees involved lost her job.

World.title: Ambiente to Open Its 35th Prague Establishment This September
World.content:
Restaurant group Ambiente is preparing to open its 35th establishment, with a second location of its Pult beer concept set to launch in Prague’s Holešovice district in mid-September.

The new venue will be located on Tusarova Street and will follow the concept of Pult in Prague 1, which opened in the Celnice building in 2021.



While both locations will focus on Czech lager, the new Holešovice branch will introduce a different food concept and its own selection of beers.

The original venue serves beers from six breweries, with an emphasis on precise storage, serving and temperature control.

A different approach to food

Food will be one of the main differences between the two Pult locations.

The original Pult in Celnice focuses largely on smaller dishes and snacks. The Holešovice restaurant will instead offer a more substantial menu designed specifically to accompany beer.

The menu is expected to focus heavily on Czech beef, including several versions of steak tartare and steaks. Unlike many restaurants where the kitchen closes earlier than the bar, the new Pult plans to serve food until closing at 1 a.m.

The restaurant will have space for around 130 guests.

Another new destination for Holešovice

The opening comes as Holešovice continues to attract new restaurants, cafés and cultural venues. The area has become home to places including Vnitroblock, Mexická, Slice Slice Baby, Eatery, Ema, Typika, Osada and Polepšovna.

Ambiente itself has expanded its presence in Holešovice this year. At the Holešovice Market, the group has opened a second location of its Myšák confectionery and Naše maso butcher shop, as well as Skô, a Slovak-focused restaurant concept.

World.title: 7 Autumn Bike Trips to Take Around Czechia
World.content:
With cooler temperatures and autumn colours arriving, September and October are among the best months for cycling in Czechia.

The country’s extensive network of marked trails makes it easy to plan anything from a relaxed day trip to a multi-day adventure.

Here are seven routes worth considering this autumn.



1. Prague–Mělník–Litoměřice

One of the easiest options for Prague residents is to head north along the Elbe. The route passes through Mělník, known for its vineyards and historic centre, before continuing towards Litoměřice.

Along the way, cyclists can see Roudnice Chateau, Mount Říp and the historic fortress town of Terezín. Mělník is particularly appealing in September, when its wine season is in full swing.

2. Znojmo Wine Route

For a combination of cycling and wine, South Moravia is hard to beat in autumn. The 63-kilometre Znojmo Wine Route connects vineyards and villages around Znojmo and is suitable for cyclists of different abilities.

September and October are also the region’s main wine-harvest season, with numerous wine and burčák events taking place.

3. Mikulov and Pálava

The Mikulov Wine Trail offers another relaxed way to explore South Moravia. The route takes cyclists through vineyards and the countryside around Mikulov, with the Pálava hills providing one of the region’s most distinctive landscapes.

It is particularly attractive in September, when the annual Pálava Wine Festival takes place.

4. Singltrek pod Smrkem

If road cycling isn’t your thing, head towards Liberec. Singltrek pod Smrkem has more than 60 kilometres of purpose-built mountain-bike trails, ranging from easier sections for beginners to more challenging routes.

The surrounding Jizera Mountains also make it a good destination for a weekend trip.

5. Bečva Cycling Trail

The almost 160-kilometre Bečva Cycling Trail follows the Bečva River across Moravia. The route can be completed over several days and is largely downhill when ridden from the river’s source towards its confluence with the Morava.

Highlights along the way include Helfštýn Castle, the Zbrašovské Aragonite Caves and the open-air museum in Rožnov pod Radhoštěm.

6. Ploučnice Cycle Path

The nearly 100-kilometre Ploučnice Cycle Path runs from the river’s source near Ještěd to Děčín. It passes through Česká Lípa, the Ralsko area and the Kokořínsko-Máchův kraj landscape before reaching the Elbe.

7. Prague–Vienna Greenway

For a more ambitious trip, the Prague–Vienna Greenway stretches 368 kilometres between the two capitals. The route passes through historic towns, castles and monasteries, including Tábor, Znojmo and Mikulov.

It takes roughly a week to complete with stops, making it better suited to a longer autumn holiday than a weekend ride.

World.title: How to Buy TikTok Followers Without Risking Your Account
World.content:
Building a TikTok audience from zero can be frustrating. Even well-produced videos may struggle to attract attention when an account has only a handful of followers.

This slow beginning encourages some creators and businesses to purchase followers in the hope of making their profiles appear more established. Follower count can influence first impressions. When visitors discover a profile with an existing audience, they may be more willing to watch its videos, explore older content, or follow the account themselves. However, purchased followers cannot replace engaging videos or genuine interaction. Low-quality services may also deliver inactive accounts that disappear quickly or create an unnatural gap between follower numbers and actual engagement. Anyone considering this approach should understand how follower services operate, what they can realistically provide, and which warning signs suggest that a seller should be avoided.

Why Creators Purchase TikTok Followers

New accounts frequently face a credibility problem. Viewers have little information to judge whether the creator is worth following, so the visible follower count becomes one of several signals they use to make that decision. A larger audience can make a profile appear more established. This is particularly relevant for businesses, influencers, musicians, and other new TikTok creators trying to build authority in a competitive category. Some creators also purchase TikTok followers to reach eligibility thresholds for particular TikTok features. TikTok commonly applies age, location, and follower requirements to features such as LIVE, although the exact conditions may differ between markets and can change over time. The important distinction is that purchased followers mainly affect appearance. They may strengthen the profile’s initial social proof, but they do not guarantee greater reach, more sales, or stronger engagement.

What Purchased Followers Can and Cannot Do

Follower count is visible to anyone who visits a TikTok profile, which means it can shape the visitor’s first impression. A profile with several thousand followers may look more credible than an otherwise similar account with fewer than 100. TikTok’s recommendation system, however, evaluates much more than audience size. Signals such as watch time, completion rate, rewatches, shares, comments, saves, and viewer satisfaction are generally more important when determining whether a video should reach a wider audience. This creates a potential problem. If an account displays 30,000 followers but its videos consistently receive only a few dozen views, the imbalance may look unnatural to both TikTok and real visitors. Brands evaluating the creator for a partnership may notice the same discrepancy. Purchased followers should therefore be understood as a limited form of social proof. They cannot:

Make weak videos more entertaining

Guarantee placement on the For You feed

Produce meaningful comments or conversations

Create loyal customers

Replace a consistent publishing strategy

Automatically generate revenue

The greatest risk comes from purchasing followers that are obviously automated, inactive, or created only to inflate account statistics. These profiles add little value and may be removed during platform cleanups.

How to Evaluate a TikTok Follower Provider

The market contains everything from established social media marketing platforms to temporary websites selling automated accounts. A professional design alone does not prove that a service is dependable, so each provider should be evaluated carefully. Platforms such as SocialWick offer clearly defined TikTok packages and a conventional ordering process. Regardless of which company is being considered, several basic checks should be completed before placing an order.

Check the Website’s Security

A provider should use HTTPS encryption to protect information submitted through its website. This can usually be confirmed by checking for the padlock symbol beside the address in the browser. Secure payment methods are equally important. Credit cards and reputable payment processors normally offer better consumer protection than cryptocurrency transfers, gift cards, or other payment methods that are difficult to reverse.

Never Provide a TikTok Password

A follower delivery service generally needs only the public username or a link to the TikTok profile. It should not require the account password, email login, recovery code, or two-factor authentication details. Requests for private credentials are a serious warning sign. Sharing this information could allow an unknown company to access the account, change its settings, publish content, or lock out the owner.

Review the Delivery Time

Instant delivery may sound convenient, but an enormous follower increase within minutes can look unnatural. A newer account is unlikely to gain tens of thousands of followers suddenly without a viral video or another clear reason. More credible providers commonly offer gradual delivery. This spreads the order across several hours or days and makes it easier to monitor the quality of the accounts being added.

Understand the Package Quality

Follower packages are often divided into labels such as standard, high quality, active, real, or premium. These terms are not standardized, so they can mean different things on different websites. A higher-priced package may include accounts with profile photos, usernames, existing posts, or more complete activity histories. Cheaper options frequently consist of empty or inactive profiles. Before paying extra for a so-called premium tier, buyers should read the description carefully and determine what the seller is actually promising. Independent comparisons of TikTok follower providers and package quality may provide additional context, but customer reviews and seller claims should still be treated cautiously.

Look for Accessible Customer Support

A legitimate business should provide a clear way to request assistance. Live chat, email support, or a functioning contact form gives customers somewhere to report missing followers, delayed orders, or payment problems. Support availability does not automatically prove that a provider is trustworthy. However, a website with no contact information, unanswered messages, and no stated resolution process presents a much greater risk.

Warning Signs That Should Not Be Ignored

Very low pricing is one of the most common signs of poor-quality delivery. Maintaining accounts that look authentic requires more resources than operating a large collection of disposable bots. Consequently, offers promising thousands of “real and active” followers for a few cents are unlikely to match their description. Other warning signs include:

Requests for passwords or security codes

Guaranteed viral results

Promises of automatic monetization

No terms of service or privacy policy

Prices far below comparable providers

Only irreversible payment methods

Broken pages or copied website content

No delivery estimate

No refund or replacement policy

Large numbers of identical customer reviews

Claims of guaranteed engagement also deserve scrutiny. No external provider can honestly promise that purchased followers will watch every video or become paying customers.

Why a Refill Policy Matters

Follower losses can occur after an order is completed. TikTok may remove suspicious accounts, users may deactivate their profiles, or low-quality followers may simply disappear. A refill policy allows customers to request replacements when the follower count drops within a specified period. Depending on the provider, this protection may last for several days or a month. The conditions should be reviewed before checkout. Some companies refill only when the loss exceeds a minimum amount, while others exclude certain packages. Buyers should also check whether the replacement is automatic or must be requested manually. A refill guarantee cannot eliminate every risk, but it shows that the provider has at least acknowledged the possibility of follower loss and established a process for addressing it.

Avoid Unnatural Growth Patterns

Sudden, unexplained growth can draw unwanted attention. An account that gains 10,000 followers overnight without publishing anything new may appear suspicious, particularly if its views and interactions remain unchanged. Gradual delivery is generally less disruptive than receiving an entire order immediately. However, spreading out a purchase should not be treated as a method for bypassing TikTok’s enforcement systems. Buying followers may still conflict with platform rules, and no delivery method can guarantee that an account will avoid restrictions or removals.

Creators who choose to purchase followers should keep the order proportionate to the profile’s existing size. Adding a modest number to an active account is less conspicuous than transforming a nearly empty profile into a large one overnight. Content should also continue to be published consistently. A larger number beneath the profile image will have little effect if visitors arrive and find outdated, irrelevant, or poorly produced videos.

Keep Engagement and Follower Numbers Balanced

Follower count is only one part of a TikTok profile. Views, likes, comments, shares, and posting frequency provide a broader picture of its actual performance. If follower growth significantly outpaces every other metric, the account may lose credibility. A profile with 20,000 followers and almost no interaction may look less trustworthy than one with 2,000 followers and an active community. Maintaining a reasonable balance requires genuine content work. Creators should continue to:

Publish videos on a consistent schedule

Capture attention within the opening seconds

Respond to real comments

Participate in relevant trends

Use searchable captions and keywords

Test different formats and video lengths

Review analytics to identify strong topics

Collaborate with creators in the same niche

These activities provide TikTok with behavioral signals that purchased followers cannot produce.

Turning Social Proof Into Organic Growth

The most practical reason to purchase followers is to improve the profile’s initial presentation. If that stronger appearance encourages more people to explore the content, it may indirectly support organic growth. This effect depends entirely on what visitors find after opening the profile. A clear bio, recognizable niche, strong video covers, and a useful collection of content can convert curiosity into a genuine follow. An inflated number without quality content is unlikely to accomplish the same result. Creators should prepare their profiles before purchasing anything. A complete profile should include:

A memorable username

A clear profile image

A concise description of the account

Several high-quality published videos

Pinned content that represents the creator’s best work

A consistent subject or visual identity

An appropriate call to action

Purchased followers may bring the profile closer to the starting line, but the content determines whether real viewers remain interested.

Final Considerations Before Buying TikTok Followers

Buying TikTok followers can improve the visible size of an account, but it should never be confused with building a real community. The number may influence first impressions, yet it cannot reproduce the value of genuine viewers who regularly interact with the content. Anyone considering a purchase should choose a provider carefully, avoid sharing login information, use protected payment methods, read the refill conditions, and remain skeptical of unrealistic guarantees. It is also important to recognize that follower purchases may violate TikTok’s rules and could lead to removals or other account consequences. The strongest TikTok profiles combine credibility with content that earns attention. Purchased followers may change how a profile looks, but sustainable growth still depends on originality, consistency, audience understanding, and videos that people genuinely want to watch.

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing is out: Migration clash, Ukraine veto and a widening budget gap
World.content:
Hungary’s political landscape remained highly active this week, with migration once again moving to the centre of the domestic and European debate, while the government continued to define its position on Ukraine, EU relations and the first major tests of the post-election political order.

In politics, the key questions centred on Hungary’s continued migration emergency, the government’s attempt to resolve the EUR 1 million-a-day EU fine, and Budapest’s decision to keep blocking parts of Ukraine’s accession process over minority-rights concerns. At home, the first signs of pressure on the new administration appeared alongside fresh polling, while Fidesz and Mi Hazánk are beginning to confront the strategic realities of opposition.

The economy and business picture was dominated by a widening budget gap, continued cost-of-living pressure and a growing list of domestic policy changes, from pensions and social spending to Airbnb regulation and the bottle-return system. Meanwhile, in diplomacy, Hungary took a firmer line on alleged Russian hybrid activity, Péter Magyar moved closer to the European People’s Party, and Budapest hosted a busy round of European and bilateral diplomatic engagements.
