World.title: K-pop in Hungary is no longer just a teenage trend: it is becoming a cultural movement – interview
World.content:
K-pop in Hungary has moved far beyond fan playlists and dance covers. What began as a niche passion among teenagers has grown into a vibrant community that leads young Hungarians towards Korean language, food, fashion, travel and even performance. In an interview with Daily News Hungary, Yu Hye Ryong, Director of the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary, explains why Hungarian fans stand out in Europe, how Budapest is becoming a stage for local K-pop talent, and why parents might want to look beyond the glitter, choreography and screaming crowds. Exclusive interview:

K-pop in Hungary: development és character

Daily News Hungary (DNH): How has the popularity of K-pop changed in Hungary in recent years?

Yu Hye Ryong, Director of the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

Yu Hye Ryong: In the late 2010s, when K-pop was still relatively new in Hungary, the scene was largely driven by teenagers and young adults, particularly fans of groups such as BTS and BLACKPINK. At the time, K-pop was consumed primarily through fan communities, with a strong focus on music and choreography.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, live performances were understandably affected, but online consumption of K-pop actually grew. The spread of short-form video content through platforms such as TikTok and YouTube Shorts made K-pop much more accessible and significantly lowered the barrier to discovering it.

Over the past few years, K-pop has developed into a much more mainstream cultural phenomenon in Hungary, with the audience growing to a point where large-scale offline events are now possible. For example, at MOKKOJI KOREA at Budapest Park in 2024, SUNMI, AB6IX and Dreamcatcher performed in Hungary for the first time. The event was free of charge, yet demand was so high that advance registration was required.

What is particularly interesting is that people are no longer consuming K-pop simply as a form of music or as individual concerts. Their interest often expands in a chain: K-pop → K-dance → K-beauty → Korean language → K-food → travel to Korea.

DNH: Why is K-pop particularly appealing to young people in Hungary? Who are the most active fans today, and is the fan base continuing to grow?

Yu Hye Ryong: One of the great strengths of K-pop is that it is not a form of content that is complete with music alone. Music, choreography, fashion, visual content, performance, the artists’ stories and fan communities all come together to create a much broader experience.

K-pop is also a culture that is easy to participate in. People do not simply listen to the music. They learn the choreography, learn the Korean lyrics and sing along, create cover videos, or form teams with friends and perform together.

From the participants we meet through our cultural centre’s programmes, teenagers and young adults are still the most active fan group. At the same time, however, the range of people interested in Korean culture is gradually expanding.

We often see people who first discovered Korea through K-pop several years ago now learning Korean, travelling to Korea, or becoming interested in Korean films, food and other aspects of Korean culture.

Ultimately, K-pop fans do not remain simply consumers of content. I think one of the most important strengths of K-pop is that it encourages people to learn about the culture they love, express themselves through it, and experience it together with others.

If you missed it: Nearly 17,000 visitors attended Korea Days – 7th KoreaON Festival on Margaret Island in Budapest – photos

DNH: Does the K-pop community in Hungary have any characteristics that distinguish it from those in other European countries?

Yu Hye Ryong: What I find particularly impressive in Hungary is the high level of participation and the strong sense of community among fans.

Hungary is not a particularly large country in terms of population, but people who are passionate about K-pop are extremely active. They form their own dance teams, practice and perform together, participate in competitions and cultural events, and regularly take part in programmes organised by our cultural centre.

We often see people who meet through one programme coming back to participate in another, forming new teams together or supporting each other’s activities.

So it goes beyond simply sharing a love of the same music. A genuine community naturally develops around that shared interest.

We consider this kind of participation very important. We believe that meaningful cultural exchange happens at a much deeper level when people do not simply watch or consume another culture, but actually learn it, practice it and create something together.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

K-pop: the gateway to discovering Korea

DNH: Does interest in K-pop also lead to interest in other aspects of Korean culture, such as fashion, the Korean language, food, film, tourism and traditional culture?

Yu Hye Ryong: Yes. This is something we see very frequently through our work at the cultural centre.

For many people, K-pop serves as a kind of gateway through which they first discover Korea. They may become interested in Korean because they want to understand the lyrics of their favorite songs. Then they start watching Korean films or dramas, trying Korean food, or planning a trip to Korea. Their interests naturally expand from one area to another.

Fashion and beauty are another example. People may become interested in the fashion or makeup styles of K-pop artists and then think, “I would like to try that myself.”

The Korean language is a particularly good example. The natural desire to sing along to a favorite song can lead to an interest in Hangul and Korean pronunciation, and eventually become the motivation to actually study Korean.

In other words, the boundaries between the K-pop fandom and the broader Korean Wave fandom are relatively fluid. People who initially come to K-pop do not necessarily remain interested in K-pop alone. They often develop an interest in Korean dramas, food, language, travel, products and Korean culture more broadly.

What is particularly interesting is that this interest does not necessarily stop with contemporary culture. We have visitors who first come to the cultural centre because of K-pop and later participate in Korean language classes, Korean food programmes, film screenings, traditional music or traditional dance programmes.

That is why we do not see K-pop and traditional culture as separate worlds. K-pop can be the first door through which people discover Korea, but it does not have to be the last.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

DNH: What role does K-pop play in the activities of the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary?

Yu Hye Ryong: K-pop is one of the important areas of our cultural centre’s activities. However, our goal is not simply to introduce popular K-pop content or bring performances to audiences. What matters to us is using K-pop as a way to encourage people to experience Korean culture directly and become active participants in it.

Through our K-POP Academy, we regularly offer K-pop dance classes. We also invite choreographers and other professionals working in Korea to conduct special workshops, giving Hungarian participants the opportunity to learn directly from and interact with professionals working in the K-pop industry.

Last October, we also hosted the Hungarian preliminary round of the Changwon K-POP World Festival with MondoCON. Through this programme, local participants have the opportunity to showcase their skills and challenge themselves on an international K-pop stage.

More recently, we have taken this one step further by focusing on the creation of original content planned by the cultural centre and made together with local participants.

Two examples are KCC IDOL and K-POP SINGERS. KCC IDOL is designed to allow participants to experience the entire process together — from practicing and building teamwork to preparing for and performing on stage. K-POP SINGERS expands the focus beyond dance to singing, allowing participants to learn and practice Korean songs and experience the process of recording and performing.

If I had to describe our approach in one sentence, it would be: “From audience to participant, and from participant to performer and creator.”

This year, we are taking this approach even further with a project called K-POP in Budapest. Local K-pop singers and dancers will practice together and perform in Budapest, while the entire journey — from preparation to the final performance — will be captured on film and produced as a music film centered around busking.

Rather than simply producing a promotional video introducing K-pop, we wanted to create something in which the people who actually love and practice K-pop in Hungary become the protagonists, and Budapest itself becomes the stage.

We believe that when people in Hungary take K-pop created in Korea and reinterpret it through their own city and their own experiences, creating new stories in the process, that itself can be a meaningful form of cultural exchange.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

Read also: 6th DAESANG Eat and Travel Film Festival happened in Budapest as its First Edition in Europe

K-pop events in Hungary

DNH: Which K-pop programmes and events are currently the most popular in Hungary? Are there any special events people can look forward to this year?

Yu Hye Ryong: Interest in K-pop dance remains extremely high. There is a steady demand for dance classes, cover dance activities and workshops with professional choreographers, and our K-POP Academy continues to offer regular programmes.

At the same time, the ways in which people enjoy K-pop are not limited to dance. Many people also want to sing Korean songs themselves, so we are expanding opportunities for participation in the vocal field through programmes such as K-POP SINGERS.

In particular, we want to create programmes in which participants do more than simply attend an event for a day. We want them to experience a process together over a period of time: learning a song or choreography, practising together, recording and filming, and ultimately performing in front of an audience.

Through this process, participants are no longer simply spectators. They become the protagonists of the programme.

Our K-POP in Budapest project this year is a good example of this approach. Local participants will prepare their own K-pop performances, take part in busking performances and filming in Budapest, and have the entire process and final performance captured as a music film.

Going forward, we want to continue expanding opportunities for people not simply to watch K-pop, but to learn it, create together and express themselves on stage.

Detailed information about our programmes and events is available through the Korean Cultural Center in Hungary’s official website and social media channels.

Soruce: Korean Cultural Center in Hungary

DNH: What are some common misconceptions among people who are unfamiliar with K-pop? What would you say to Hungarian parents who see K-pop simply as a teenage trend?

Yu Hye Ryong: For people who are not familiar with K-pop, the first things they may notice are the spectacular performances and the enthusiastic young fans. So it is understandable that they might see it simply as a form of popular culture that happens to be fashionable among teenagers.

Of course, K-pop is popular culture, and trends inevitably change. But when we meet young participants directly, what interests us is not only what they are listening to, but what they are doing because they love it.

They learn a new language because they want to understand the lyrics of their favorite songs. They practice for hours and sometimes for months to perfect a piece of choreography or a song. They learn how to work with teammates, overcome the nervousness of performing on stage, make new friends and gain confidence.

For some, K-pop becomes the starting point for studying Korean or developing an interest in Korean food, films, history and society — and eventually even visiting Korea themselves.

So if their children are interested in K-pop, I would encourage parents to look not only at what their children are watching and listening to, but also at what they are learning and creating through that interest.

Interests naturally change as young people grow older. But the confidence they gain on stage, the discipline they develop through repeated practice, the ability to cooperate with others, and their curiosity about a new language and culture can stay with them for much longer.

K-pop can be the first door through which someone encounters Korea. I believe the role of a cultural centre is to help people who enter through that first door discover all the many other doors that lie beyond it.

Read our exclusive interview – South Korean Ambassador: Hungary is no longer just an investment destination; it’s a strategic innovation partner

Daily News Hungary is the official media partner of the Korean Cultural Centre in Hungary.

World.title: Hungary fuel prices face first major test as oil climbs and government rules out costly cap
World.content:
Hungary fuel prices are heading towards their first serious test since the government scrapped the protected-price system earlier this summer. With global oil prices climbing again, Prime Minister Péter Magyar says his government is preparing targeted help for motorists – but this time, it wants a solution that does not create shortages or cost taxpayers tens of billions of forints every month.

Global oil markets have turned sharply higher again amid renewed tensions between the United States and Iran and fears over supplies from the Middle East. Brent crude climbed above USD 96 a barrel on Saturday, putting renewed pressure on fuel prices across Europe.

That creates an uncomfortable economic and political test for the Hungarian government: what happens when fuel becomes substantially more expensive, but simply fixing the retail price is no longer considered a sustainable answer?

Hungary fuel prices back in focus

In a Saturday Facebook post, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said he had discussed the challenges facing Hungary’s economy and energy sector with Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány.

The government, Magyar wrote, was working to provide motorists with “effective and targeted” assistance as soon as possible amid what he described as an increasingly difficult global market environment.

Crucially, however, he also appeared to draw a line under the previous model of intervention.

Magyar said Hungary needed a solution which, unlike the protected fuel price, would not lead to shortages and would not cost the state budget – and therefore taxpayers – tens of billions of forints every month, equivalent to tens of millions of euros.

The statement marks a notable change in tone after months in which government intervention in fuel prices became increasingly familiar to Hungarian motorists.

From Orbán’s protected price to a market-based system

The protected fuel price was introduced by Viktor Orbán’s government on 9 March 2026 following a surge in international oil prices. Petrol was capped at HUF 595 per litre, around EUR 1.64, while diesel was limited to HUF 615, approximately EUR 1.69 at current exchange rates.

After winning the election, Magyar initially announced that the incoming government would maintain the scheme. In April, he said an agreement had been reached with Hungarian oil and gas company MOL to preserve the protected prices without imposing additional costs on the budget.

By June, however, market conditions had changed. With filling-station prices falling below the official ceiling, the new government moved to abolish the system. Legislation nevertheless retained the possibility of introducing regulated prices again if market conditions changed disproportionately and government intervention was deemed necessary to protect consumers.

Now the international environment is deteriorating once again – and this time the government appears reluctant to reach immediately for the same tool.

If you missed it: Cost of living in Hungary: Inflation has fallen – so why do people still feel poorer?

The first real test for the new approach

The challenge is not merely the price displayed at petrol stations.

Artificially suppressing fuel prices can offer motorists immediate relief, but the previous Hungarian system also demonstrated the potential costs of broad price intervention. Magyar’s latest comments explicitly acknowledge two of those problems: supply shortages and a significant burden on public finances.

That makes the coming weeks an important test of economic policy.

For years, Hungarian consumers have repeatedly seen the state intervene when politically sensitive prices rise sharply. The risk is that such intervention gradually creates an expectation that the government should prevent market prices from increasing even when the underlying cause comes from abroad.

Magyar’s government now appears to be looking for a narrower alternative: helping those most exposed to rising fuel costs without once again fixing the price for the entire market.

The prime minister said he and Kapitány had also reviewed the direction of Hungary’s new domestic and foreign economic policy, as well as measures needed to establish a stable energy sector.

With global oil prices moving higher, those discussions may quickly become more than long-term economic planning. Hungary fuel prices could soon show whether the government is genuinely ready to move away from broad price controls when doing so becomes politically difficult.

Fidesz reacts

The Fidesz party, which suffered a defeat in April, is now launching a fierce attack on the Tisza government’s economic policy, in the hope of winning back voters.

At the same time, we must not forget that, on the one hand, this state intervention runs counter to the development of a healthy economy, and, on the other, Viktor Orbán has close ties with none other than Trump, who was in fact responsible for the rise in oil prices through the attack on Iran.

And if the war in Iran is not set to end any time soon – for which there is no indication – then further price rises are to be expected, for example in flights: Ryanair and Wizz Air sound the alarm – what could happen to air fares?

World.title: Hungary weather: Cold front this weekend, then heat, heavy rain and sharp cooling next week
World.content:
Hungary’s weather is about to change several times within just over a week. A cold front crossing the country on Saturday will bring a temporary drop in temperatures for Sunday, before summer heat quickly returns. From the middle of next week, however, a much more significant change could arrive, bringing substantial rainfall and eventually genuinely autumnal temperatures.

A cold front is moving across Hungary from the north and north-west on Saturday, 5 September. Despite increasing cloud cover, significant widespread rainfall is not expected, although scattered showers and thunderstorms may develop.

HungaroMet has warned of possible thunderstorms in several counties, particularly in the north-east and south, with storms also possible in the south-west later in the day. Wind gusts of 60–70 km/h, locally exceeding 70 km/h, may accompany stronger storms, and isolated hail cannot be ruled out. Temperatures will nevertheless remain summery, with afternoon highs between 25 and 34°C.

Sunday: Cooler, sunny and mostly dry

The cold front will be more noticeable on Sunday, 6 September, when temperatures fall by several degrees.

Mostly clear or lightly cloudy weather is expected across Hungary, with no significant precipitation. More cumulus clouds may develop in the north-east, while north-westerly and northerly winds could occasionally strengthen.

Morning temperatures will generally range between 10 and 18°C, although sheltered areas could fall slightly below 10°C. Afternoon highs are forecast between 24 and 29°C.

The cooler weather will not last long, however. Temperatures will begin rising again almost immediately as Hungary heads into another short spell of late-summer heat.

Hungary weather next week: Day-by-day forecast

Monday, 7 September: Summer returns

Temperatures will begin climbing again on Monday, with mostly dry and warm conditions expected. Forecasts currently indicate afternoon highs of roughly 27–32°C, meaning the weekend’s brief cooling will already be fading.

Tuesday, 8 September: Temperatures above 30°C again

Tuesday could be one of the warmest days of the week. Maximum temperatures are expected to reach around 28–33°C, bringing summer-like heat back to much of Hungary.

For anyone hoping that Saturday’s cold front marked the beginning of autumn, the answer will therefore be a clear no – at least temporarily.

If you missed it: another popular Hungarian lake dries out, Bölömbika lookout shows critical conditions

Wednesday, 9 September: A major change begins

The first wave of a more substantial weather change is currently forecast to arrive from Wednesday, when another cold front reaches Hungary.

One of its most striking effects could be a large temperature difference between different parts of the country. Western Hungary may already experience much cooler conditions while the east remains hot, potentially creating a 10–15°C difference between the two sides of the country.

Unlike Saturday’s front, this system is also expected to bring more significant rainfall.

Thursday, 10 September: Cold front spreads across Hungary

The effects of the front are expected to become much more widespread by Thursday.

Temperatures should fall across larger parts of the country, while rain could affect numerous regions. Current forecasts suggest this will be the point when the first major cooling phase becomes established.

The exact location and amount of precipitation remain uncertain several days in advance, so the forecast may still change considerably.

Friday, 11 September: Sharp cooling possible in western Hungary

By Friday, some western parts of Hungary could experience a dramatic change compared with the heat seen earlier in the week.

Current projections suggest temperatures in some western areas may reach only around 15°C – potentially almost 20 degrees below Tuesday’s highest values.

Eastern parts of the country may remain somewhat warmer, but the overall trend will be firmly towards cooler weather.

Catch up on the week’s biggest stories from Hungary — politics, economy, business and diplomacy, all in one place. Subscribe here: Substack

Saturday, 12 September: Autumn weather and heavier rain

A second phase of the weather change could begin around Saturday.

Forecasts currently indicate that a Mediterranean cyclone may start influencing Hungary, bringing widespread and potentially substantial rainfall. From this point, autumnal temperatures are expected across the country rather than only in western regions.

Sunday, 13 September: Widespread rain could continue

Sunday could remain cool and wet as the Mediterranean system affects Hungary.

Between 12 and 15 September, current projections suggest that repeated rainfall could bring approximately 30–70 millimetres of precipitation across the country, with larger amounts possible in western Hungary.

Such rainfall would be particularly notable after the prolonged dry conditions of recent months.

Summer first, then a real taste of autumn

The coming days could therefore bring an unusually sharp weather contrast to Hungary: temperatures above 30°C on Tuesday, the arrival of a cold front from Wednesday, highs potentially around 15°C in parts of the west by Friday, followed by widespread autumnal weather and significant rainfall over the weekend.

Meteorologists stress that forecasts for the second half of next week still carry considerable uncertainty, particularly regarding the timing and strength of the expected Mediterranean cyclone and the amount of rainfall it may bring. Nevertheless, current models increasingly point towards a much more substantial change than the brief cold front crossing Hungary this Saturday.

World.title: Water-law permit in Hungary: 3 hidden traps only insiders discover
World.content:
My previous article examined how a water-law permit can affect property value: how a source with valid permits differs from one without them, and why official recognition as natural mineral water is an important condition for market access. This article adopts a different register. It is not about principles, but about reality. I have been involved in the permitting processes for two very different water-related property projects: a mineral-water well in the Börzsöny hills and a thermal well on the Great Hungarian Plain. Both lead to the same conclusion. The regulatory maze is not only slow and costly; it is also difficult to predict. The most serious obstacles often emerge not at the beginning, but years into the process.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Parallel jurisdictions: when several bodies are involved

A water-related property development in Hungary will usually bring the investor into contact with several authorities and specialist bodies. Regional water-management and water-protection authority functions are exercised by the county government offices designated in Government Decree 223/2014 (IX. 4.). The National Directorate General for Water Management (OVF) and the regional water directorates are water-administration bodies. A regional directorate may, among other things, issue asset-management consent and a water-infrastructure identification statement during the procedure, but it is not the permitting authority.

The mining authority acts in relation to the exploration, extraction and use of geothermal energy in the cases specified by the Mining Act; the exceptions applicable to certain forms of thermal-water extraction must be examined separately. Where a Natura 2000 site is affected, nature-conservation rules and authorities may become relevant; agricultural-land-protection, building and land-registry rules and bodies may also play a role. The municipality defines the framework for land use through its local building regulations (HÉSZ) and other local decrees.

This fragmentation is not accidental. The regulatory framework has accumulated from legislation enacted at different times for different purposes. In a single project, the relevant procedures may proceed in parallel, but at independent speeds. A decision in one procedure does not automatically create a right in another. The investor is therefore not walking down one corridor, but navigating several intersecting systems at the same time.

The Natura 2000 collision: consequences that are not apparent at the outset

In the Great Plain thermal-well case, the Natura 2000 designation, specifically the HUBN10004 Heves Plain Special Protection Area, was not a late surprise. According to the case files available to me, the Natura 2000 legal designation was already recorded in the land register when the well was drilled in 2007. What became clear only during the permitting process was how far its consequences could extend.

Under Section 10 of Government Decree 275/2004 (X. 8.), the first question is whether a plan or development may affect the Natura 2000 site; a detailed impact assessment is required if the possibility of a significant effect cannot be ruled out. In this case, the assessment focused primarily on the potential effects on the species for which the site was designated, including the red-backed shrike. The authority imposed mitigation conditions, including the retention of woodland buffers and existing shrub belts and the exclusion of certain lower-lying areas from development. The process took years, while the well remained unused.

If you missed it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ

The seven hectares discovered only years later

The most striking experience, however, was unrelated to Natura 2000 and arose through a separate regulatory channel. The local building regulations in force designate part of the Great Plain project’s development site, nearly seven hectares, as green space, specifically a public park. The owner did not learn this through the service of an authority decision. It emerged during a review of documents in an ongoing procedure, years after the property had been acquired: under the HÉSZ, that part of the site could not be built on or developed for the intended purpose because the municipal decree classified it as a public park.

This situation, which is not unique, illustrates a systemic feature of Hungary’s rural property market. The effect of a water-law permit on property value does not depend solely on the water-law procedure. Land-use classification, local building regulations, zoning and the land register are partly independent systems.

A property’s title sheet does not necessarily disclose every restriction contained in the HÉSZ. The municipal decree that determines what may be built on a plot is not automatically reproduced in the land register. A buyer who reviews only the title sheet, without separately checking the current local building regulations, may acquire property whose development potential is fundamentally constrained by a municipal decree of which the buyer was unaware.

What this means for the long-term viability of a water-law permit

The operating water-law permit for the Great Plain well expired in 2018. The proposed use, which required a larger water allocation, called for updated water-use plans and a fresh examination of the permitting conditions; the absence of the necessary asset-management consent delayed the procedure.

While the permit reserving 320,000 cubic metres per year remained in force, the absence of actual abstraction did not automatically eliminate liability for the water resource charge (vízkészletjárulék). Under Section 15/B(3) of the Water Management Act, where actual use is lower, the general calculation base is 80 per cent of the authorised quantity, which in this case would be 256,000 cubic metres.

The amount payable cannot, however, be determined from that volume alone. The formula under KHVM Decree 43/1999 (XII. 26.) also takes account of the type of water, the purpose of use, metering, the status of the water body and any applicable exemptions. Under certain combinations of parameters, the annual amount may exceed HUF 10 million. Any liability arising after the permit expired must be assessed separately by reference to the relevant period and the actual legal position.

The Börzsöny lesson: the value of patience and preparation

The Börzsöny mineral-water project followed a different course. There, the process from hydrodynamic modelling to official recognition as natural mineral water advanced with careful preparation. The interdependence of the procedures was planned in advance, and where one decision was a prerequisite for the next, the project waited for that decision to become final. Questions concerning the water-law regime, the HÉSZ, zoning and neighbouring properties were addressed before development began. This may extend the preparation phase, but it substantially reduces the risk of surprises later. Whether procedures should run in parallel or sequentially must be decided separately for each project on the basis of a tailored timetable.

Also interesting – From the offer to the land registry extract: how a safe property purchase works in Hungary

What every investor needs to understand

Together, the two cases offer three lessons.

Map the parallel constraints before purchase. The value created by a water-law permit can be realised only if Natura 2000 implications, HÉSZ zoning, agricultural-land-protection obligations and any green-space or public-park designation are known in advance. A permit is not perpetual. Its validity period, conditions and scope for amendment must be examined separately. A buyer acquiring property associated with an existing permit should have an expert verify whether the permit remains valid, who holds it, the conditions for changing the permit holder or owner, whether it can be amended, and whether its validity can be extended. The HÉSZ and the title sheet are separate sources. They must be checked independently of one another.

In closing

Hungary’s water resources, from mineral-water wells in the Börzsöny hills and thermal sources on the Great Plain to the use of geothermal energy, embody genuine and still underexploited value. That value does not realise itself. Regulatory procedures, interlocking specialist rules and long lead times stand between the resource and the investor. The outcome, a legally final permit, a recognised source and a properly protected water base, may constitute an asset that the market can rarely replicate. That is its cost, and that is its value.

Legislation cited

Emese Széll, an expert in Hungary’s premium property market. premiumingatlanok.com

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal, water-law, mining, nature-conservation or investment advice. The project-specific data and authority history described above should be verified against the original permits, decisions, registers and expert documentation. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

World.title: Where centuries-old Hungarian folk traditions are still alive – PHOTOS
World.content:
Hungarian folk traditions are still very much part of community life in the small village of Kiscsősz, in western Hungary. A new Anadolu photo series captures residents in traditional dress as they perform folk dances, play music and preserve customs that have been passed down through generations.

The photographs were taken in Kiscsősz, Veszprém County, on 13 August. They show villagers wearing authentic traditional costumes and taking part in folk dances accompanied by traditional music.

According to Anadolu, the local community actively preserves centuries-old Hungarian rural traditions, folklore and cultural heritage. The images also highlight indigenous musical instruments and community gatherings designed to ensure that these customs are passed on to younger generations.

Hungarian folk traditions remain part of village life

What makes Kiscsősz particularly striking is that these traditions are presented not simply as historical exhibits, but as part of a living community.

Folk dance and traditional music have long played an important role in Hungarian cultural identity, with regional variations in costumes, choreography and musical styles reflecting the country’s diverse rural heritage.

In Kiscsősz, that heritage remains visible through community events and performances where different generations take part together. Anadolu’s photographs show both the elaborate detail of traditional clothing and the social side of folk culture, with musicians, dancers and residents gathering in an intimate village setting.

The emphasis on transmitting traditions to younger people is particularly important, as many rural customs across Europe face the challenge of surviving demographic change and increasingly urban lifestyles.

A different side of Hungary

For international visitors, Kiscsősz offers a glimpse of Hungary far removed from Budapest’s grand architecture, ruin bars and thermal baths.

Small communities such as this one preserve another layer of the country’s identity: one shaped by village life, traditional music, colourful costumes and customs that have survived for generations.

The Anadolu gallery captures that atmosphere particularly well. Rather than presenting Hungarian folk traditions as something frozen in the past, the photographs show a culture that continues to be practised, shared and celebrated today.

World.title: Cost of living in Hungary: Inflation has fallen – so why do people still feel poorer?
World.content:
The cost of living in Hungary remains a major source of anxiety even as inflation has fallen sharply and real wages are rising again. A new PwC Hungary survey suggests that many households still feel financially stretched, with a sizeable share struggling to build savings, cover unexpected setbacks or even make their salary last until the next payday.

The findings highlight a gap between Hungary’s improving headline economic indicators and the way many people perceive their own financial situation.

According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), consumer prices were just 1.2 percent higher in July 2026 than a year earlier, while prices actually fell by 0.1 percent compared with June. Food prices were down 1.1 percent year on year, although services were still 4.7 percent more expensive.

Wages have also been gaining purchasing power. Real earnings rose by 7.6 percent year on year in June, according to the latest KSH figures.

Yet the latest survey from PwC Hungary shows that the improvement in the macroeconomic picture has not necessarily translated into a feeling of financial security.

Cost of living in Hungary continues to squeeze households

According to PwC Hungary’s Financial Wellness survey, 42 percent of respondents said their salary was generally failing to keep pace with rising living costs, while only 4 percent believed their pay was fully keeping up.

The survey also suggests that a substantial proportion of households have little room for a serious financial shock.

Thirty percent of respondents said their household would not be able to cover basic expenses if its main earner were unable to work for six months. Another 20 percent were unsure how long their existing reserves would last.

Day-to-day finances are also proving difficult for some. Fourteen percent said they often or always run out of money between paydays, while another one in five said this happens from time to time.

PwC found that 45 percent of respondents experienced at least a moderate level of stress when managing their finances, while 16 percent described themselves as particularly stressed. For 35 percent, financial anxiety had increased during the previous year.

The numbers are particularly notable because falling inflation does not mean that prices have returned to where they were several years ago. It simply means they are now increasing much more slowly. Households may therefore still be adjusting to the cumulative price rises of previous years even as current inflation becomes less severe.

If you missed it – Cost of living in Hungary in 2026: rent, groceries, transport and monthly budgets

Long-term savings are another weak point

Financial pressure is also affecting preparations for the future.

Among respondents who had not yet retired, 36 percent said they were not saving anything specifically for retirement. A further 13 percent said they intended to start but had not yet done so.

Concerns about the future extend beyond retirement savings. Around 32 percent of those surveyed said they believed their generation was financially worse off than previous generations had been at the same age. A similar proportion expected the next generation’s financial prospects to be no better.

This suggests that the debate around the cost of living in Hungary is increasingly about more than immediate inflation. Financial resilience, housing plans, retirement and the ability to build wealth are becoming part of the same conversation.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

Financial pressure is spilling into the workplace

PwC’s research also found signs that money worries are affecting working life.

Some 42 percent of employees surveyed were at least somewhat concerned about the future security of their jobs. Meanwhile, 45 percent felt that their employer did little or nothing to support their financial wellbeing.

The consequences can extend beyond personal budgeting. Respondents reported that financial stress can affect sleep, health, self-esteem, relationships and performance at work.

Why the figures matter despite falling inflation

For foreign observers, the survey offers an important qualification to Hungary’s improving inflation and wage statistics.

Lower inflation and rising real wages are positive developments, but they do not immediately undo several years of higher prices or rebuild household savings. The PwC findings suggest that many Hungarians remain focused on financial security rather than feeling the full benefit of the improving headline numbers.

The Hungarian survey was carried out in July 2026 in two waves among more than 3,200 adult Hungarian internet users who shop online, using a nationally representative sample for that group. The results should therefore be interpreted within that methodological scope rather than as a survey of every Hungarian household.

For now, the picture is mixed: inflation has eased substantially and purchasing power is recovering, but for a significant share of those surveyed, financial confidence appears to be recovering much more slowly.

World.title: Could Hungary back EU countries’ Rwanda plan?
World.content:
A plan to send migrants with no legal right to remain in the European Union to “return hubs” outside the bloc is rapidly moving from theory towards policy. Rwanda is emerging as a possible destination, raising a particularly interesting question for Hungary: would Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s new government support such a solution to Europe’s migration crisis? Budapest has not yet endorsed the Rwanda proposal, but its recent statements suggest it could be receptive to the idea.

Rwanda returns move to the centre of Europe’s migration crisis

Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands have been working together on the creation of return hubs outside the European Union. Representatives of the five countries recently travelled to Rwanda, where negotiations are under way over the possibility of hosting people ordered to leave EU territory.

According to Euractiv, one location being discussed is the Gashora Transit Centre, around 60 kilometres from Kigali. The facility has previously housed migrants evacuated from Libya while longer-term solutions were arranged. Rwanda has confirmed that preliminary negotiations with European governments are taking place.

The initiative has progressed quickly. The five governments have now set a target of establishing their first return-hub system by 2027, while Rwanda and Uganda are among the potential partner countries being considered. Denmark has said it hopes transfers could begin by the end of next year.

The proposal has become possible because EU migration policy itself is changing. The European Parliament approved new return rules in June allowing member states to conclude agreements with non-EU countries and transfer people who have received a return decision to facilities there. Unaccompanied minors are excluded, while partner states would have to respect international human rights standards and the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits sending people somewhere they face persecution or serious harm.

Importantly, this is not identical to the controversial British Rwanda scheme abandoned in 2024. The emerging EU model is primarily aimed at people who have already been found to have no legal right to remain in the EU, rather than simply moving asylum processing abroad.

Even so, considerable legal and humanitarian questions remain. The UN Refugee Agency has argued that return hubs should be used only where a person has undergone a full and fair asylum procedure and direct return to their country of origin is not possible within a reasonable period. The Council of Europe has also called for strict independent monitoring and legally enforceable human-rights guarantees.

If you missed it yeasterday: Hungary extends ‘mass migration crisis’ until end of 2026, PM Magyar vows no easing of border rules

Britain already tried Rwanda – and it failed. But Europe’s new plan is different

The obvious question is whether Europe is now repeating an experiment that has already failed.

Britain agreed its controversial Rwanda scheme in 2022, planning to relocate certain people who had arrived irregularly in the UK to Rwanda, where their asylum claims would be processed. In practice, however, the policy never became operational on the scale intended.

In November 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled that the scheme was unlawful in its existing form because of the risk that asylum seekers sent to Rwanda could ultimately be returned to countries where they faced persecution or inhumane treatment. The Conservative government subsequently negotiated a new treaty with Kigali and passed legislation declaring Rwanda a safe country, but the planned deportation flights still did not take place before the government changed.

According to the British Home Office, during more than two years of the programme only four people travelled to Rwanda voluntarily, while no asylum seekers were forcibly relocated under the scheme. The Labour government discontinued the policy after taking office in July 2024.

The emerging European proposal, however, is different in one crucial respect. The British scheme was designed largely for people whose asylum applications would not be considered in the UK and would instead be processed in Rwanda. The EU return-hub concept is primarily intended for people who have already received a return decision and therefore no longer have a legal right to remain in the European Union.

That distinction could make the European model easier to defend politically and legally. Rather than outsourcing the asylum procedure itself, return hubs would be intended as destinations for people whom EU governments have already decided must leave – particularly in cases where returning them directly to their country of origin proves difficult.

The British experience nevertheless provides a warning. Any European system involving Rwanda or another third country is likely to face intense scrutiny over human rights safeguards, legal responsibility and the risk of unlawful onward deportations.

Péter Magyar’s government has kept Hungary’s tough migration policy

The question for Hungary is particularly significant because the change of government in May did not bring the major reversal in migration policy that some foreign observers might have expected.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar said this week that, while individual measures introduced by Viktor Orbán’s previous government could be debated, Hungary had been fundamentally right in its assessment of migration. He specifically backed both the southern border fence and the country’s strict migration rules.

Magyar also said there could be no relaxation of Hungarian asylum regulations and that his government wanted to ensure that not “one more” irregular migrant entered the country. At the same time, he is seeking an agreement with Brussels rather than another prolonged confrontation over EU migration rules.

That stance is important for understanding how Budapest might approach the latest migration crisis proposal.

Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai has repeatedly said since the new government took office that Hungary’s position on irregular migration remains unchanged. In July, his ministry also revealed that Hungary was closely monitoring the practical experience of Italy’s controversial agreement with Albania – another attempt to handle aspects of migration outside normal EU territory.

Then, following renewed migration pressure at the EU’s external border in August, the Hungarian government explicitly called for “innovative policy tools” going beyond existing solutions, while stressing stronger external border protection and action against abuses of the asylum system.

Hungary has also discussed the support of returns directly with Austria, one of the five countries now pushing the return-hub initiative.

Migrant crisis in the EU. Photo: depositphotos.com

What’s next: Hungary joins 21 EU leaders in criticism of Spain’s migration response after mass arrivals

Could Hungary support the Rwanda return hubs?

Taken together, those positions provide a credible basis for believing that the Magyar government could support return hubs in principle.

Such a policy fits several elements of Budapest’s current approach: preventing irregular entry, maintaining strict asylum rules, strengthening the EU’s external borders and making it easier to remove people who have no right to stay.

It could also be politically easier for Magyar to support than parts of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact involving solidarity between member states. Sending people with final return decisions outside the EU is fundamentally different from requiring Hungary to receive asylum seekers transferred from another member state – something Budapest has strongly resisted.

However, there is an important distinction between saying the Hungarian government would probably find the concept attractive and saying it supports Rwanda specifically. Hungary is not currently part of the five-country initiative, and neither Magyar nor Pósfai has publicly committed Budapest to the Rwanda negotiations.

What happens next?

The next few months should provide a clearer answer. The five participating governments are expected to continue negotiations with potential host countries, with another meeting planned in Munich in September and concrete agreements targeted before the end of 2026.

For Hungary, much will depend on the final legal and financial structure. If return hubs remain voluntary, comply with EU and international law and do not require Hungary to accept migrants from other member states, the proposal would sit comfortably with much of the migration policy the Magyar government has outlined so far.

That makes Hungarian support a plausible scenario – but not yet a government position. The Rwanda debate may therefore become one of the first major tests of how much Hungary’s approach to Europe’s migration crisis has really changed under Péter Magyar: less confrontational towards Brussels, perhaps, but not necessarily more permissive on migration.

World.title: Netopia Payments expands license to include money remittance services after Romania’s Central Bank approval
World.content:
Romanian payments and technology platform Netopia Payments is entering a new stage of development after it received the authorization of the National Bank of Romania (BNR) to expand its payment institution license to include money remittance services, the company said.

The company, which processes more than RON 10 billion annually, is preparing new embedded finance solutions and developing an integrated financial platform for merchants, it said.

The company aims to expand its portfolio of services for merchants beyond traditional online payment processing and toward a comprehensive financial ecosystem.

At the same time, it is preparing to diversify the payment methods it accepts, including through the integration of account-to-account (A2A) solutions such as RoPay, and to expand financing options offered through partners, including merchant cash advance products.

Netopia’s priorities for the coming period include operationalizing its newly licensed activities, developing new financial products, and expanding its technology and operational infrastructure.

“Obtaining the license from the National Bank of Romania validates our security and compliance standards, but more importantly, it provides the foundation on which we are building Netopia’s future. Our vision is to become a comprehensive growth partner for entrepreneurs in Romania,” Raluca Micu, CEO of Netopia, said.

In the medium term, the company aims to build a one-stop shop model for merchants, a unified platform integrating multiple payment methods, rapid funds collection, automated transaction reconciliation, and complementary financial services.

Netopia Payments is a Romanian payments and technology platform for merchants, providing digital payment infrastructure and financial solutions to thousands of companies. Since 2023, private equity fund Innova Capital holds a majority stake in the company.

World.title: Romanian construction company Concelex appoints Daniel Spiridon, Carol Șerban to strategy and transformation roles
World.content:
Romanian construction company Concelex announced it was strengthening its management team by bringing in two professionals with international backgrounds in strategy and transformation.

Daniel Spiridon, with over 20 years’ experience in management consulting and executive leadership, has joined Concelex as Deputy CEO Strategy.

Carol Șerban, a construction engineering graduate with international experience in strategic consulting, has joined as Director of Strategy and Transformation.

The two appointments “support Concelex's current phase of accelerated growth and strengthen the company's capabilities in strategy, organizational transformation, and business development,” the company said.

Daniel Spiridon (in opening photo) spent more than 15 years at McKinsey & Company, where he rose through every stage of his career to become Managing Partner of the local office. He subsequently joined eMAG as VP Business Development and Strategy and, as CEO, led eMAG's operations in Hungary. A graduate in economics, he also holds a Master's degree in International Business and Finance from BI Norwegian Business School. As Deputy CEO Strategy, he will oversee the implementation of Concelex's strategy, develop the Strategy and Transformation function, and be involved in developing and optimizing the company's business portfolio, with the goal of strengthening its competitiveness and profitability.

Carol Șerban

Carol Șerban brings a construction engineering educational background paired with experience in international strategic consulting. A graduate of the Technical University of Civil Engineering Bucharest, he holds a Master's degree in Structural Engineering from the University of Manchester and an MBA from the University of Oxford. He began his career in the UK, where he spent seven years in civil and structural engineering and project management, before joining Kearney's Romania office. He has also held the position of Commercial Director at Glovo Romania. As Director of Strategy and Transformation at Concelex, he will coordinate organizational transformation programs, with a focus on optimizing business processes, accelerating digitalization, and identifying strategic initiatives to support the company's performance.

“Concelex has reached a stage where the scale of the projects we manage and the company’s accelerated growth prospects require us to continuously strengthen our leadership team. Daniel and Carol bring complementary experience and a valuable perspective on how we build, organize, and prepare for the next stage of growth. They are professionals with a solid track record in their fields, and I am confident they will make a significant contribution to Concelex's development in the coming years," Radu Pițurlea, chairman and CEO, Concelex, said.

World.title: Central Romania: Restored castle in Covasna reopens to the public
World.content:
The Miko Castle in the village of Olteni, Covasna County, which has been restored with EU funding, is set to reopen its doors on Saturday, September 5, Agerpres reported.

Built in 1827 by Count Miko Miklos, the castle is notable for the murals discovered on its interior walls during the restoration work. The paintings depict scenes from the social life of the period, as well as scenes from the Napoleonic Wars.

The property was returned to the descendants of Count Miko in 2007. Seven years later, they sold it to the Covasna County Council and the Bodoc Local Council.

The restoration was carried out as part of a project worth approximately RON 20 million, co-financed by EU funds through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The castle will house the Székely Equestrian Museum, a section of the Székely National Museum in Sfântu Gheorghe.

The castle is also set to become part of the Transylvanian Manor Houses Route, one of 12 national cultural tourism routes financed through PNRR, the Covasna County Council said.

The reopening will also be marked by a screening of the Italian film Vita mia, directed by Edoardo Winspeare, which features several scenes filmed inside the castle. Other events for the opening weekend include a tour focusing on the history of the castle, and a guided tour of the Székely Equestrian Museum.

(Photo: Consiliul Județean Covasna)

simona@romania-insider.com

World.title: Swedish man wanted over Stockholm shooting apprehended in Romania
World.content:
Romanian organized crime prosecutors have apprehended a Swedish citizen wanted by authorities in his home country over his alleged involvement in a shooting targeting two people in Stockholm. The suspect had lived in Romania for approximately three years, according to the Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT), as reported by Biziday.ro.

Prosecutors searched two properties in Bucharest and nearby Otopeni as part of an investigation into organized crime and aggravated murder.

According to investigators, several individuals tried to kill two people at a Stockholm address in September 2024. One of them allegedly fired at the building, with bullets passing through the entrance door and entering the home.

DIICOT said the suspect helped those involved in the attack, with his actions considered serious illegal threats aggravated by the use of a firearm.

Swedish authorities issued an arrest warrant for the man. He will be brought before a judge at the Bucharest Court of Appeal, with Romanian and Swedish law enforcement agencies cooperating in the case through Eurojust.

During the searches, authorities seized an air gun, a gas pistol, a bulletproof vest, quantities of plant material, data-storage devices, and bladed weapons.

According to DIICOT, another Swedish citizen suspected of belonging to a rival organized crime group was located in Romania in late July. A Romanian court ordered his detention pending extradition in connection with an alleged conspiracy to commit murder.

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/George Călin)

World.title: Estée Lauder Romania renews SkyTower lease, moves to new office
World.content:
Estée Lauder Romania has extended its lease at Bucharest’s SkyTower for a third time and relocated its headquarters to a newly fitted-out space on the building’s ninth floor. The beauty company has operated from the office tower since 2017.

The announcement did not disclose the duration or financial terms of the renewed lease, nor the size of the new office.

“This extension reflects our commitment to our team and our activities in Romania,” said Adrian Simionescu, country manager of Estée Lauder Romania.

The company also uses SkyTower’s SkyHub and board meeting areas to organize events.

Located in northern Bucharest, SkyTower is owned by Raiffeisen Property Holding International.

The 137-meter building has 37 floors and is Romania’s tallest office tower. Its underground structure extends to a depth of 60 meters and provides parking and storage space.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Romanian tech group Arobs sells Polish subsidiary to WB Electronics
World.content:
Arobs Transilvania Software, one of the largest technology companies listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, has sold its entire stake in Arobs Polska to WB Electronics.

Before the sale, the company acquired the 5.66% stake held by Michal Drogosz, enabling the subsequent transfer to WB Electronics of 100% of the share capital of Arobs Polska, the company said in a filing with the Bucharest Stock Exchange. The filing did not disclose the value of the transaction.

The decision to sell comes as the company pursues a focus on “areas where the group has established capabilities, can leverage international synergies and sees the most relevant growth opportunities.” These areas include software and engineering services for the automotive industry, IoT and telematics, enterprise software, life sciences and travel.

Arobs Polska focuses on developing electronic solutions for satellite applications, giving it a distinct profile compared with the group’s core business lines. Its activity is characterized by extended development cycles, projects carried out predominantly under institutional programs, and specific capital and infrastructure requirements, Arobs explained.

The integration of Arobs Polska into WB Electronics will ensure the continuity of ongoing projects and provide the team with access to an industrial platform and a portfolio of programs suited to the specific nature of its activities, the company said.

The transaction does not affect the current operations of Arobs Transilvania Software.

(Photo: Arobs Facebook Page)

World.title: Romanian court lifts house arrest for mercenary Horațiu Potra in alleged coup plot case
World.content:
Romania’s High Court of Cassation and Justice lifted the house arrest imposed on mercenary Horațiu Potra on Thursday, September 3, allowing him to remain free under judicial supervision while standing trial. The court granted Potra’s appeal against the previous preventive measure, Agerpres reported.

Horațiu Potra is one of the main defendants in a case concerning an alleged plot to destabilize Romania following the annulment of the 2024 presidential election.

The High Court released him from pre-trial detention in mid-June and placed him under house arrest, ordering him to wear an electronic monitoring bracelet. He had been in custody since November 2025, when he was brought back to Romania from Dubai together with his son and nephew.

Prosecutors indicted Potra on charges including attempted actions against the constitutional order, illegal possession of weapons and ammunition, violations of rules governing explosives and pyrotechnic materials, and public incitement. He is being tried alongside 20 alleged members of his mercenary group and former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu.

Prosecutors claim Horațiu Potra and his associates planned to infiltrate protests held after the December 2024 election annulment to provoke unrest and violent confrontations.

According to investigators, Cãlin Georgescu and his associates devised the plan during a meeting at a farm in Ciolpani shortly after the election was annulled. Potra allegedly coordinated efforts to bring a group of mercenaries to Bucharest and escalate the demonstrations into actions capable of destabilizing the constitutional order.

The allegations remain subject to examination by the court, and the defendants are presumed innocent until a final ruling.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea)

World.title: Romania’s 2026-2027 school year begins on September 7
World.content:
Students across Romania will return to classrooms on Monday, September 7, for the start of the 2026-2027 school year. The calendar includes 36 weeks of classes divided into five modules, with five holiday periods between them, Digi24 reported.

The school year officially runs administratively from September 1, 2026, to August 31, 2027, but classes begin on September 7. Each school will determine the timetable for opening-day ceremonies, access for parents, and other activities.

The first module will run until October 23, although no classes will be held on October 5, International Teachers’ Day. The autumn holiday is scheduled from October 24 to November 1.

Students will return for the second module on November 2 and continue classes until December 22. The winter holiday will run from December 23, 2026, to January 10, 2027.

Then, the third module begins on January 11, with its closing date varying by county. Local school inspectorates selected a one-week holiday between February 15 and March 7 after consulting students, parents, and teachers.

Classes will subsequently continue until April 23, followed by the spring holiday from April 24 to May 4. The final module will run from May 5 to June 18, with the summer holiday beginning on June 19 for most students.

Graduating high school students will complete 34 weeks of classes and finish on June 4, while eighth graders will end their 35-week school year on June 11. Most students in technological and vocational education will continue until June 25.

One of the main changes this year affects students entering ninth grade, who will be the first to begin the phased introduction of Romania’s new high school curriculum.

The new school year begins amid continued concerns about access to education, particularly in rural areas. According to Education Ministry data analyzed by the Friedrich Ebert Foundation Romania’s Monitorul Social (Social Monitor) project, only 75.2% of children and young people aged 3 to 23 were enrolled in some form of education in the 2024-2025 school year.

The gross enrolment rate in preschool education stood at 86.3% in 2025, but there was a considerable gap between urban areas, at 98.4%, and rural communities, at 74%. Among three-year-olds in rural areas, the rate was only 60.2%.

The divide was even wider in primary education, where the gross enrolment rate reached 98.5% in urban areas but only 71.5% in rural areas. At lower-secondary level, the corresponding figures were 96% and 65.6%, a gap of more than 30 percentage points and the largest recorded over the past five school years.

The overall gross enrolment rate was 85.1% in primary education, 80.7% at lower-secondary level and 78.6% in high school and vocational education. Monitorul Social said participation generally declines as students advance through the education system, while distance, transport costs and limited nearby options can create additional barriers for rural pupils.

World.title: Serbian, Bosnian Serb Officials Join Hundreds at Ratko Mladic Commemoration
World.content:
The man, who preferred to withhold his name, now lives in the Serbian capital. He decided to come along and pay tribute to Mladic, who he considers a “hero who defended his country” and who, in his view, Serbia “betrayed” when it extradited him to the UN war crimes tribunal in The Hague in 2011.

A large number of people with similar views, mostly men, gathered in front of the Army House before the commemoration began. Some of them were wearing T-shirts depicting Ratko Mladic, with messages expressing support for him.

Three men wearing identical T-shirts stood together and posed for journalists’ photos. As well as an image of Mladic, the shirts bear the phrases often used as a message of support for him: “General, are you afraid of anyone? ‘I fear no one but God.’”

World.title: Serbia’s Vucic Slates EU Condemnation of Mladic Tributes as ‘Stupid’
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled her planned visit to EU candidate state Serbia on Friday, the day after Ratko Mladic’s body was transported on a government plane to Belgrade, where it was met by officials and an army honour guard.

Groups of supporters of the former Bosnian Serb military chief also greeted the motorcade carrying his body into Belgrade with banners praising Mladic, hung from roadway overpasses, with messages such as “Thank you, General” and “Welcome home, General”.

“The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history,” Kos wrote on X.

“The glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built … The values that underpin our common future are not negotiable. In this context, I have decided not to proceed with my planned visit to Serbia at this time,” she added.

Her criticisms have been echoed by ministers from several other EU member states.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic dismissed Kos’s criticism as “extremely brief, but stupid, as usual”.

“‘Glorification’ of General Ratko Mladic, except it doesn’t say who was glorifying anything. And when they can’t find anything concrete, then they deal with underpasses and overpasses [where pro-Mladic banners were displayed]. I suppose we were meant to ban people from showing up, to ban the funeral,” he told the media on Friday.

Mladic’s body was returned to Serbia on Thursday evening on a Serbian government plane.

Ratko Mladic’s son, Darko, confirmed on Friday that the funeral will be held on Monday at the Topcider Cemetery in Belgrade.

Before the funeral, a tribute to Mladic will be held in a church where the coffin will be placed, and on Saturday, a public commemoration will be staged at the Home of the Army of Serbia, in central Belgrade.

Darko Mladic said a procession would be organised on Monday from the church to the cemetery and emphasised that he expects a large turnout.

“This is a people’s funeral, and, as you all know, I do not engage in politics and would not mix politics into this. The only thing I can say is that regarding our requests [to the Hague for Mladic’s conditional release because of illness], of which there were many in the past, President [Vucic] was always there for us, and I would like to publicly thank him for that support in defending General Mladic, which meant a lot to us,” Darko Mladic said.

Neither Darko Mladic nor the Minister of Justice, Nenad Vujic, who was sitting next to him at the press conference, specified whether there would be army or state honours at the funeral.

On August 27, when Mladic died, Vujic initially said Mladic would be buried with state honours. “General Mladic is a general and there are protocols that apply,” he said then.

Mladic held the rank of general in the Yugoslav People’s Army, JNA, during the 1990s but legal experts in Serbia are divided on whether there is any basis for a funeral with state or army honours, given that he was convicted of genocide.

President Vucic has since cast doubt on the idea of a funeral with state honours. Minister Vujic on Friday, when quizzed about state honours, just said that the state would provide all the family was entitled to, out of “respect for the family’s wishes … [and] according to the laws of the state of Serbia”.

Asked whether he will attend the funeral in person, Vucic on Friday pleaded a packed schedule. “I have an official visit from the President of Uzbekistan [Shavkat Mirziyoyev] for the whole day on Monday and Tuesday, scheduled four months ago,” he said.

Several European dignitaries have echoed EU commissioner Kos in criticising the glorification of Mladic.

Belgium’s Foreign Minister, Maxime Prevot, wrote on X on Friday that “it is shameful and disrespectful to the victims and their families to reserve such honours for his funeral.

“It’s a step distancing Serbia from EU’s fundamental values of respect for human dignity, human rights and the fight against impunity – going in the opposite direction of what is expected from a EU candidate country,” Prevot said.

Ireland’s Minister for European Affairs and Defence, Thomas Byrne, told media on Friday that it was “not acceptable” if there were “senior figures from government memorialising that man”.

World.title: Kosovo Charges Serbian Security Officers Over Jashari Compound Massacre
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Blerim Isufaj (C), Chief Prosecutor at the Kosovo Special Prosecution, with prosecutor Valdet Gashi on September 4, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Special Prosecution announced on Friday that it has filed an indictment charging 35 suspects with involvement in the murder of 26 civilians at the compound of Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA commander Adem Jashari in the village of Prekaz in Skenderaj/Srbica in March 1998.

“After years of work, we have succeeded in finalising the investigation into the Prekaz case by filing an indictment. We have managed to substantiate the well-founded suspicion that the accused committed the criminal offence of war crimes against the civilian population – specifically on March 5, 6, and 7, 1998, in the village of Prekaz, more precisely in the Jashari neighbourhood,” prosecutor Valdet Gashi said.

BIRN has seen the indictment which, among others, includes the names of Jovica Stanisic, the former head of the Serbian State Security Service; Vlastimir Djordjevic, a former high-ranking Serbian Interior Ministry official; Sreten Lukic, a wartime head of the Serbian interior ministry’s staff for Kosovo and Milorad ‘Legija’ Ulemek, a former commander of Serbia’s State Security Unit for Special Operations.

“Based on material and testimonial evidence, we have identified 35 accused individuals in this case who held high command positions within the Serbian special police units,” Gashi added.

Serbian police and military forces besieged the Jashari family compound in Prekaz from March 5 to 7, 1998, leaving 59 dead, including the founder of the KLA, Adem Jashari, himself.

The assault caused outrage among Kosovo Albanians and is seen as the incident that encouraged widespread armed resistance against Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic’s regime.

Gashi told media on Friday that the indictment was filed in absentia as the authorities could not secure the presence of the suspects.

Stanisic is currently serving a sentence for war crimes in another case after being convicted by the Hague Tribunal, while Ulemek is in prison for his role in the killing of Serbian Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic. Djordjevic and Lukic have been released after serving war crimes sentences for other crimes.

Chief Special Prosecution Prosecutor Blerim Isufaj highlighted the indictment as “the first one concerning the killing of civilians in the Jashari family compound in Prekaz, Skenderaj”.

In cases concerning war crimes committed during the 1998-99 Kosovo war, legal cooperation between Kosovo and Serbia remains almost non-existent, so it appears unlikely that most of the indictees will be available for trial.

World.title: Serbian President Launches ‘Non-Political’ Podcast as Election Looms
World.content:
Ahead of elections expected in the next few months, Serbia’s head of state has started doing podcasts, while promising to give politics a big miss on his show.

The first episode of Vucic’s PodcAVst aired on Friday at noon on his official YouTube channel. In it, Vucic interviewed the basketball coach Miroslav “Muta” Nikolic, introducing him as a “pal” and a “legend of Serbian basketball”.

“When I was a boy, I applied to become a radio reporter. At the time, my dream was to become a sports commentator or reporter. I didn’t make it – Radio Belgrade rightly rejected me because I had a slight speech impediment,” Vucic reminisced in the introduction.

Vucic said he decided to try the podcast format for a simple reason: to have conversations with successful people.

“I’ve missed having conversations with successful people, with people who are different from me, so that I can learn something from them, gain a different perspective and listen to them, rather than having them listen to me,” he said.

“I’ll try not to be someone who argues or disagrees with guests, but instead to be here to learn as much as possible from people working in completely different fields. And there won’t be a single word about politics,” he added.

During the interview, Vucic and Nikolic spoke about basketball strategies, teams, players and coaches. They also reminisced about Vucic’s own sports efforts and his brother Andrej’s life.

Since the podcast premiered live, it had a live chat filled with supportive comments like “Serbia Wins” and “Serbia United”, and emojis including the Serbian flag, a wolf, hearts and flexed biceps. Some presented opposing views, however, such as “The students will win against Vucic”, referencing the wave of student-led protests against his government.

By launching his own podcast, Vucic is following a trend already embraced by political figures in the region, notably Albania’s Edi Rama with his weekly “Flasim” (“Let’s Talk”) podcast, as well as politicians further afield, such as California Governor Gavin Newsom and US Senator Ted Cruz. It has not been announced when Vucic’s next show will be aired.

The podcast’s launch comes amid Vucic’s already extensive presence in traditional media ahead of nationwide elections expected to be held in the coming months.

According to Serbian election watchdog CRTA, by August 18 he had made 64 live television appearances that month, already surpassing his previous monthly record of 61, set in March 2025.

World.title: Week in Review: Ghosts and Guns
World.content:
Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic died in The Hague at the age of 84 on August 27, having spent his final years serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. BIRN covered the death of Mladic extensively, with profiles, features, analyses and opinion articles.

Mladic’s death has shown just how far the former Bosnian Serb military chief’s legacy extends beyond the judgments that established his responsibility for some of the worst atrocities of the Bosnian war.

Across Bosnia’s mainly Serb Republika Srpska entity, Mladic supporters took to the streets, lit candles and publicly celebrated Mladic, including in towns where his forces committed crimes, while politicians in both Bosnia and Serbia joined in paying tribute. For genocide survivors, the sight of young people who may not even have been born during the war glorifying Mladic was particularly disturbing, proving that nationalist narratives have passed to another generation.

The reactions have also prompted deeper questions about what justice has achieved. Former Hague Tribunal intern Ahmet Gumusbas observed that Mladic’s conviction established criminal responsibility and an authoritative record of the crimes, but could never end disputes over memory and denial. Journalist Kristina Ljevak Bajramovic reflected on the gulf between Mladic, who was able to grow old, and the thousands of his victims who were denied that chance.

In Serbia, meanwhile, Youth Initiative for Human Rights director Sofija Todorovic argued that official tributes to Mladic demonstrate how the glorification of convicted war criminals has become embedded in Serbia’s politics, media and public life.
