World.title: Rights activist Siranush Sahakyan: ‘Lives of all Armenians held in Baku are in danger’
World.content:
Trials of Armenian prisoners in Baku

“The lives of all Armenians held in Baku are in danger. They may even express views that are contrary to their own will,” Siranush Sahakyan, who represents the interests of Armenian prisoners at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), told a news conference.

She said this was also reflected in statements dictated to the prisoners. Many of those who have returned to Armenia told human rights activists that they had signed documents under torture that “in no way reflected the information known to them”.

At the same time, Sahakyan said some prisoners express their views while “being prepared to face the consequences”. She specifically referred to statements from prison by Ruben Vardanyan, Davit Babayan and Davit Ishkhanyan.

“We should be cautious and attentive when analysing these statements. We need to understand whether they were dictated by the authorities in Baku or reflect the prisoners’ free will, because we cannot rule out coercion under torture. Those making these statements are simply in a situation where they have no choice. They are forced to make a statement under threat of reprisals,” the rights activist said.

Responding to questions from Armenian journalists, Sahakyan commented on the trials of Armenian prisoners held in Azerbaijan, described the conditions in which they are being held and detailed alleged violations of their rights.

According to official figures, 19 Armenian prisoners are being held in Baku, including former leaders of the self-proclaimed Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. On 5 February, an Azerbaijani court sentenced former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, deputy commander Davit Manukyan, parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and Foreign Minister Davit Babayan to life imprisonment. Former presidents Arkadi Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison. The lighter sentences for the two former presidents were attributed to their age. Under Azerbaijani law, people over the age of 65 cannot be sentenced to life imprisonment. The case of former State Minister Ruben Vardanyan was heard separately from those of the other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders. On 17 February, he was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Baku pursues ‘hostage diplomacy’

“The release of the prisoners requires, first and foremost, a political decision, since their detention itself was linked to the conflict,” Siranush Sahakyan said.

Siranush Sahakyan

She argues that resolving the conflict entails an obligation to release the detainees.

At the same time, she believes Azerbaijan is using the prisoners to pursue what she described as “hostage diplomacy”, treating them as a bargaining tool in the conflict settlement process.

According to the lawyer, this applies particularly to the former Karabakh leaders: “Holding them is particularly valuable in terms of hostage diplomacy.”

Charges not supported by any evidence

The representative of the Armenian prisoners at the European Court of Human Rights has not been able to examine the judgments in the cases of 15 of them.

“We only have an extract containing information about the charges and the sentences handed down to those convicted; it is not the full text,” she said.

However, she has access to the indictment and an English translation of the judgment in the case of former State Minister Ruben Vardanyan. The document runs to 3,302 pages.

Sahakyan has studied it and believes it demonstrates an unprecedented violation of the defendant’s rights:

“The entire trial was a farce and its outcome is illegitimate. We have submitted our arguments to the ECHR. Ruben Vardanyan’s case has already been assigned a number and will be considered by the court.”

According to the rights activist, the Azerbaijani authorities, “using an unknown methodology”, calculated the number of victims and declared that more than 18,000 people had been killed during the years of the conflict:

“And because Ruben Vardanyan joined this criminal organisation [meaning the NKR and its leadership] in 2022 and took up a position there, Vardanyan himself is held responsible for all these lives.”

The lawyer says Ruben Vardanyan is accused of crimes that have nothing to do with his activities or reality.

Moreover, according to her, the Baku court regarded the following as “criminal activity”:

implementing various social and charitable programmes in Karabakh,

renovating schools and kindergartens,

funding a large joint wedding for 250 couples.

His Aurora Humanitarian Initiative was also deemed to constitute activity linked to “terrorism”, while award recipients who visited Karabakh were described as members of a “criminal organisation”.

The Aurora Humanitarian Initiative is an international philanthropic project established on behalf of the survivors of the Armenian genocide of the early 20th century. Its founders are Ruben Vardanyan, Vartan Gregorian and Noubar Afeyan. They described the initiative as a gesture of gratitude to all those who sought to save the victims of the tragedy. Each year, the Aurora Prize is awarded to individuals and organisations that have “dedicated themselves to saving human lives and advancing humanitarian causes”.

“For example, one of the laureates is an Iraqi citizen. His receipt of a [monetary] award was classified as financing Iraqi Kurdish mercenaries,” Sahakyan said.

She stressed that Vardanyan’s case goes beyond the fate of one individual. In her view, it concerns the right to a fair trial, the quality of justice and the protection of fundamental human rights and democratic principles.

“The professional community has serious work ahead of it. It must not allow charges and convictions that have no evidentiary basis to become a precedent and standard practice,” the lawyer said.

Prisoners are isolated from outside world

The rights activist stressed that the Armenian prisoners held in Baku have no contact with the outside world:

“They do not see their relatives, consular officials, independent doctors, independent lawyers or representatives of the ICRC. In short, they are being held in conditions of complete isolation from the outside world.”

According to Sahakyan, their only means of communicating with family members is by telephone:

“However, all calls are monitored and permitted at the authorities’ discretion. Depending on their content, they may be forcibly terminated. The permitted frequency of calls also varies. For example, three prisoners are allowed to make a call once every 40 days, while the others are allowed to call once a week. The duration of calls also varies: two minutes, three minutes and, in some cases, 10 minutes.”

Some prisoners suffered fractures after beatings

According to Sahakyan, in recent months the prisoners have frequently spoken during telephone calls about health problems and a lack of medical care:

“After a certain hour, there are no medical staff at the facility. If emergency care is needed, there is no possibility of providing it. At most, they may be given medication to relieve certain symptoms.”

There have also been documented cases of prisoners suffering fractures as a result of beatings. The lawyer said she had information about which prisoners had sustained fractures but could not disclose their names.

Alleged torture over religious symbols

According to Siranush Sahakyan, religion also plays a role in the treatment of the prisoners, with such cases documented in international reports:

“Those who had cross tattoos had them burned, with the crosses removed from their skin through torture.”

She also said that although prisoners had been allowed a limited number of books, they were not permitted to receive copies of the Bible.

“There have been cases, which we have documented, in which they were forced to read the Koran,” the rights activist said.

Proposal by Ruben Vardanyan’s wife

Veronika Zonabend, the wife of former State Minister Ruben Vardanyan, has proposed creating an international women’s humanitarian delegation to travel to Baku in September. Zonabend hopes that a group of female human rights activists, under the auspices of Azerbaijan’s ombudsman, will be allowed to visit the Armenian prisoners and deliver personal belongings, photographs and letters to them.

However, it remains unclear whether the visit to Azerbaijan will take place. The proposal is currently being discussed with the Armenian authorities.

Sahakyan explained that because of visa requirements, security considerations and procedures governing access to prisons, the project could not be carried out as a private initiative.

Representatives of the relevant Armenian agencies have already met Veronika Zonabend and Vardanyan’s defence team.

“We have not yet received an official response. The matter is still under discussion,” Siranush Sahakyan said.

World.title: Drug for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to become available in Georgia early next week
World.content:
Givinostat for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to arrive in Georgia

According to Georgian Health Minister Mikheil Sarjveladze, the drug givinostat, used to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy, will arrive in Georgia early next week. He said all the necessary preparations have already been completed so that doctors can begin using the drug in the country as soon as possible.

“Today we have another piece of good news: we have received confirmation that the drug givinostat has been sent to Georgia by air mail. This means the medicine will arrive in Tbilisi by the beginning of next week.

We have carried out extensive preparations together with Italfarmaco. In particular, we have recorded patient data with the utmost accuracy, created a dedicated registry, approved the relevant regulations, and had foreign specialists train doctors. Everything is now ready to start using the drug in practice as soon as possible,” Sarjveladze said.

He said parents can call the ministry’s hotline for information and advice on how the medicine will be used.

Sarjveladze also spoke about another drug for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The ministry has been negotiating with its manufacturer in parallel with the talks on givinostat. The minister said he hoped the two sides would sign an agreement within days.

The drug in question is Elevidys, which doctors use to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

“In this case, I would like to share some good news with the public: we have completed negotiations on all the key commercial issues. We have already prepared and issued all the necessary legal acts on our side and confirmed that we are fully ready to sign the agreement.

We are now waiting for the company’s response and are confident that we will sign the procurement agreement for this medicine within days.

It is worth noting that the negotiations took longer than expected. This was mainly because of our firm position that we must clearly define and insure the responsibilities and obligations of the relevant parties regarding the quality of the medicine,” Sarjveladze explained.

The minister also thanked the parents of children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy for their active involvement in the process.

Background

On 31 July, Sarjveladze announced that the government would purchase givinostat for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

Parents of children with the condition first met Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze on 3 June. After a second meeting on 4 June, Kobakhidze announced the creation of a working group to address the supply of the medicines the children need.

After the meeting, the parents said the authorities had agreed to provide the medicines. They expected two specific drugs to arrive in Georgia in about two months.

On 8 July, after meeting Health Minister Mikheil Sarjveladze, the parents said negotiations on making one of the drugs available in Georgia had reached the final stage. They added that they would announce details of the talks on the second drug the following week.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a rare genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and muscle damage. It mainly affects boys, with symptoms usually appearing in early childhood. As the disease progresses, it can also affect the respiratory and heart muscles. There is currently no cure, but treatment can slow the progression of the disease.

Givinostat for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to arrive in Georgia

World.title: Abkhazia to review how effectively agricultural grants are being spent
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to review how agricultural grants have been spent. President Badra Gunba has ordered the government to return to the budget any money spent on ineffective projects.

The grants come from the Agriculture Ministry’s “Agricultural Development for 2025” programme and the Economy Ministry’s programme supporting small and medium-sized businesses.

The president’s decision to review how the grants are used was most likely prompted by numerous complaints from farmers on social media, who say the government is providing little or no support to actual producers.

Badra Gunba does not rule out some violations given the large amount of funding involved.

“If violations are found — and with such a huge amount of funding, they are bound to occur — we must respond to them. But most importantly, we should not simply punish those responsible. We must make sure they compensate the state for all the costs it has incurred and return the money to the budget,” the president said.

The opposition media outlet Respublika believes that the president’s decision to order law enforcement agencies to set up an interagency group to oversee state support programmes for small and medium-sized businesses can only mean one thing: something is clearly wrong with these programmes.

“It looks like someone has already decided to make a tidy profit from state support for entrepreneurs. Now law enforcement agencies have several options:

simply scare them so they stop stealing;

investigate what they have already managed to steal;

or get in on the deal themselves.

Which option do you think they will choose?” Respublika asks, making it clear that it believes the answer is obvious.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Agriculture in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian businessman Elizbarashvili charged over alleged threats
World.content:
Elizbarashvili charged with making threats

Prosecutors have charged businessman and animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who is known for his outspoken criticism of the government, with making threats. He is accused of an offence under Article 151, Part 1 of the Criminal Code, which carries a maximum prison sentence of one year.

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Lekso Svimonishvili, seven alleged victims are involved in the case. Prosecutors say Elizbarashvili threatened them and that they regarded the threats as genuine.

Svimonishvili said his client categorically rejected the charges and maintained that he was completely innocent.

What do investigators accuse Elizbarashvili of?

According to the Georgian Prosecutor’s Office, an investigation by the Interior Ministry established that at around 2340 on 30 August, Tamaz Elizbarashvili and one of the alleged victims encountered each other by chance at a restaurant in Tbilisi. A verbal altercation broke out over a comment Elizbarashvili had previously posted on social media about the individual and his family.

According to investigators, during the altercation Elizbarashvili threatened the alleged victim and the people accompanying him. In particular, he allegedly said he would not let the matter rest and would return in about 30 minutes, while demanding that they remain at the restaurant.

“Since the alleged victims knew that Tamaz Elizbarashvili possessed a weapon that could be used against them, they had reasonable grounds to fear for their lives and safety and therefore decided to leave the restaurant.

At around 0020, Tamaz Elizbarashvili returned to the scene intending to carry out his threat. He was armed and attempted to enter the restaurant, conspicuously keeping his hand on a weapon tucked into his waistband. He also continued to threaten and insult the alleged victims. Those who had not managed to leave and remained near the restaurant had reasonable grounds to fear that the threat would be carried out.

Despite being barred by security staff, Tamaz Elizbarashvili nevertheless entered the restaurant premises. After establishing that the alleged victims were no longer there, he left,” the Prosecutor’s Office said.

What does the lawyer say?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, prosecutors cite comments previously made by the businessman on social media as the reason for the confrontation. However, the defence says the indictment makes no mention of any personal conflict between Elizbarashvili and the alleged victims.

“Mr Tamaz does not admit guilt, and his account of what happened is radically different [from the one presented]. During the incident, he left his wife and children at home to shield them from any potential confrontation and returned alone, believing that if anyone had questions, they could put them to him in person. However, no-one was there when he arrived,” Svimonishvili said.

The case materials also refer to a firearm, although Elizbarashvili denies possessing one illegally. According to his lawyer, he has not at this stage been charged with the illegal acquisition, possession or carrying of a firearm.

Svimonishvili said the only firearm seized during a search of Elizbarashvili’s apartment was officially registered in his name and had been sent for forensic examination.

The defence will ask the court not to impose any pre-trial restrictions on Elizbarashvili. Alternatively, the lawyer will request that he be released on bail.

Prosecutors have not yet specified what pre-trial measure they will ask the court to impose.

Background

On 1 September 2026, Elizbarashvili was placed under administrative arrest for allegedly failing to comply with a lawful police order. His arrest followed searches of his car and home conducted as part of an investigation launched under Articles 151 (threats) and 236 (illegal acquisition, possession and carrying of firearms) of the Criminal Code.

Elizbarashvili said the complaint against him had been filed by employees of the Imedi TV channel, with whom he had a verbal altercation at a restaurant on 30 August. He alleged that the Imedi employees had initiated the confrontation and threatened him over his political views.

World.title: Ex-Georgian PM questioned in prison over his statements on a human rights defender who died by suicide
World.content:
Georgia: Gharibashvili questioned in Jorbenadze case

As part of the ongoing investigation into the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, law enforcement officers questioned former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili at Prison No. 12 in Rustavi on September 3.

Jorbenadze had publicly criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. Gharibashvili recently published a letter expressing doubts about the officially stated cause of the human rights defender’s death — suicide.

Following several hours of questioning, prosecutor Medea Tsiramua and Gharibashvili’s lawyer, Natia Tamazashvili, spoke to journalists.

Former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in January 2026 for legalising illicit income on a particularly large scale. He pleaded guilty and reached a plea deal with the prosecution. On August 24, he was charged with a second offence — accepting a particularly large bribe. Gharibashvili denies the new charge.

What the lawyer and prosecutor said

How it started. On September 1, 2026, Irakli Gharibashvili published another letter from prison on social media, calling on government officials to answer questions about the true circumstances of Lazare Jorbenadze’s death. Gharibashvili pointed out that Jorbenadze, a former human rights defender, had criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze in an article by journalist Dito Chubinidze and died by suicide shortly after its publication. Gharibashvili also noted that the newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, where the article was published, had publicly questioned the suicide theory.

According to the prosecution, Gharibashvili’s public suspicions about the circumstances of Jorbenadze’s death have no direct factual basis. The prosecutor said the former prime minister provided investigators with no new or significant information.

She said the questioning showed that Gharibashvili was neither a direct witness to Jorbenadze’s death nor someone with specific information about it.

“Gharibashvili’s public letters were based solely on information from various publications, rather than any specific facts. He categorically stated that he has no specific information about Lazare Jorbenadze’s suicide,” prosecutor Medea Tsiramua said.

Gharibashvili’s lawyer, Natia Tamazashvili, who is his wife’s sister, said the former prime minister’s questions arose after he read specific publications while in prison and later learned of Jorbenadze’s death.

“His questions arose after he was sent a letter containing an article by journalist Dito Chubinidze in Asaval-Dasavali. The article was critical of Irakli Kobakhidze. Gharibashvili later learned about Jorbenadze’s death, put the facts together and raised questions publicly. During the questioning, he repeated the same questions he had raised in his public letter,” the lawyer said.

According to the defence, Gharibashvili was not trying to provide investigators with previously unknown sources or information. His questions were based on suspicions about a possible connection between the articles published in the media and Jorbenadze’s sudden death.

Series of interrogations in the Lazare Jorbenadze case

Before Gharibashvili was questioned, politicians and public figures were questioned at the Digomi police headquarters in Tbilisi. They were asked about the former prime minister’s letter published on social media.

Investigators questioned Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the opposition coalition For Change, analyst Gia Khukhashvili and several activists.

Gvaramia said he had no information about the details of the case and knew only what had been published on social media.

Opposition politicians Khatia Dekanoidze and Tazo Datunashvili, as well as journalist Nanuka Zhorzholiani, refused to appear for questioning at the police station. They told investigators they would give evidence only in court, in the presence of a magistrate judge.

World.title: ‘If Russia decides to withdraw its military base, we will not object’ – Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on the withdrawal of Russia’s military base from Armenia.

“If Russia decides to withdraw its military base from Armenia, we will not object. But if they want to stay, we are ready to discuss that too,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during his regular weekly briefing.

He also said Yerevan does not consider the presence of Russia’s 102nd military base in Armenia vital.

Putin raised the issue after his meeting with Pashinyan in Bishkek, although the Armenian prime minister says they did not discuss the issue either during those talks or before them. Putin said:

“If Armenia believes that Russia’s military base is not needed in Armenia, we will leave tomorrow if necessary. Is Armenia ready for that? Fine, we will not impose anything on anyone. But if the Armenian people want some kind of Russian military ‘wing’ there, we will stay. We will work and cooperate.”

Pashinyan also commented at the briefing on the issues he discussed with Putin in Bishkek. In particular, he once again explained Armenia’s position on its membership in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union, Russia’s concession to operate Armenia’s railways and the construction of a new nuclear power plant.

Armenia cannot be forced to hold a referendum

“And who said that all EAEU member states swore allegiance and would remain members of the EAEU for their entire existence?”

That was Pashinyan’s answer to a question about Armenia’s membership in the Russian-led EAEU. He gave it among the first answers at the briefing. The issue also dominated the open part of the Pashinyan-Putin talks.

For several months, Russia has been calling at various levels for Armenia to hold a referendum on membership of the EAEU or the European Union. The Russian president also insisted on this at the meeting in Bishkek.

“The adoption of the law to begin Armenia’s accession to another organisation amounts to a declaration that it is leaving ours,”* Putin said.

Pashinyan explained to the Russian president, and repeated at the briefing, that under the union’s charter, a country must give six months’ notice before ending its membership. However, Armenia has no such intention for now.

He said he continues to explain this to his Russian partners, trying to make Armenia’s position “clearer and more acceptable”.

One journalist who raised the issue described Putin’s tone towards Pashinyan as “harsh”. He said Moscow was taking a tough line and forcing Yerevan to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenia’s prime minister replied:

“I am also giving the Russian president a tough choice. I say: this cannot continue, the issue of the railway concession must be resolved. Why is there no headline saying ‘Pashinyan gives Russian president a tough choice’?”

Pashinyan himself believes Armenian media do not use such headlines because the country still follows the “logic of subordination to the Central Committee of the USSR”. In his view, that logic produces the following reaction: “They called from Moscow, we urgently need to bring out the cognac.”

At the same time, the prime minister stressed his position: Armenia cannot be forced to hold a referendum.

He said the country’s Constitution requires a referendum before joining a supranational organisation. However, Armenia should hold one only when the issue “is ripe”. This would mean, in particular, when Armenia applies for EU membership or at least sets out its roadmap. Holding a referendum before that, he argued, would mean asking citizens to go to polling stations before anyone has formulated the question or decided what answers they can choose.

Selling the railway concession is the best solution

Pashinyan said he discussed the future of South Caucasus Railway with Putin. This issue is, incidentally, more important to the Armenian side. For a long time, Armenia’s authorities have been telling their Russian partners that the country is losing its competitive advantage in developing regional railway links because Russia controls the Armenian railway.

Since 2008, the company South Caucasus Railway has operated Armenia’s railway under a concession agreement. Russian Railways owns 100% of the company. The agreement grants the concession for 30 years. However, since 2008, freight traffic on Armenia’s railways has halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the investment commitments have remained unfulfilled.

The Armenian prime minister therefore proposed selling the concession to a third country that is friendly to both Armenia and Russia. Russian partners described the proposal as “strange and largely unacceptable”.

However, Pashinyan said the following about the outcome of his meeting with Putin:

“We reached an understanding that the current situation cannot continue for much longer. We need to resolve this issue somehow. Both Armenia and Russia understand that one possible solution would be to sell the concession rights to a third party acceptable to both Armenia and Russia. Frankly, I think this is the best solution. The other options seem unrealistic.”».

Moscow to present proposals for building a new nuclear power plant

According to Pashinyan, Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev will visit Armenia in September.

“He will present Armenia with proposals on what Russia can offer today for the construction of a new nuclear power plant. I have already said that we do not see the nuclear power plant as a geopolitical choice. We need the best value for money. We will go with whoever makes the best offer,” the prime minister said.

He said Armenia would consider all possible options, whether a small modular reactor proposed by Western partners or a conventional Russian nuclear power plant:

“We have never said that the Russian proposal cannot be the best one, including in terms of modular reactors. It is not the case that Russia has no proposal for modular reactors. However, there are a number of important factors: the price, the payback period, the construction time and the financing arrangements.”

Nikol Pashinyan said work on the issue had intensified and that Armenia should make a decision within a year.

He said Armenia initially favoured a small modular reactor, but “desire is one thing and reality is another”.

The problem is that experts are concerned about the lack of experience in building modular nuclear power plants and the potential risks.

According to the prime minister, if there are no operating or licensed modular nuclear power plants anywhere in the world when Armenia makes its decision, this will create “uncertainty” and make the decision very difficult.

At the same time, he said work was continuing to extend the operating life of the existing Metsamor nuclear power plant beyond 2036.

No plans to introduce visas for Russian citizens

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that “if Armenia suddenly introduces visas as well, it will not introduce them against us — it will introduce them against its own citizens”. She also said the move would affect Russian citizens who have relatives in Armenia.

Importantly, no one in Armenia had suggested introducing a visa regime for Russian citizens before her statement.

“We have absolutely no such intention, and never have. It has never even crossed our minds. We are very happy to welcome tourists from Russia. We can see that they have now become very active in promoting Armenia’s tourism attractions. Society also welcomes these people. And they themselves seem to feel quite comfortable in Armenia. We are happy to have them, just as we are happy to welcome tourists from other countries,” the prime minister said.

Pashinyan on the withdrawal of Russia’s military base from Armenia

World.title: Georgian politicians questioned after ex-prime minister’s claims about Lazare Jorbenadze’s death
World.content:
Death of Georgian human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze

Georgian politicians have been summoned for questioning over public statements by former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili about the death of Lazare Jorbenadze.

According to the Georgian Prosecutor’s Office, investigators have confirmed the suicide theory without ambiguity following investigative work into Jorbenadze’s death on 4 April 2026 and interviews with members of his family.

Nevertheless, because convicted former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili and others have made public statements about the case, investigators will question several political figures further: Irakli Garibashvili himself, Nika Gvaramia, Irma Inashvili, Nanuka Zhorzholiani, Khatia Dekanoidze, Tazo Datunashvili, Gia Khukhashvili, Giorgi Liluashvili, Zaza Davitaia and Ermile Nemsadze.

What happened

On 1 September 2026, former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili published another letter from prison. He called on the authorities to answer questions about the circumstances surrounding the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, a human rights defender who had criticised Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

Garibashvili writes that Jorbenadze died by suicide shortly after journalist Dito Chubinidze published an article based on an interview with him.

The newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, which published the interview, questioned the suicide theory. In his letter, Garibashvili stresses that the public should receive an answer about the true cause of Jorbenadze’s death.

The former prime minister says he decided to speak publicly about the issue after comparing the contents of a letter he received from government representatives in February with other circumstances.



Lazare Jorbenadze

According to Garibashvili, on 12 February, officials acting on the instructions of Irakli Kobakhidze and Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze gave him an article that the newspaper Asaval-Dasavali had published on 2 February 2026.

The article featured a conversation between Dito Chubinidze and Lazare Jorbenadze. Garibashvili says it focused mainly on criticism of Kobakhidze and serious allegations against him.

The former prime minister says the message he received suggested that he was behind the article. “I received a message expressing the suspicion — based on a completely false assumption — that I was behind the article in question,” Garibashvili writes.

Garibashvili says he categorically rejected the accusation and told government representatives that he had never engaged in publishing “commissioned articles”.

What do politicians say?

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, said she would appear in court to testify in the Lazare Jorbenadze case. She said Bidzina Ivanishvili bears responsibility for the system he created, so investigators should question him as well.

“Bidzina Ivanishvili created a system in which people fight for positions and money, testify against each other, fabricate cases and, of course, are deeply involved in corruption. That is why Bidzina Ivanishvili, Kobakhidze, Mdinaradze and everyone who fabricates all sorts of dirt for money should be summoned for questioning. As for the investigation itself, I have made my position clear: I will go to court,” Dekanoidze said.

Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili said he did not understand why authorities had summoned him for questioning in the Lazare Jorbenadze death case, as he had made no specific statements about Jorbenadze and only learned of his existence after his death.

“I only learned of Jorbenadze’s existence after his death. I did not comment specifically on the situation involving Jorbenadze. I spoke more broadly about suicide cases that raise questions. Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze should be here instead of me, because Garibashvili named them, but they are not being summoned — I am. And now this has turned into nothing more than a tragicomedy,” Khukhashvili commented.

According to Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, investigators did not ask him about any other subjects during his questioning in the Jorbenadze death case. Gvaramia believes the case may serve two purposes: one could be political propaganda, while the other could involve bringing new charges against the former prime minister.

“The next step, I am sure, will be to bring new charges against Garibashvili, under the article concerning illegal wiretapping. As far as I know, investigators are currently questioning him in prison. Mdinaradze and Kobakhidze should themselves be concerned about such allegations if they are true, although Garibashvili should also provide further explanations,” Gvaramia said after the questioning.

Death of Georgian human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze

World.title: Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?
World.content:
Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

In Azerbaijan, the authorities have raised the income threshold for classifying families as low-income. It would be logical to expect this to increase both the number of people receiving assistance and the amount of support they receive. However, official statistics show the opposite trend: both the number of families receiving targeted state social assistance and the amount paid per person are falling.

According to the State Statistics Committee, as of 1 July, 349,300 people from 78,900 families received targeted social assistance. A year earlier, the system covered 353,300 people from 80,300 families. This means that over the year, the number of families receiving assistance fell by 1,400, while the number of recipients fell by 4,000.

The decline becomes even more striking over the longer term. In mid-2017, 498,400 people received this type of assistance. Over nine years, that figure fell by 149,100, or about 30%. Meanwhile, the country’s population increased during the same period.

These figures raise an important question: have the incomes of low-income families increased enough for them to no longer need social assistance, or has the system stopped reaching some people who still need support?

The income threshold has risen, but social assistance has fallen

Targeted social assistance is not a fixed payment. The authorities calculate it as the difference between the needs-based threshold for all family members and the family’s average monthly income. The calculation takes into account income from the previous 12 months.

In 2025, the needs-based threshold stood at 285 manats (approx. $167.65) per person. In 2026, the authorities raised it to 300 manats (approx. $176.50), an increase of 5.3%. Despite this, the average payment per person fell from 100.37 to 97.94 manats (approx. $59 to $57.70). In nominal terms, the payment fell by 2.43 manats (approx. $1.43), or 2.4%.

Applying the current formula to the average figures suggests that the system calculated recipients’ average monthly income per person at 184.63 manats (approx. $108.60) in 2025 and 202.06 manats (approx. $118.90) in 2026. This represents a nominal increase of 9.4%. Mathematically, the lower payments reflect the fact that, according to the system’s calculations, family incomes grew faster than the needs-based threshold.

However, these figures do not prove that the financial situation of all low-income families has improved. The average for families that remained in the system in mid-2026 is being compared with the average for families that received assistance a year earlier. Families whose payments stopped or whose applications were rejected no longer form part of the new average.

Our calculations, based on official data, show that total monthly payments to recipients fell from about 35.46 million (approx. $20.86 million) to 34.21 million manats (approx. $20.12 million). The government therefore reduced its monthly spending on this group by about 1.25 million manats (approx. $735,300), or 3.5%, in nominal terms.

The assistance has lost even more purchasing power

According to July 2026 data, annual inflation stood at 5.8%, while food inflation reached 7.3%. After taking price rises into account, the purchasing power of the 97.94-manat payment fell by about 7.8% compared with the 100.37-manat payment a year earlier. If we consider only food price increases, the decline approaches 9%.

After receiving assistance, the system brings a family’s calculated income per person up to the needs-based threshold of 300 manats. However, this represents only a 5.3% increase from last year’s level of 285 manats. That increase falls short of overall inflation and especially of food price growth. As a result, even the minimum income of families that remain in the social assistance system has not increased in real terms.

The number of people receiving assistance is not the number of people living in poverty

The State Statistics Committee’s final data for 2025 put the poverty line at 286 manats (approx. $168.20) and the poverty rate at 5.2%. With a population of 10.26 million, this amounts to roughly 534,000 people.

At the end of the same year, 336,000 people received targeted social assistance, or about 3.3% of the population. The authorities use different methodologies and reporting dates to calculate these figures, so we cannot directly compare them. Nevertheless, the gap of about 198,000 people clearly shows that the number of assistance recipients cannot serve as a measure of poverty in the country.

Moreover, earning less than 300 manats does not in itself qualify a person for assistance. Under the rules, a family must show that factors beyond its control have caused its low income. The official criteria allow authorities to reject an application if the family owns or uses a car, has two properties of the same type at different addresses, or has carried out purchase or sale transactions worth more than 12 times the subsistence minimum over the previous 12 months. Authorities can also reject an application if an able-bodied family member has turned down two suitable job offers.

Based on the 2026 subsistence minimum, the threshold for purchase and sale transactions stands at 3,600 manats (approx. $2,118). Authorities can also reject assistance if a family spends 45 manats (approx. $26.50) or more per person each month on utilities and communications. For a family of four, that amounts to 180 manats (approx. $106) in total. The authorities also count money and gifts from relatives, as well as estimated income from a household farm or garden, when calculating family income.

These criteria may help identify hidden income and assets. However, the same rules can exclude a family with a low cash income if it owns an old car, faces high utility bills or mainly survives on financial support from relatives.

The number of pensioners is falling, while more people receive age-related benefits

Another question arises when we examine other social security figures. On 1 July 2025, Azerbaijan had 1,103,300 pensioners. A year later, the figure had fallen to 1.1 million. At the same time, the average pension rose by 10.5% to 594.4 manats (approx. $350). However, the number of pensioners fell by 3,300.

Meanwhile, the number of people who do not qualify for a labour pension but receive a 220-manat age-related benefit (approx. $130) rose from 166,200 to 177,500. We cannot say that the changes in these two groups involve the same people. However, the fall in the number of pensioners as the elderly population grows, alongside the rise in recipients of a lower benefit, requires a separate explanation in terms of access to labour pensions.

What data the government should disclose

To treat a decline in the number of assistance recipients as evidence of falling poverty, we need more than one headline figure. The Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population should report how many families entered the system over the past year, how many stopped receiving assistance, how many applicants faced rejection and why authorities rejected their applications.

The government should also report how many families failed to qualify under each criterion, including car ownership, purchase and sale transactions, utility costs, discrepancies in income data and refusal to accept an offered job. It should also disclose how many decisions authorities reviewed following complaints and what share of assistance recipients are children.

Without this data, we cannot conclude that poverty has fallen. So far, the official statistics show only this: the number of people covered by targeted social assistance has fallen, the average payment has declined in nominal terms, and its purchasing power has fallen even further.

Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

World.title: Man in Nepal tunnel and woman rescued 10 days after flash flood
World.content:
Rescuers in Nepal have rescued two more survivors, 10 days after devastating floods hit the country.

The man and woman were freed in separate operations on Saturday, local time, with teams continuing the search for thousands of missing people.

A Chinese man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country's prime minister's office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project.

Two Nepalese workers were rescued on Friday.

Lu Haitao is the third person pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. (AP: Nepal Army)

Nepal's army said a joint rescue team of Nepali military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre tunnel and that he was undergoing a health assessment.

Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight.

A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man, called Lu Haitao, out of the tunnel.

CCTV shared audio of Mr Lu talking to an officer, saying how he repeatedly shouted whenever he saw the rescue crews' lights, but they could not hear him.

"When they rescued me today, when they shone [the light] before my eyes, I couldn't believe it," he said.

Mr Lu was taken to a hospital and was in stable condition, according to CCTV.

Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.

Specialised rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.

Woman's rescue 'has given hope to the entire nation'

A damaged residential building along the swollen Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district. (AP: Rajesh Kumar Singh)

In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman named Chandika Kumari Shrestha was rescued alive from a house, Nepal's army spokesperson said Saturday.

Officials said she was airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said Ms Shrestha's rescue "has given hope to the entire nation".

Images released by Nepal's army showed rescuers finding the woman covered in mud inside the damaged house.

They gave her bottled water before pulling her to safety, wrapped in a grey blanket.

At least 1,300 people were killed in the August 26 floods — which were likely caused by a glacier collapse — and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

The United Nations has warned that the "magnitude of the destruction" makes delivering aid an immense challenge, as it launched a $US50 million ($69 million) appeal to help more than 84,000 people affected by the disaster.

On Saturday, the Nepali government released a provisional damage assessment, saying more than 7,500 houses, 48 public buildings and about 100 bridges had been destroyed.

With morgues overflowing, about 1,030 bodies have been buried in mass graves after having DNA samples taken for future identification, Nepal Police said on Saturday.

In a sign of progress, a team was able to reach the remote Nepal-China international border crossing at Timure in Rasuwa district on Saturday.

They placed Nepal's flag at the location, the prime minister said.

"After three days of continuous efforts, Nepal's national flag has been reinstalled along the Nepali border," he said on Facebook.

"It was extremely difficult to identify the border from the Nepali side and erect the flag."

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

AP/AFP

World.title: Mother feared 'failing' baby after months of inconsistent advice postpartum
World.content:
Maddy Barrett wanted more than anything to feel "empowered" enough to make informed decisions after becoming a first-time mother.

But after receiving inconsistent advice from multiple practitioners while struggling to breastfeed her newborn daughter, she was left feeling "frightened that I was doing something wrong".

In the first 24 hours after giving birth, Ms Barrett said nurses, lactation consultants, and midwives gave her conflicting advice on how to get her daughter to latch.

Despite the volume of advice, in the end she left the hospital with no feeding plan or ongoing support with breastfeeding.

"What I found incredibly confusing was the huge variation in advice and approaches from different healthcare professionals," Ms Barrett said.

If you, or someone you know, needs help: PANDA (Perinatal Anxiety and Depression Australia) on 1300 726 306

Sands (miscarriage, stillbirth and newborn death support) on 1300 072 637

Pregnancy, Birth and Baby helpline on 1800 882 436

Lifeline on 13 11 14

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

Beyond Blue on 1300 22 46 36 or online resource Dadvice

In the weeks that followed, her daughter began to lose weight because she was not receiving enough milk from breastfeeding alone.

Emotionally exhausted and sleep-deprived, Ms Barrett said she was then put on a "triple feeding" plan by nurses, which involved breastfeeding, pumping milk and formula feeding her daughter.

"It absolutely broke me," she said.

"I was up around the clock, trying to pump every three hours to establish and protect my supply.

"My daughter was often unsettled and unhappy throughout the process, and I felt like our entire lives revolved around feeding."

Ms Barrett's postpartum experience was similar to several other women the ABC spoke to, who reported inconsistent advice from care providers after they'd delivered their babies.

According to a 2024 review of antenatal care guidelines used in Australia, several commonly used guidelines for parents were found to be inconsistent in their recommendations for childbirth and early parenting.

The independent review, published in the Journal of Midwifery, evaluated five guidelines for antenatal care across six domains: scope and purpose, stakeholder involvement, rigour of development, clarity of presentation, applicability, and editorial independence,

All five guidelines scored low in each section.

Mental health, social media and 'overwhelm of information'

Getting conflicting advice could increase a new parent's level of distress and worsen their mental health, according to the executive director of the Centre of Perinatal Excellence (COPE), Nicole Highet.

"It undermines their confidence because they have got no reference point as a new parent. They don't know what to expect. Then they're constantly getting conflicting advice, which increases their stress and their levels of anxiety," Dr Highet said.

People might delay getting help early because they fear being "judged" for not being a successful parent, Dr Highet said.

"The overwhelm of information, all of these things together make it an extremely stressful and vulnerable time for parents when it comes to mental health."

'I cried all the time': What it's like to have postnatal depression Postnatal depression is a common experience among new mums and dads, but many still struggle with how to talk about it.

Information may not be uniform across all health practitioners for multiple reasons, including practitioners giving personal or anecdotal advice, she said.

Guidelines are reviewed every five years, which could make some information outdated, she added.

The national guidelines only recommend screening for postnatal depression before and after birth, but that is not enough according to Dr Highet.

"We know that for most people who develop postnatal depression, that will occur after six weeks. It might occur between six to eight months, yet no one is screening after that," she said.

"This is an example of where we have guidelines, but we don't have policy that aligns with the guidelines … and guidelines are not being reflected in practice," she said.

Erin Seeto, director of clinical services at the Gidget Foundation, said postnatal depression and anxiety could occur in one in five women and one in 10 men.

"Depending on whether you're a woman or a man, you might seek help differently," Dr Seeto said.

"We know that men tend to delay help-seeking until things are more acute, whereas women tend to have multiple touch points with health practitioners, but maybe not then be directed to the help that works for them within the time frame that they need."

US mum on trial for murder says voice told her to 'kill the children' A mother who says she was suffering postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children and attempted to take her own life is now on trial for their murder.

A lack of continuity in care for a parent could lead to missed diagnoses, prompting large-scale calls for more consistency among practitioners, she said.

She said social media can contribute to mental health stigma postpartum, making some women hesitant to seek help.

A recent example is a woman on trial for killing her three children, which has sparked comments on social media about postnatal psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth, she said.

"The problem is when we have these very high-profile media cases, often they add stigma, and they deter people from help-seeking because they worry about what's going to happen and what this means for them," Dr Seeto said.

"In some ways there are benefits to it. In other ways, it can be very detrimental to vulnerable women and families that are going through the perinatal period right now."

'Feeling as though I was failing my baby'

Women say they need to feel more heard postpartum. (Adobe: Grooveriderz)

Looking back at the beginning of her postpartum journey with her now 11-month-old daughter, Ms Barrett said the way advice was delivered without consistency had a "profound" impact on her.

Eventually, it was identified that her daughter had a severe tongue-tie that was affecting her ability to latch effectively.

The mixed advice continued up until her daughter began starting solids, at about six months.

"The hardest part was constantly feeling as though I was failing my baby," she said.

"As a first-time mum, hearing variations of 'your baby isn't getting enough' every few days was incredibly distressing.

" I felt like I was starving my child, even though I was doing absolutely everything I could. "

She stressed that it was important that new mothers received support that was consistent, evidence-based and compassionate.

"But they also need to feel heard," she said.

"When you're exhausted, vulnerable and responsible for a tiny human, conflicting advice can make an already overwhelming experience feel impossible."

World.title: AI chatbots like Buddy at Bunnings years from becoming norm
World.content:
AI chatbots are already in use by Australia's biggest retailers, from Buddy at Bunnings to Olive at Woolworths.

But experts say it will be years before these company-built artificial assistants can do more than just chat to shoppers.

Grocery prices up In the past 16 months, the rise in grocery prices has outstripped wages growth.

During their full year financial results presentations, all major retailers earmarked "agentic commerce" — letting an AI program shop for you — as a key space to invest in.

"Olive, our much-loved digital shopping assistant, has transformed into a personal shopping companion," Woolworths CEO Amanda Bardwell said.

Coles, which has yet to develop its own AI chatbot, has flagged conversational shopping as an opportunity for further investment.

Australia's major retailers reported a combined profit in the last financial year of more than $5 billion.

"The earnings growth came out of cost, not out of customers spending more," Retail Customer Advisory's director Trent Rigby said.

Retailers also highlighted the growth in private label and online sales during their financial results presentations.

One in three purchases to be online, expert says

Some of the largest revenue growth for retailers came from online orders with Coles seeing a 26.4 per cent increase with sales reaching $5.6 billion, representing almost 14 per cent of all sales.

Woolworths saw its online orders grow by 18 per cent, which represented almost $11 billion.

As many as one in three products could be purchased online soon, according to Queensland University of Technology's Gary Mortimer.

But high transport and logistics costs will curb the profit margins for online sales, he said.

Since 2019, Coles has partnered with e-commerce company Ocado Group for its automated deliveries.

According to Ocado Group's 2024 annual report, the cost per item picked for its British clients was 52 British pence ($1.06).

Some retail experts have said as many as one in three products could be purchased online in the next few years. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Professor Mortimer said the growth could see store sizes and ranges shrink with repeat purchases such as toilet paper and cleaning goods delivered to homes.

"It is certainly cheaper to fill shelves and have shoppers physically select, scan and take their purchases with them," he said.

US supermarket chain Kroger announced last year it was closing three of its automated warehouses, which was in partnership with Ocado, due to sites not meeting financial expectations.

University of Sydney retail expert Lisa Asher said customers could soon bear the additional costs associated with online orders.

"Groceries will continue to go up if they're going to push forward with this as an option because the price point that you pay online versus in store is the same," she said.

AI privacy concerns as retailers move to 'agentic commerce'

Ms Asher said regulation was needed to curb "surveillance capitalism", and protect the privacy of shoppers as supermarkets deliberate how to roll out AI in stores and online

Facial scans in supermarkets Industry groups say the move to facial scans in supermarkets is about safety, but analysts say that once the technology is installed, its "scope creep" paves the way for options like discriminatory pricing.

"They are essentially monetising our shopping habits and data points from a customer perspective to make more money from us," she said.

"We are not the product because we are trying to buy food to feed our families with rising cost of living."

Mr Rigby said it will take at least three years before agentic shopping becomes a standard practice in Australia.

"Woolworths is beta testing Smart Basket, which builds a basket from your previous purchases. [It] still puts a human at the check-out," he said.

"Nobody here is letting an agent complete a grocery shop unsupervised at any scale."

Mr Rigby said agentic shopping was expensive technology years away from being a part of people's routine shop. (ABC News: Harriet Tatham)

Mr Rigby has tested 'agentic shopping journeys' across a number of retail categories, and said grocery was the hardest to hand over.

"My read is grocery will be one of the last categories to go agentic, not the first," he said.

"People are particular about fresh. Substitutions are personal. Get one item wrong in a $200 basket and you've lost trust in the whole thing.

"When it lands it will be more routine replenishment, not fresh. Not to mention this tech is very expensive to rollout."

Home-brand growing as retailers become suppliers

Private label, or home branded products represent about 36 per cent of consumer sales across all supermarkets in Australia, and the category is growing according to Mr Rigby.

At the major supermarkets, Coles saw a 6.1 per cent lift in private label sales, while Woolworths saw that figure increase by 5.5 per cent in the year to June 30.

Mr Rigby said home-branded products have created savings for retailers but the growth was due to the quality gap closing between them and branded products.

"It's a rational trade rather than a sacrifice for a household under genuine financial pressure that's the difference between making the week and not," he said.

Kmart's brand Anko now supplies retailers from countries in the United States, Canada and India. (ABC News: Elizabeth Pickering)

Mr Rigby highlighted Kmart's home-brand Anko which expanded to supply overseas retailers from Walmart in the United States, Hudson's Bay in Canada, Flipkart in India and Amazon.

"An Australian discount department store has turned its private label into a product design and sourcing business it sells to retailers overseas," he said.

"There's no other example like it here."

But the growth in home branded products especially at supermarkets could, over time, displace other competitors, and potentially impact costs for consumers.

"Where it goes wrong is conflict of interest," Mr Rigby said.

"The moment a retailer is also a supplier, every ranging and pricing decision it makes about a competing brand is open to question."

Home branded products were a short-term sales strategy to improve profitability but could limit customer choice long term, according to Ms Asher.

"So when they delete our competition, they delete the brand, we lose out from price competition … and they can do this because it's not unlawful," she said.

World.title: One Nation, Coalition bank on cheap cigarettes being uncool
World.content:
Is smoking cool again?

Better not ask singer Charli XCX, who was photographed at the height of her Brat summer, receiving a birthday bouquet stuffed with cigarettes.

At the time Vogue noted the tongue-in-cheek gift was the kind of thing a Swiftie might "baulk" at.

No shade to Taylor Swift, but the subtext was clear: smoking was, regrettably, cool.

Singer Charli XCX was photographed at the height of her Brat summer receiving a birthday bouquet stuffed with cigarettes. (Reuters: Daniel Cole)

Australia considers dramatic change

Fortunately for Australian health advocates, that aesthetic does not appear to have penetrated the psyche of the average teenager.

Smoking among 14 to 17-year-olds has fallen to levels almost too low to reliably track, while local research found teens generally described young smokers as "losers" or "trying too hard to be cool".

Has tobacco tax gone too far? The Liberals and One Nation have a simple solution to end Australia's tobacco black market. But Labor says there's no easy fix.

But there remain concerns. A poll released this year found 26 per cent of 12 to 17-year-olds had tried some form of nicotine, while another 15 per cent were considering it.

All of these factors matter if Australia is seriously considering a dramatic change in how nicotine is regulated.

More than half the cigarettes sold in the country are now purchased illegally, while the estimated nicotine black market share jumps to 80 per cent when vapes and pouches are included.

In addition to money for more law enforcement and a public education campaign, the Coalition wants to legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches. (AAP: Pip Farquharson )

Coalition releases its plan

The solution proposed this week by the Coalition is to slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent, just edging out One Nation's 75 per cent in what Labor has dubbed a "race to the bottom" with organised crime.

But the policy unveiled by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor this week went further than the excise.

In addition to money for more law enforcement and a public education campaign, the Coalition wants to legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches.

That has Labor and medical experts very worried.

A young person who has vaped is five times more likely to take up smoking, according to one study cited by the Cancer Council.

Australia has to date taken a highly restrictive approach to alternative nicotine products, restricting the sale of vapes to pharmacies and banning pouches.

Enforcement has become much more aggressive, though it plainly has not eliminated the retail black market.

But where reforms can claim some success has been in youth vaping rates, which have dropped by about a third since 2024.

It is this progress in particular the federal government and health advocates fear would be undone by the Coalition's policy.

Loading...

One question opponents care about

There is only one question that matters to opponents of the idea Australia can tax and regulate its way out of a very dangerous organised crime-fuelled tobacco black market: Is a rise in smoking and nicotine addiction a price worth paying?

It's a premise either avoided or outright rejected by those who believe a more affordable legal option is preferable to the status quo.

Taylor this week has argued the "horse has already bolted" on higher smoking rates, suggesting things couldn't get worse.

He can argue that because this debate has been riddled with selective use of statistics and preferred sources of information.

While a national household survey has tracked a drop in smoking rates and stabilisation of vaping, there was about 30 per cent more nicotine detected in wastewater last year compared to 2021.

These two seemingly incongruous points are used to either argue that making cigarettes prohibitively expensive remains an effective tool for reducing smoking, or that people are turning to illegal alternatives and not reporting it.

Loading

Black market situation untenable

There isn't a politician of any stripe who believes the current black market situation is good.

Cigarettes have become more accessible with no checks and balances — no one has any clue what is in those products or who they're being sold to.

It is financing organised crime, which has led to terrifying firebombings — including one that led to the death of an innocent woman.

The federal budget will be billions of dollars poorer over the next four years because of the drop in excise revenue.

But consensus around a problem does not mean all solutions are equal.

A legal packet of cigarettes retails for generally between $40 and $50, of which about $30 is excise, while an illegal pack can be bought for $10 to $20.

A 75 to 80 per cent excise cut would reduce the cost of a 20-packet by $23 to $24.

The Coalition and One Nation are both arguing their respective proposals hit the sweet spot of making legal cigarettes competitively priced enough to compete with the illicit market. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

One Nation and Coalition argue proposals hit sweet spot

The Coalition and One Nation are both arguing their respective proposals hit the sweet spot of making legal cigarettes competitively priced enough to compete with the illicit market.

They are betting on several things for this to work.

The first is that Australians, rule followers that we are, will happily revert to the legal product for the right price.

And the second is that an enforcement squeeze combined with market competition will destroy the criminals' profits.

Both plausible outcomes — it worked in Canada, advocates will tell you.

In 1994 the country successfully quashed its thriving black market by slashing tobacco taxes in half.

But there's a third factor this strategy relies on, and it's important.

The Coalition and One Nation are hoping that the next generation of Australians will enter young adulthood and see a legal pack of cigarettes on the shelf for $20 and think, "nah, I'm good thanks".

Re-enter the Canadian example.

Killing off the black market came at a high cost: Canada has about 190,000 excess daily smokers among the generation born from 1977 to 1985.

To risk a similar result in Australia by making legal cigarettes cheaper and vapes more convenient to access would be a serious gamble.

Health Minister Mark Butler has accused the Coalition of having "no understanding" of what its policy would do to Australia's smoking and vaping rates. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Health minister questions Coalition

Health Minister Mark Butler has accused the Coalition of having "no understanding" of what its policy would do to Australia's smoking and vaping rates.

Labor's claim to progress in those areas will forever be undermined as long as the black market flourishes — something it does not dispute.

Spending more on enforcement is inevitable, and there is speculation some movement on the excise is possible.

But there is no chance Labor would come near the deep cuts or further legalisation proposed by its political opponents.

That sets up the next federal election as a contest of very different ideas about how to tackle Australia's illegal nicotine problem.

Perhaps against the odds, Australian teens are currently proving impervious to the return of smoking in pop culture.

The Coalition and One Nation will have to prove they believe a generation that has grown up thinking cigarettes are both deeply uncool and prohibitively expensive will continue to resist when the last of those barriers disappears.

World.title: 'I was the void': What happens when meditation goes wrong
World.content:
"Everybody thinks meditation's hunky-dory … there's just this automatic assumption that it couldn't possibly come in and totally blow up your brain."

Three years ago, Sue discovered pranayama, a type of meditation involving modifying the length and timing of breaths.

But the self-described "spiritual seeker" in her 70s from Florida stopped after having "an acute traumatic experience … caused by meditation".

Sue is not alone.

Research suggests one in 10 meditators will experience an adverse effect that lasts more than a month or is associated with impairment and functioning.

Loading...

This is significant given the growing popularity of meditation, particularly mindfulness-based meditation.

In the US, the number of people meditating has increased from 10 to 20 per cent of the population over the past two decades.

In Australia, that figure is even higher, with one third of the population practising some form of meditation.

There are a wide range of proven mental and physical health benefits of mindfulness and meditation.

But the potential negative or adverse effects of meditation remain relatively unknown and under-researched.

The evangelical meditator

Willoughby Britton, an associate professor of psychiatry at Brown University and director of the Clinical and Affective Neuroscience Lab, is a pioneer and world-leading researcher into meditation-related adverse effects.

But 20 years ago, Dr Britton was what she now considers an "evangelical meditator".

"I spent my first 20 years of meditation research promoting the benefits, stating there were no adverse effects even though I never measured them," she admits.

In the US alone, the mindfulness and meditation industry via apps, books and retreats is worth billions of dollars each year. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Dr Britton was first introduced to meditation following the death of a childhood friend.

"I was really devastated and anxious and I didn't know what to do and I really didn't want to take medication."

Instead, Dr Britton's father sent her a book on meditation that she describes as "my gateway drug".

After quickly establishing a daily mindfulness routine, she decided to research the impact of meditation on sleep.

"I was going to prove to everyone that not only was meditation good for sleep, but how it also improved depression because lingering sort of problems with sleep can lead to relapse in depression."

But she was surprised by the results.

Instead of improving sleep quality, the study showed participants' brainwaves got faster and they woke up more after meditation.

At the time, Dr Britton chose not to publish her findings.

A couple of years later while working as a resident doctor at Brown University's psychiatric hospital, she treated two patients with psychotic symptoms who had been on separate meditation retreats.

" It was like some of the most extreme patients that I saw in that hospital all year. "

Following those encounters, Dr Britton sought advice from a trusted meditation teacher.

"I said, 'Well, have you ever seen this before?'

"She didn't say anything but I remember the look on her face was like, 'Oh yes, this is definitely a thing that she's seen before'.

The conversation prompted Dr Britton to embark on decades of research into the field of meditation-related adverse effects.

Very quickly, she says, all her "fantasies about meditation were sobered up".

What are meditation-related adverse effects?

In 2017, Dr Britton and her team published a 10-year study based on interviews of more than 100 Buddhist meditation practitioners describing challenges they had experienced personally or observed in meditation students.

Insomnia, as Dr Britton had previously discovered, was just one of more than 50 adverse meditation-related symptoms reported.

Sue described a particularly frightening experience she had while driving. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Many of the adverse symptoms people in the study reported fell into two categories:

Hyperarousal, such as anxiety, fear, insomnia, involuntary movements and emotional flooding; and hypoarousal, such as a lack of emotion, motivation and sense of self.

Many people described feeling dysregulated, experiencing a combination of both hypo and hyper arousal.

They also reported psychosis symptoms that lasted on average between one and three years.

"There was a considerable amount of impairment where some people were hospitalised, some people became suicidal, many people had to take time off work, or were fired or had to take time off school.

"So it can be quite a significant impairment in functioning," Dr Britton says.

Sue experienced symptoms of hypoarousal and dysregulation after using a meditation app a couple of times each week.

One experience was particularly frightening.

"I was all by myself in my car and I had this profound sense of myself dissolving … so it was just the void and I was the void … it was really terrifying".

Sue remained in this dysregulated space for about a year and a half.

While Sue experienced negative symptoms after meditating regularly over time, short exposures right through to intensive meditation practices can trigger adverse effects.

Twenty years ago, Jane, a retiree in her mid-seventies who had practised Zen meditation for several years, experienced a serious and prolonged mental health episode after attending her fourth five-day retreat.

Jane distinctly remembers the first night of that retreat.

"My mind was just fizzing, like a sort of lemonade bottle, I knew something wasn't right," she says.

"I made an appointment the next morning with the teacher, and she just looked at me and said, 'Oh, you don't need to sleep when you meditate.'"

When Jane returned home after completing the course, her husband contacted their local GP who diagnosed her "as being psychotic and manic".

Over the next two decades, Jane was hospitalised multiple times and treated with a range of antipsychotic medications.

In hindsight, Jane believes she was likely slightly psychotic before starting the retreat, but she thinks if the teacher she sought advice from had a greater awareness of the risks, they may have recognised she was clearly unwell.

Clues in plain sight

While Dr Britton's research has contributed to growing awareness of meditation-related adverse effects, she is not the first person to recognise the problem.

In Buddhist tradition there are a range of terms used to describe meditation-related adverse effects including meditation sickness, Zen sickness and wind disorder. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

The earliest understandings of these problems date back as ancient Buddhist traditions, according to Pierce Salguero, a professor of Asian history and health humanities at Penn State University.

"I came across some writings from about 1,500 years ago that were talking about meditation as a form of healing … and what I noticed was that those texts were also talking about meditation as a source of both mental and physical problems and conditions," he says.

Benefits of meditation

Yet there is plenty of evidence that supports the benefits of meditation, specifically mindfulness meditation.

"It can help with a wide variety of mental health issues, anxiety, depression and some substance use problems," Nicholas Van Dam, director of the Contemplative Study Centre at the University of Melbourne, explains.

Meditation can also help with the management of pain associated with physical health conditions such as arthritis and cancer recovery by helping train attention and shifting focus away from pain.

The relaxation aspect of meditation is also beneficial.

"Many times, in meditation you are engaged in a process where you're slowing down your breathing, you're potentially seeing the mind quiet," he says.

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

So, given the benefits, how can it prove dangerous for some?

"Much like a lot of other treatments … in medicine and mental health, it would be remiss not to acknowledge that what we do know about meditation is that it's potent, it's powerful," Dr Van Dam explains.

He believes informed consent is "missing" in the conversation about meditation and participants should be made aware of the potential risks.

The beginning of Cheetah House

Dr Britton says she was overwhelmed by the public's response after her study, which is part of the Varieties of Contemplative Experience project, was published in 2017.

"We had so many calls at the lab that we had to turn off our phone because it was interfering with research," she recalls.

"[Callers] were like, 'You're the only ones I've ever seen who knew anything about this … everyone I've been to is like, 'meditation doesn't have side effects.''"

For the past decade, Cheetah House has provided assistance for meditators in distress. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

In response, she set up Cheetah House, a not-for-profit service that offers support to meditators in distress and aims to educate meditation teachers and clinicians about the risks of meditation.

A decade later, Dr Britton says the service has on average 150 appointments each month and has treated thousands of meditators in more than 20 countries.

"There is a problem that is being systematically ignored, it's a pretty common problem and there's just this kind of system of denial and gaslighting," Dr Britton says.

Jane agrees.

"I think people who do these practices … almost feel [meditation] is the answer to everything and it just isn't," Jane says.

"Sometimes it doesn't suit a certain person."

World.title: Why this El Niño is different from all the others
World.content:
This El Niño is unlike those before it. ( )

Climate scientists have been closely monitoring what is happening off Australia's east coast over recent months and are increasingly concerned by what they are seeing. Pacific Ocean temperatures, a key driver of El Niño, are rising at an extraordinary pace and starting to enter uncharted territory.

Ocean temperatures are forecast to be 5 degrees above average in the central and eastern Pacific in December. ( )

The dark, red tongue spreading in the Pacific is growing at a rate not seen in living memory. The El Niño brewing there is already breaking records, and it is months away from its peak. The sheer magnitude of the event and the uncertainty over what is driving it have alarmed experts.

Among them is senior climatologist at the Bureau of Meteorology Felicity Gamble, who said the rate of warming over the past six months was the fastest ever recorded.

"We're actually seeing record values and record values by quite a significant margin as well," she said.

"So very warm ocean temperatures across much of the equatorial tropical Pacific.

"That does raise a lot of concern by meteorologists, oceanographers and marine scientists."

Across the globe, anxiety over its backlash is growing, triggering a stark warning by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
