World.title: How cheap drones are upending the big business of defence
World.content:
Analysis BusinessThe economyAviation How cheap drones are upending the big business of defence Chris Zappone September 6, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The lower price and high impact of drone warfare is pushing down the financial costs of aerial bombardment, forcing a rethink from militaries and governments. At the same time, the blistering pace of drone innovation is also disrupting traditional defence manufacturing by lowering the barriers and opening the door to favour smaller, more nimble companies. Iran’s Shahed drones on display in a 2023 photo. Drones have come to define the Ukraine-Russia conflict and their effects are playing out daily in the Middle East. Salvos of drones are overwhelming conventional air defence systems; swarms of cheap drones are being shot down with expensive Western-made missiles; and inexpensive small drones are taking on tanks. In the process, long-standing practices of how defence gear is designed, built, and sold are being repriced at a lower cost, much in the way computers, once the province of university labs in the 1960s, became ubiquitous PCs in the 1990s, then laptops, and iPhones.



In the defence world, this has created a gap in capabilities between drone-savvy militaries and ones relying on high-tech, expensive weapons of the past. UK-based Jay Guthrie says SMEs are essential for rapid drone production and innovation. The US, for instance, has been hamstrung in defending its Middle East bases because it doesn’t have enough drone interceptors. Nations quickly building stocks of drones to meet government-directed goals are practicing what Ukrainian analyst Lesia Bidochko describes as “drone Keynesianism”. Economist John Maynard Keynes believed governments could solve economic problems through massive, sustained spending on production. For companies, the goal shifts from marketing complex and elegant systems to fielding drone units that can deliver on a battlefield.



Today, for example, Ukraine incentivises 500 small suppliers to work fast and respond to near-daily changes on the battlefield. The government creates the market, allowing small companies to focus on rapid innovation while literally “under fire”. The US is looking to emulate this model through its “Drone Dominance” program. Loading Jay Guthrie, a British ex-service member who has spent time in Ukraine, said drones can be simultaneously “low cost” to build and deploy and “high impact” in what they destroy. At the same time, large legacy defence companies can’t produce drones at the speed or cost needed to be effective on a modern battlefield, he said.



Major Western defence companies are “all looking at the 100 per cent solution” made up of “a really shiny drone that looks really pretty when it takes off”. “But in reality, at the end of the day, it’s going to end up a big lump of plastic anyway, so it doesn’t need to be shiny. Just robust enough to get to the target,” he said. An assembly line at Melbourne-based Freespace Operations. The company, which provides sovereign capability in drone manufacturing, makes heavy lift drones for defence, energy, mining, infrastructure and emergency services. Chris Zappone Iran pioneered the strategy of building cheaper drones that could seek to overwhelm Israeli and US defences. Iran built thousands of Shahed drones, costing a fraction of the price of US interceptor missiles. The Ukrainians played catch-up after Russia expanded its war against Kyiv in 2022. The rise of drones is also changing the big business of defence procurement because drones can be produced quickly and at low cost by smaller companies rather than the traditional corporate giants, which rely on long-lead times, that supply militaries.



Related Article Aviation Welcome to the era of the ‘affordable’ cruise missile While there some large-scale makers of civilian drones, smaller nimble drone players have been driving much of the disruption in the defence sector. Guthrie notes that it takes Western-based defence companies 18 months to two years to incorporate major innovations into a product, but takes Ukrainians or (Iranians) only a couple of weeks. The technology of drones – cheap electronics, 3D-printed parts, rapidly updated designs – is transforming part of the defence industry dominated for decades by major companies known as “prime subcontractors”. Parts of downed Shahed drones launched by Russia are piled in a storage room of a research laboratory in Kyiv, Ukraine, in 2024. AP



Companies such as Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Airbus, and Thales act as systems integrators, which manage “complex supply chains and manage risk around delivery of major projects”, he said. Ken King, CEO and Co-founder of Melbourne-based Freespace Operations. Chris Zappone The prime contractors can see the shift. Some are learning from it. Boeing, for instance, is trialling an ultra-low cost guidance system, which could be used on drones and missiles, “to dramatically reduce per-unit costs and enable precision munition employment at scale across programs”. Guthrie, who works for UK-based Merlin Power Defence, said that at issue is the scale of the companies doing the production. “What you need is a load of mini primes, where you build that framework agreement (with the defence departments), but there’s still the man-in-the-shed mentality,” where new features can be tried quickly.



The learning curve around drone economics is steep, and Guthrie said that, typically, nations’ defence departments stick with the primes “because it’s easy” and the framework for contracts is already in place. But the prime contractors have “many investors and the need to return an investment”. So what is a $10 drone becomes about $200 because everyone has a “piece of the pie”, said Guthrie. Small and medium enterprises, he says, are more agile. They can build. They can innovate. They’ve got fewer people on their shoulders saying: “You need to make a big profit out of it”. Melbourne start-up Freespace Operations uses ArduPilot, an open-source autopilot system to guide its drones, says co-founder chief technology officer Leonard Hall. “This whole industry is based on that simple factor,” Hall said.



Freespace Operations doesn’t build combat drones, but drones designed to lift equipment, some used for defence, to “last for years”. Hall said that if not for open-source autopilot code, it would cost $100 million to code the autopilot before his company’s drone could be tested. Instead, “open source allows small companies to share the developmental burden of the impossible task”. To take advantage of the rapid development once it’s done. “It’s really a first-to-market enabler.” Such speed is key. CEO and co-founder Ken King said his company’s growth since 2019 has essentially followed a Moore’s law “type of trajectory”. (Moore’s law is the idea that the number of transistors on computer chips doubles roughly every two years.)



In conflict, even contenders to be the new defence prime contractors face a challenge in producing enough drones, cheaply enough. Anduril’s Bolt-M kamikaze drones run an estimated US$26,000 to $40,000 apiece including the required support system, far above the price tag of units in use in Ukraine. Bravo Ordnance CEO Devan Plantamura sees drones becoming “commoditised”. Bravo Ordnance “First-person view drones have pretty high attrition rates due to reliability or jamming,” said a spokesperson for Anduril. “Bolt is designed to be much more reliable, resilient, and to bring the firepower necessary to actually take out targets with one shot.” The speed of the innovation also makes drone manufacturing an unpredictable industry. CEO and co-founder of US-based Bravo Ordnance Devan Plantamura said that currently in conflict “first world countries cannot afford to use” the high-end missile technology they’ve created, such as Patriot missiles.



At the same time, increasingly, the global industry is “commoditising drones”, he said, making them a product bought on price rather than specific brands. That makes for a rapidly shifting landscape. Capabilities change, too. Plantamura said that once countermeasures are developed to beat the Shaheds, for example, the price of Shaheds could rise as they’ll need “more technological advancements”. “So it’s a game of cat-and-mouse that’s going to go on for the next 10 to 15 years.” In this world, production capability is everything. Anduril founder Palmer Luckey last year said that “a country can only mass manufacture arms if it designs arms that can be mass manufactured by the industrial base it already has. The current defence industry has not been done this way”.



Guthrie said: “It’s a huge cultural change”. One he doesn’t see democracies are ready for. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: The winning formula: Do you have what it takes to be the next footy star?
World.content:
So how do the clubs in the national league (18 men’s, 18 women’s) find the next generation of elite players? What sets a future professional apart from a skillful amateur? And how can young people maximise their chances of playing at the ’G one day?

More than 624,000 children and adults play football in Australia. Whittling down the best young players takes years, money and skill. The stakes are high: the best players, like artists, can create something out of nothing while players with poor character or decision-making can drag down a whole team for years.

Theirs is not a glamorous job. At games, you’ll spot them in puffer jackets, perched on camping chairs with binoculars, pen and notebook. Other times, they’ll be hunkered down scrutinising footage, crunching player data. Many fans like to think they could do a better job. “I think every sports fan in Australia is picking their footy team or cricket team,” veteran AFL talent expert Kevin Sheehan tells us. “It’s a tough business, the business of drafting, and it’s make or break for the careers of not just the boys [and girls] but the scouts who are looking at them.”

Australian rules football has a rich history of freakishly talented players ( Buddy Franklin , Nick Daicos , Erin Phillips ) and legendary coaches ( Leigh Matthews , the late Ron Barassi and Walls’s own father, Robert ). Less lauded but no less critical to success are the recruiters and list managers. They determine who is in and out of a club, how to mix new blood – a handful of teen draft picks each year – with existing teams, a painstaking task that culminates in the nerve-wracking annual draft in November (for the men) and December (for the women).

But the picture is never complete until he visits them at their family home. “You can’t bullshit in front of Mum or Dad,” says Walls, once a fresh-faced rookie himself, now head of player personnel at Fremantle footy club. “Even siblings will start to say, ‘That’s not true’,” Walls tells us. “Dads, generally, are trying to sell them as footballers and mums just want to make sure they’re good people.”

In his nearly 30 years of finding footy talent, David Walls has sat down to talk with thousands of young people who dream of becoming professional footballers. He’s watched them play from the sidelines at games and on countless hours of video; reviewed their psychological tests and physical tests; analysed their statistics; met with their coaches, employers, schoolteachers; and spent time in their orbit on training camps – to work out who they are, and who they could become.

Van Hattum has signed up with a manager, a crucial step in a junior’s progress to the AFL, and has, meanwhile, been playing footy for a dizzying array of sides: Ivanhoe Grammar, his school in Melbourne’s east; Vic Metro in the AFL national championships; the AFL academy; and the Northern Knights in the AFL Talent League, Victoria’s top under-18 competition, from which most draft picks are drawn. (Gifted players also come from state leagues, or the northern academies run by Sydney, Greater Western Sydney, Brisbane and the Gold Coast, or from next-generation academies run by all clubs for Indigenous and multicultural youth.) Van Hattum considered an invitation to play for Richmond’s VFL team, too, but enough was enough. “It’s pretty busy,” he says.

On a trip to New Zealand with the AFL national academy squad , made up of 50 of Australia’s most talented draft contenders, his every interaction was noted by recruiters, on the field and off. “You sit down with them and have lunch, dinner and different meetings with them on different days,” Van Hattum says, “so you get a really good sense of what their point of view is and what they are looking for from that. I was definitely pretty nervous the first time I had a meeting with someone from a club, so I was trying to be super-professional and really well-behaved. But you have just got to be yourself, don’t lie, don’t make anything up – because obviously they will find out.”

Yet it was only last year that Van Hattum put aside his other sporting pursuit, basketball – which he played at state level in under 12s and 14s – to focus on footy, and recruiters became part of his life. “It was around then I started talking to recruiters a fair bit and getting calls from them and organising home visits and stuff like that over that summer,” he tells us.

‘I was definitely pretty nervous the first time I had a meeting with someone from a club, so I was trying to be super-professional and really well-behaved. But you have just got to be yourself …’

At 205 centimetres, Harry Van Hattum stands out in a crowd. The year 12 student is confident, warm and mature. He also has a massive running leap, 103 centimetres into the air, just a touch higher than West Coast icon Nic Naitanui’s 102 centimetres jump as a junior. High-flying ruckmen are back in vogue after the AFL changed the rules this year to stop other players wrestling them away from the centre bounce, although Van Hattum wants it known ruckmen are about more than their aerial manoeuvres: “It doesn’t matter your size when you’re using it [the ball] well … I pride myself on having elite skills,” he told ESPN in August. In short, the 18-year-old has the makings of a very modern ruckman and, consequently, he’s a top prospect in November’s draft.

She is ready to take the plunge and relocate if she’s drafted interstate. “I understand it would be extremely scary,” she says, “but the support that you get given is huge and, on top of the salary that you get given as an AFLW rookie, you also get extra money if you go interstate, to pay for your rent.” Clubs sometimes house newbies with a host family, another player, or a coach for a short while. Draft picks will be paid a minimum of $125,000 in 2027 in the men’s game; women will be on a base salary of $72,363.

Her hard work has paid off: Meagher has signed with a player agent, toured St Kilda’s facilities and met with several clubs. “Collingwood’s was just online, and Carlton’s was going to their club, and Essendon, they came to training to have a 30-minute conversation with me and a couple of other girls,” she explains, “and I’ve got Freo coming to my house.”

Among attendees will be year 12 student Maddy Meagher, who plays on the wing for the Northern Knigh t s in the Talent League, the top under-18 competition in Victoria. “I base a lot of my game just off my speed,” the 18-year-old tells us. With a background in athletics, Meagher has climbed the footy ranks since she started about six years ago, this year juggling study with two three-hour training sessions a week for the Knights, games on the weekend and private coaching to “focus on the nitty-gritty”.

Just days after the AFL grand final, Van Hattum and other promising teenage footballers (a total of 102 men and 89 women) will attend an event called a draft combine, either in Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth, where they will talk with clubs and compete in various trials (think sprints, agility tests, vertical jumps from a standing start).

Through it all, he is trying to live a normal life: studying, playing golf, hanging out with schoolmates and getting on the tools to help his dad, Rod, build a granny flat in the backyard of his family’s Kangaroo Ground property. He admits he sometimes feels like a lab rat. “It always lingers in the back of my head that there is an expectation about me and I have to perform well, but I just try to block it out of my mind and try to play to my best level and don’t think about the expectation on me every time.”

Very few players possess all of these attributes at a high level – now-retired Adelaide Crows champion Erin Phillips, a former basketballer, came pretty close – but you are better off with a laser kick or elite-standard speed than being average at everything. “If you watch where even AFL and AFLW was five or six years ago to now, the game is so much quicker,” says Alec Morgan. Walls agrees: “The distance they’re covering at high speed is just getting bigger and better.” Seven-time best and fairest, Richmond’s Monique Conti, is known for her explosive speed; Joel Wilkinson, who played briefly for Gold Coast then moved to the US National Football League, still holds the 20-metre sprint record (2.75 seconds) at a draft combine in 2010.

On the left is FOOTBALL: clean hands to control that odd-shaped ball without fumbling, aerial game (marking), ground game (running) and cue response, which, says Clayton, means, “You react in instinct and action in super-quick time [to] what is actually happening. Perhaps at times it is predicting the future and making a decision on what action you must actually take.”

Scott Clayton has built playing lists for Brisbane, the Bulldogs, Gold Coast, West Coast and North Melbourne. “You’ve got to have talent,” he says. “Without that, we can’t help you.” Clayton, who these days is a future talent consultant, shows us a piece of paper on which he’s jotted the qualities he wants in a draft pick.

Recruiters watch players for up to three years before making a move, which they can’t do until the player is 18 by December 31 of their draft year, under both leagues’ rules. Even then, being picked can be down to timing and luck. “Often,” says player agent Alec Morgan, who represents both the men’s and women’s league players, “recruiters will have a whiteboard and they’ll have a whole list of names at the start of the year on that, and then as the year goes, they cross names off and they add names on. So you could be the third-best key-position defender on everyone’s list, but if the other two ahead of you don’t get taken right until the end, you might keep coming second or third. So it’s not necessarily a knock on you, the footballer.”

Next on Clayton’s list is something less obvious: self-efficacy, a term that describes possessing a belief in your ability to achieve an outcome. In footy, Clayton asks, “Do they go in knowing that they’re going to affect the outcome? Because in a competitive sport, that’s what you need: you need instinctive people who just want it, want to affect the outcome, and they’re bold.”

Top of Clayton’s list is “competitiveness”, and he’s not the only one. “I think the biggest thing that we find with clubs is competitiveness, that’s what they love,” says agent Alec Morgan. “One of the things recruiters really look out for is, do you compete? And if you’re a competitive person on the ground, you’re going to be doing all the little things off the field to make sure you’re as good as you can be.” David Walls wants players who go all out: “You know that they’re going to give the same amount of effort, it doesn’t matter what game it is, it doesn’t matter if they start slowly and things aren’t going their way, or if the team’s getting belted.”

On the right side of Clayton’s ledger is CHARACTER. For many recruiters, it’s what sets apart the most desirable players from those who are merely technically very good. But what aspects of character, in particular, are they looking for?

As well as athletic flair, recruiters have to predict whether players’ bodies will cope. “We get our medical department involved heavily because players change so much physically,” says Walls. “Sometimes they can’t handle the training loads and their bodies break down and they get injured a lot.” Geelong premiership coach Mark Thompson used to have a theory that if a player was injured often in junior football, they would continue that pattern in the adult game. But with advances in medical science and more nuanced approaches to training, that theory is less fiercely held.

Take Joel Selwood, now retired but who still holds the league record for games as captain. A troublesome knee deterred some clubs (although not Geelong) from drafting him in 2006, but he devised his own leg-strengthening exercises — “the Joel Selwood program,” he’s joked — which he followed religiously for 16 years, barely missing a game. “Pick a player who you’d have in your side,” said Blues coach Mick Malthouse in 2014, after Selwood had kicked the winning goal against his team. “I’d pick Selwood every day of the week.”

The jubilation is plain to see after Cats captain Joel Selwood, right, takes decisive action, kicking a winning goal in the final moments of a 2014 game against Carlton. Getty Images

Research backs up the importance of self-efficacy and its related traits in everyday life, too. The Dunedin Study, from New Zealand’s University of Otago, has followed the health and fortunes of 1000 boys and girls since 1972 and found that their capacity for self-control – self-discipline and perseverance – was the single biggest predictor of their success, more than IQ or class. “We also found that children whose self-control increased with age tended to have better adult outcomes than initially predicted, showing that self-control can change and with desirable results,” wrote research leader Terrie Moffitt in 2011.

‘We had a kid who went to the snow ... but he wouldn’t ski because he was worried about getting injured. He just trained all day ... You go, OK, this kid’s really, really serious.’ David Walls

Similarly, self-motivation appears on Clayton’s list, too, a close cousin of that propulsive inner desire we call “drive”. “The players that are really driven to be the best they can be are usually the players that succeed,” says Katrina Gill, AFLW general manager at Melbourne Football Club. “You obviously need a level of talent, but talent combined with the work ethic tends to be the winning formula.”

That applies off the field, too. Fremantle’s Walls will sometimes quiz aspirants about what they do in their spare time. “We had a kid who went to the snow [with his family], went to Canada,” he recalls, “but he wouldn’t ski because he was worried about getting injured. He just trained all day, he worked out where the gyms are, where he could find an oval, where he could get a treadmill. We’re looking for things like that – where they’re giving you examples of they’re getting up early, they’re doing extra work, they’re doing recovery, they’re doing gym. You go, OK, this kid’s really, really serious.”

Fremantle’s David Walls has spent countless hours getting the measure of would-be recruits. Getty Images

A term not on Clayton’s list but that is often heard in Aussie rules circles is “footy IQ”: the ability to read, indeed predict, the play in all its fast-moving complexities, to understand the game and tactics at a deep level, to make smart decisions in a split second. If footy IQ is tricky to pin down, Walls knows it when he sees it: he drafted Murphy Reid in 2024 after 11 clubs overlooked the youngster. Reid, 20, is regarded as one of the most astute draft selections in recent history, having won the Rising Star award in his first season, and been named All-Australian in his second. Says Walls: “Footy IQ is … really, really big. Murphy Reid, for us, is one that stands out with how smart he is and how much composure [he has] and how calm he is.”

Can they back themselves to take highly consequential, calculated risks without over-thinking and second-guessing?

Also known for footy nous is Daisy Pearce, who balanced delivering babies (she was a midwife) with playing for the Demons in the early days of the AFLW. After having twins of her own, Pearce led Melbourne to a premiership, and now coaches the West Coast Eagles women’s team. Pearce’s footy IQ was “nothing that I’d seen before,” said football trailblazer Debbie Lee as Pearce was inducted into the Australian Football Hall of Fame. “She was a player who had so much time, she created so much space for herself, her skills were silky.”

Daisy Pearce in 2013: the first No. 1 pick in the first AFLW draft, when the first exhibition games were played, she is well known for her footy nous. Scott McNaughton

Why is “risk” on Clayton’s list? On a footy field, big risk-takers will be prepared to take the kick that, as Clayton says, “changes the course of events”, in front of 100,000 people and millions watching on television – even if a mistake might make them look foolish. He tests a rookie’s risk appetite with a line of questioning that he adapts to them. If they surf, he asks how big a swell they are prepared to paddle out in. If they play golf, he asks which club they would use to attack a par four. Can they back themselves to take highly consequential, calculated risks without over-thinking and second-guessing?

‘Are they supportive? Are they encouraging? And it goes the other way too, where you see people speak poorly to teammates and don’t treat them well, and play in a selfish manner.’ David Walls

If many of these qualities suggest ruggedly individual star power, how players relate to others – being a “good teammate”, as Clayton puts it – is a must. Gill agrees: “You want good people who are going to come in and have a positive impact on your program and be a good teammate as well.” Walls loves going out to huddles and listening to the way players talk to each other. “Are they supportive? Are they encouraging? And it goes the other way too, where you see people speak poorly to teammates and don’t treat them well, and play in a selfish manner.”

Monique Conti, at left, in 2021 is known for her explosive speed. Getty Images

Similarly, “ability to learn”, or coachability, is another prerequisite: recruiters will observe how a player reacts to instructions, including their body language. Off the field, they’ll check school reports and find out how the kid is with their classmates. Players do need to be able to follow rules. Their ability to do the right thing goes into the recruitment mix, as does whether the club culture and the coach are good matches for them. If the standards in the club, upheld by coaches and senior players, are positive then players, regardless of their proclivities, will generally fall into line. The best coaches can mould all types into elite players while creating an environment where positive decisions are made on and off the field, more often than not.

‘… their coachability, their resilience, their grit, their fire in the belly, their self-confidence, and those things that are a bit more intangible, such as their … fear factor.’ Elissa Morley

For kids with dreams of excelling in other sports, take note of these insights from Elissa Morley, who is performance pathways manager at the Australian Institute of Sport, which assesses more than 2900 athletes across 46 sports, each with their own “what-it-takes-to-win profile”. After a battery of physical tests, athletes are invited to trial with a sport to see if they have the right “psychological and behavioural factors”. “So, their coachability, their resilience, their grit, their fire in the belly, their self-confidence, and those things that are a bit more intangible, such as their feel for the water or their fear factor.” She adds there are some characteristics all athletes need, no matter the sport: resilience, persistence, self-belief, self-regulation and being proactive about solving problems.

Elissa Morley from the Australian Institute of Sport at the Northside Wizards basketball facility in Brisbane. She says elite athletes all need qualities such as persistence and problem-solving, no matter the sport. Dan Peled

It’s an impressive alchemical mix that makes up a player’s F.D.P., or future development potential. Kevin Sheehan says the sport gets drafting “right” about 80 per cent of the time. “You will make errors when you’re trying to assess talent very early. But even the NFL makes mistakes, and their entry age is post-college, 21 or 22,” he says of the US football league.

‘I’m always, would you want to work with this guy for the rest of your career, for the next 10 years?’ David Walls

The Demons’ Katrina Gill says recruiting still requires a touch of instinct. “You’re crystal-balling, to an extent.” Fremantle’s David Walls agrees, and says it makes him “sick to his stomach” when his team recruits the wrong player. “We’ve done it before, where they’re hard work and there’s issues off the field and they cause problems,” he tells us. “I’m always, would you want to work with this guy for the rest of your career, for the next 10 years? Because we’re dropping them off with these players, and is he going to make the most of the opportunity? And is he going to be a great teammate for the players that are already there?”

Ultimately, this is what recruiters want: future development potential. (The highlighter is added but the circle, underline and red pen are Clayton’s.) Courtesy Scott Clayton

What’s survivability? And how can parents help?

Being a young footy star can be tough. Living the dream will include strangers critiquing them and their team, yelling over the fence at games, writing negative comments online, and placing bets (literally) on their performance. So there’s another factor that plays into how a player is chosen: their survivability. “It’s a pretty full-on environment that you’re going into if you’re drafted at 18 and you’re straight out of school,” says Walls. “Are they going to be able to come in and work and be resilient and deal with setbacks? And if they’re playing reserves and developing for two years, are they going to be able to grind for that amount of time?”

One recruiter from a non-Victorian club tells us survivability includes coping with travel: basic self-management, being organised, being able to manage emotions. The Dockers take notice of what sort of company a prospect is over dinner – after all, they’ll have to spend a lot of time away with teammates. Says Alec Morgan: “Sometimes you can get a vibe from players that they’re really big homebodies and the club, if they’re going to bring them interstate, they’re going to have to have a lot of support.” The Brisbane Lions changed their selection process and welfare support program after five young players requested trades back to their home states at the end of 2013. Now, all northern states ensure “resilience” is weighted heavily in assessing players.

Player agent Alec Morgan: “The game is so much quicker now.” James Brickwood

Some factors are beyond a player’s control. In a group from the same school-year level, for instance, those born in the first six months of the year tend to have had a head start on their development, are likely to have more confidence and so be elevated – a much-noted pattern that applies in other areas of education, too.

Also known to help carve a contenders’ path to selection is attending a school with a high-performing footy program, which often offer scholarships to gifted players, too. Twenty-two per cent of last year’s draft attended an Associated Public School in Victoria, such as Geelong Grammar or Scotch College, says Luke Soulos, chief executive of APS Sport. In Melbourne, particularly, school footy is “big”, says Scott Clayton, with some clashes attracting several thousand fans. The AFLW isn’t yet dominated by APS schools, says Soulos. “We’re at, I would say, the embryonic stages in regards to girls’ football. We do get one to three players drafted in a given year.”

Former footy (and basketball) player Erin Phillips with her father Greg ahead of her induction into the Australian Football Hall of Fame in 2025. Getty Images

Some youngsters might also hail from a family of sportspeople, which can confer genetic advantages and/or the chance to model their parents’ athletic drive; or their father might have played footy, in which case they can be admitted under the AFL’s father-son or father-daughter rules. (Close to 100 players arrived at AFL clubs as father-son picks from 1998 through to 2025; over the short history of the women’s league, at least 13 players joined under the father-daughter rule, including sisters Abbie and Sophie McKay, who followed their father Andrew to Carlton.)

“Dad taught me the game, Mum took me to all my games,” the Crows’ Erin Phillips said when she was inducted into the Australian Football Hall of Fame in 2025. Phillips’ dad Greg played for Collingwood and Port Adelaide, and she was a “cross-coder”, playing footy until age 13, when pathways for girls ended, then switching to pro basketball before going back to footy for the women’s league’s first season, in her early 30s. “Having experienced being in an elite environment since I was 16 years old, I feel like I have a good grasp of what makes really successful teams.”

Harry and Maddy are both chasing their dreams while studying hard at school. Wayne Taylor

The Darcy family has produced three generations of footballers: the late David Darcy played 133 games, his son Luke notched up 226, and his grandsons Sam and Will are both Bulldogs. Luke, now a podcaster, has warned that hyper-competitive parents are destroying their children’s love of team sport. “They [teens] actually don’t care that much at 14 about winning or losing, but they get in the car and what happens is Mum or Dad say, ‘Why didn’t you play harder?’” he said. “You’re not their coach, you probably weren’t good enough to do it, so why are you trying to overlay your world on to your kids? If they’re there, and with their mates, end of story.”

‘They’re not going to draft someone who isn’t committed and who isn’t going to do their part.’ Maddy Meagher

The APS’s Soulos offers this: “The better parents are the ones that stand to the side and don’t interfere and don’t get involved, other than maybe a quiet word in the car of how well they played, or [saying], ‘It was exciting to watch you play’.” Katrina Gill concurs. “Ultimately, it’s going to be the athlete that drives their own career and determines how far they go.”

Maddy Meagher as a girl. Courtesy the Meagher family

Maddy Meagher’s dad Steven, who originally coached his daughter, says he has been lucky to “watch her play a sport that many girls before her simply didn’t have the opportunity to play”. “She had a dream of playing AFLW, and once we knew how much she wanted it, our role became more about giving her opportunities to develop and see how far she could go,” he tells us. “She could potentially end up anywhere in the country, or she might not get drafted at all. Whatever happens, it certainly won’t be because she didn’t put the effort in.”

Meanwhile, Meagher and Van Hattum are chasing their dreams with level heads. “They’re not going to draft someone who isn’t committed and who isn’t going to do their part,” Meagher says. After school, she plans to combine football with a TAFE course in myotherapy (a form of physical treatment) then do university studies in it or physiotherapy. Amidst the whirlwind, Van Hattum often reminds himself why he is doing what he is doing: “Keep it enjoyable, because you have to love footy to be there [on draft night]. It’s a big commitment at this age.” His agent Max Hayes says Van Hattum is locking in on what is important now the business end of the year has arrived, and it’s not all football. “He’s hitting the books hard right now,” Hayes said.

World.title: On a trip to a remote island with Dad, I unlocked memories I hadn’t thought about in years
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life On a trip to a remote island with Dad, I unlocked memories I hadn’t thought about in years Riley Wilson September 6, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 6 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

“Riles, check out this one.” I’m crouching over a rockpool. A mangled, tumbled conch is thrust into my sightline. My father looks pleased with his find, a sunbleached coil that barely resembles the shell it once was. “I’ve always preferred the inside of shells to the outside,” Dad says, turning it over. “Isn’t it incredible that a creature builds all of this around themselves?” Photo: We keep combing the pocked, tessellated shore of Picnic Island, a one-hectare seabird rookery and private rustic luxury escape a kilometre offshore from Coles Bay on Tasmania’s east coast. Dad gently picks up a small crab that sits unfazed in his hand until it scurries away, then collects fractures of a sea urchin dome smashed between cairns. The last time we were in Coles Bay together was over two decades ago, when we visited with my mother and American aunt. There’s a picture of me as tall as Dad’s knee, in rolled-up denim overalls, splashing in the rocky pools off nearby Muirs Beach. Dad was still in the navy, kept away for long stretches on ships as big as small towns. This morning, we watched seals from leather benches on a gun-metal- grey Van Diemen speedboat with Sam Graudins, Picnic Island’s adept and accommodating host, before mooring at one of two timber jetties on the island, which hosts up to eight people in all-inclusive comfort.



Dad joined the military at 15 and traversed the globe for 23 years. He and Mom, who left rural Illinois at 17 and worked around the world before I was born, taught me how to travel. Dad sent postcards from Vietnam, Hong Kong and Europe. He took us on adventures near and far, and impressed upon me the importance of packing an extra zip-lock into my bag, turning my undies inside out when delays became days, and unashamedly pocketing an apple from the hotel buffet for mid-afternoon fuel. By the time I left home at 17, I’d been to over a dozen countries, typically with a carry-on, surplus socks and Dad a few paces ahead of me. On the island, bar the boat squeaking against rubber buoys or the occasional helicopter flying above en route to Wineglass Bay, our peace is uninterrupted. It’s Dad, me and the penguins for six rounds of cards, a deep-dive into the state of the world, and stretches of companionable fireside silence. By the time I left home at 17, I’d been to over a dozen countries, typically with a carry-on, surplus socks and Dad a few paces ahead of me. RILEY WILSON I wake to blindingly crisp skies. In the communal lodge, known as the Birdhouse due to its elevation and large louvred windows, I make coffee for Dad and tea for me and stroll to his newly built one-bedroom suite (my studio suite, designed within the structure of the island’s old shacks, is on the other side of the island). True to form, Dad is already dressed and prepared for the day. We loop the walking track before breakfast, marvelling at the pink granite Hazards sparkling in the morning sun. This view alone could surely convince a jet-setting traveller to purchase an island while on holidays – exactly how Picnic Island’s latest ownership resulted. Dad tops homemade chai Bircher with berries while I juice carrots, oranges and apples. He’s sliced blueberries on top of my muesli, like he did with grapes for me as a kid. Some things, wonderfully, never change.



Our plans, however, do. Sam had scheduled us in for a whisky tasting, winery visit and guided tour of a local oyster lease, but we forgo the tasting for a trek to the rocky, peach-coloured cove of Sleepy Bay in Freycinet National Park. Studying lichen-covered rock faces and the ocean’s surface, Dad spots textures invisible to me. “Look into the land, not at it. That’s how you see things, Riles,” he says. “See its soul?” I quip. He replies with grave seriousness. “Exactly.” After lunch at Devil’s Corner winery, we head to Melshell Oyster Shack in Dolphin Sands, where owner Cassie Melrose proffers a chain-mail glove and her knife. I owe my obsession with oysters to Dad, who would hoist me onto his shoulders for jaunts through Melbourne’s Queen Victoria Market, and Dad’s beloved uncle, who taught me to love the taste of raw oysters. I shuck the final bivalve and pass it to Dad, who declines.



“I know how much you love them. All yours.” Related Article Sunday Life This remote Tasmanian island is known for its dairy. But a stay here reveals much more This picnic table, surrounded by discarded shells, reminds me of a lunch in France. Driving through the countryside, we paused next to a pétanque court. Dad sliced tomatoes and fat burrata with a pocketknife he kept in his sock while my brother picked leaves off a basil plant we’d bought and Mom tore bread. The sun-kissed memory remains one of my fondest. Back in our island retreat, private chef Mark Jensen (of Sydney’s now-closed Red Lantern) chats with us as he stacks Bass Strait scallops – two to a shell – in homemade XO sauce and serves rich, vibrant fish curry with rounds of crisp roti. An indulgent tiramisu and three-cheese platter await us after the table is cleared. Sated, Dad and I lie on parallel couches, me nursing a postprandial hot chocolate and him a dram. Penguins rustle outside.



“Shall we explore?” I ask, waving a red-light torch. He swings his legs off the couch. “Absolutely.” I follow him into the dark. The writer travelled as a guest of Picnic Island and Tourism Tasmania. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Michelle Lim Davidson dated a fellow actor for 10 years. Now she’s happily single
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Michelle Lim Davidson dated a fellow actor for 10 years. Now she’s happily single Jane Rocca September 6, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 6 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Actor Michelle Lim Davidson is best known for her roles in TV shows such as Play School and The Newsreader, and her new play, Koreaboo. Here, the 39-year-old talks about meeting her Korean birth parents, the end of her last relationship, and why she’s happily single for now. Michelle Lim Davidson was adopted from Korea when she was just a baby. Jedd Cooney I was adopted by my Australian parents from Seoul in 1987, and have lived in Australia since I was 4½ months old. My parents also adopted my Australian sister, who is five years younger than me. My father was born in Newcastle and raised in a working-class family. He worked in sales for a confectionery company. He played guitar in a cover band most Saturday nights in Newcastle. While Dad’s day job was all about interacting with customers, he was quite an introverted person – very private, quiet and happy to potter around at home. His father used to deliver bread and milk on a horse and cart through the streets of Carrington [NSW] and my mother’s father was a coalminer. My parents never told me I was adopted, but it was pretty obvious.



My birth parents in Korea are still together. I saw them a few months ago. They are similarly from a working-class background. When I first met them at the end of 2019, they were running a small convenience mart. They worked there for over 30 years from 6am to 11pm every day without taking a holiday. I first saw my birth father in an old black-and-white photo when he was quite young. If you cut the photo in half, I have his eyes and eyebrows. I am also half of his personality. One of the first things he sent me was a YouTube link to a song that reminded him of me. He is also a deep and serious thinker, quite introverted, too. We go from wistful and poetic to giving out facts quite quickly. It’s a common experience to have a big relationship end in your early 30s. This was a critical time for me. In year 11, at Hunter School of the Performing Arts, I was cast as the lead in Bye Bye Birdie. There was a guy in the play who was funny, charismatic, and the girls always crowded around him. I was the opposite – a quirky theatre nerd. I remember we had our first kiss at the after-party – it took me by surprise. We always talked and got along well, but I never thought he would entertain a closeness with me. A couple of years later, after I left school, we ended up in a relationship together. My teacher, Mr Carol, encouraged me to do drama as an elective. He cast me in an adaptation of Waiting for Godot, where I played Lucky and won an award for outstanding performer. It was so unexpected. I remember Mr Carol saying, “See, you can act.” He’s the reason why I even entertained the idea of becoming an actor.



My celebrity crush growing up was John Farnham. I really liked his voice and watching him perform on TV. He was more of a talent crush. I had a boyfriend when I was 22 at WAAPA [Western Australian Academy of Performing Arts]. We dated as professional actors and lived and worked in Sydney. We were together for a decade. Michelle Lim Davidson (centre) with her co-stars in The Newsreader, Sam Reid and Anna Torv. ABC-TV It’s a common experience to have a big relationship end in your early 30s. This was a critical time for me. I had just met my Korean family; my biological clock was ticking. We broke up during this time. I realised we had loved each other for the right amount of time; there was no more love to grow. I didn’t need anything from him or anyone else to fix me, and learned to love in a different way – that had come from connecting with my family in Korea. Michael Lucas brought me into the writers’ room to be part of a great creative collaborative process for [ABC-TV series] The Newsreader. I’d never had that experience before. It meant I was able to build a character that felt true, because I was playing a Korean-Australian woman in the show.



I worked with Stephen Peacocke for three seasons of The Newsreader. He is a wonderful

actor – generous and curious. I felt safe with him. Related Article Sunday Life After The Bachelorette, Brooke Blurton’s sister died. It profoundly impacted her relationship I’ve also been on Play School for 14 years and am close friends with co-presenter Alex Papps. He did my callback audition and we have toured the live show – you really get to know someone in a hire car on a six-hour drive to Wagga Wagga. I’ve never been somebody who wanted to get married. It’s not that I’m not open to it, but it would have to involve a discussion of what marriage means to that other person. But at the moment, I’m very happy to be Aunty Mish. I am happily single. World.title: Like many, I’m an expat kid. When my parents get sick, the distance feels crippling
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Like many, I’m an expat kid. When my parents get sick, the distance feels crippling Amy Molloy September 6, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 6 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

My older sister and I have a mental list of the places we’ve stood when she’s called to tell me, “Dad has cancer.” We’ve laughed about it, in the way you do when life has shown you so much darkness, and there is no other option. The first time, I was a teenager at a theme park, queuing for a rollercoaster. Two years later, when it spectacularly recurred, I was on my way to a university lecture, while my sister was on a ferry. My dad had woken up unable to walk; a tumour had been discovered around the base of his spine. We’re the lucky ones. After Dad endured years of gruelling chemo and a stem-cell transplant which, 20 years ago, was ground-breaking, our family has been gifted decades of “bonus” time, once unimaginable when his stage four non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma was first diagnosed. Amy Molloy with her father, Steve, who has had multiple bouts of cancer. Now 70, Dad has watched us get married and welcomed the birth of my three children. His three-monthly scans became six-monthly, then yearly – so normal, I stopped worrying about them at all. That is, until November 2025, when my sister and I added a new location to our list.



This time, I was standing in the clutter of my garage at 5am; with the time difference between the UK and Australia, I knew my dad would have received his scan results by then. As my kids slept, I had snuck out of the house and messaged my sister: “I’m ready.” I wasn’t ready, of course, even though I suspected what was coming. On this occasion, there were two differences in our conversation: a “new” type of cancer – myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), which can be caused by intense chemotherapy – and my actual geographic location. Raised in the UK, I immigrated to Australia nearly 15 years ago. My sister lives a few hours’ drive from our parents’ home on the outskirts of London; I live 17,000 kilometres away, a 24-hour plane ride. Our familial distance is increasingly common. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, 8.8 million people living in Australia were born overseas – 32 per cent of the population. That’s a lot of people living apart from their families. Every immigrant has run the “cost analysis” in their head. In the NSW South Coast town where I’m based, I live the Aussie dream: surfing before school with my kids, writing in cafes by the beach, earning a wage that felt impossible in England.



But after a certain age, the downsides sharpen. In my 30s, expat friends started moving back to their home countries to raise their kids. In my 40s, British mates started buying one-way tickets back to be closer to ageing parents. I’ve always known that, if my dad got sick again, moving back to the UK wasn’t an option. And then there are people, like me, who stay. As my dad’s news sank in, I found myself Googling “How to be a long-distance carer” at 2am – and discovering I’m far from the only one asking. The question is: if you choose to stay in your “chosen” life while a loved one fights to survive, how do you help – without hating yourself for not doing more?



I’ve always known that, if my dad got sick again, moving back to the UK wasn’t an option. The socially acceptable reasons? My kids are settled at school; my surf-obsessed husband wouldn’t cope; the cost of living is lower here. But really, it’s because I’m scared of being too close – and I suspect my dad shares that fear. In the past, proximity had been my coping mechanism. During our first rodeo with cancer, I wanted to do everything – to meet Dad’s little buddy in “chemo club”, to learn the alphabet of drugs he was taking, to disinfect every surface. Adrenaline and the novelty of fresh trauma carried me – until months became years. Any Molloy and her dad, Steve, when she was a child. Unlike my doting mum, who didn’t have the choice to leave, I did – and I needed to. I was “sick” in my own way, with an eating disorder that had become my coping mechanism. So, during a university summer break, I booked a flight to Sydney – a three-month trip that became a year, then a life choice. Dad tried to ease my guilt: “It’s easier when I don’t have to worry about you, too.” Those well-meaning words became part of my identity.



Fast-forward to November 2025, and we both went through the motions again. “I can come back,” I messaged him. “It’s better you don’t,” he said, blaming his compromised immune system. “I won’t be able to see anyone anyway.” Related Article Sunday Life After becoming a parent, I developed an intense fear of dying Not for the first time, we made a pact: “I’ll see you on the other side.” At the end of this year, he’s scheduled for a bone marrow transplant: a perfect match, donated by a stranger in the US. If it “takes”, he’ll no longer be transfusion-dependent or immunocompromised, and he’ll be able to fly to Australia to see his daughter and grandchildren again. We’d made a similar promise once before. When I left for my gap year, Dad was still learning to walk after his paralysis and on crutches at the airport. Before I went through the departure gates, he swore, “When you get back, I’m going to be standing on my own.” Twelve months later, he kept his word. It’s proof that no decision is ever clear-cut – especially where life and death are concerned. Some will call my choice to stay in Australia selfish. I’ll admit it: there’s self-protection at play. But it also fits a dynamic my dad and I have danced with for decades.



Unlike my older sister, a scientist who works in medical trials, I don’t speak in facts; I speak in big feelings – and I know I can be a loose cannon because of it. I understand why, in the depths of healing, my dad doesn’t want his wildest child and her three young kids turning up on his doorstep. The truth is, I have said goodbye to my dad a thousand times in big and small ways. However, that doesn’t erase the ache of being the absent one. Right now, my dad is in the “honeymoon stage” of treatment, on a light kind of chemo. He chats to my kids on FaceTime and sends photos of his e-bike outings. That will change as he nears his transplant. We’ve been here before, and we remember it too well. Before he gets better, he’s guaranteed to get worse. Of course, there are practical ways I can express care – letters from my kids, photos uploaded to his digital photo frame – but I know it can go deeper. And, so, I turned to an expert. Casey Beros, author of Next of Kin: What to Expect When You’re Expecting to Care for Someone You Love, says the “do I stay, or do I go?” tug-of-war is common.



“I have complete strangers dropping into my DMs saying, ‘I’m based here but my parents are there, and I don’t know the right thing to do,’” she says. “I understand that angst. My first response is: there is no right decision.” Related Article Sunday Life I am paid to be an oversharer, but when my life took a tragic turn, I clammed up When her own dad was diagnosed with cancer in 2021, she “got straight on a plane” with her family, moving from Sydney to Perth until he died in 2023. But, as she points out, everyone’s circumstances differ. “It also depends on your context of grief,” she says. “This was my first experience with it. If you’ve walked through that fire before, it can be a different context.” For long-distance carers, Beros offers three tiers of advice: harness technology, “support the supporter”, and realise that guilt is a wasted emotion. “I recommend showing parents how to voice-note doctors’ appointments, especially when they’re high-stakes. Another role you can play from afar is being carer for the carer.” This can be as simple as a weekly text with a sibling, or a call with the other parent. “The patient is the star athlete and the carer is the coach – they need space to vent.”



Her final piece of advice may be the most pertinent: whatever you do, it might not feel like enough – so let yourself off the hook. “I could not have juiced one more drop from the last year I spent with my dad, and it will still never feel like enough,” says Beros. “We all want a pure grief that doesn’t contain disappointment or remorse, but grief is messy. Anybody in this situation needs to ask: what can I live with?” Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Rugby: Springboks outmuscle All Blacks to win third test, take 2-1 series lead
World.content:
The Springboks have beaten the All Blacks 29-24 in the third test in Soweto to take a 2-1 lead in the four-match series.

The Springboks again started well, but the All Blacks absorbed the pressure and began to apply their own. With the All Blacks close to the line the hosts' first-five Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu knocked the ball down and was yellow carded for a professional foul.

The All Blacks made the most of the extra man, with captain Ardie Savea barging over from close range for the first try of the match after some good work from hooker Asafo Aumua.

Love kicked the conversion to give New Zealand a 7-0 lead after about 10 minutes at FNB Stadium in Johannesburg.

The Springboks were back to 15 men in the 20th minute with Feinberg-Mngomezulu re-entering the game, and the hosts would score moments later with wing Kurt-Lee Arendse going over in the right-hand corner. Feinberg-Mngomezulu missed the conversion, leaving the score 7-5 to the All Blacks midway through the first half.

The All Blacks struck back with another try to Savea after a break down the left edge by wing Leroy Carter, the skipper picking up a loose ball before diving over for his second try of the match. The conversion was unsuccessful, with the score 12-5 to the All Blacks after 27 minutes.

All Blacks winger Leroy Carter in action against the Springboks. Photosport

Savea though would leave the field soon after with what appeared to be a shoulder injury, dealing a sizable blow to the tourists. He was replaced by Wallace Sititi, with openside flanker Luke Jacobson taking over as captain.

The All Blacks had a player sent to the sin bin in the 37th minute with Love yellow carded for being offside when the Springboks were hot on attack in the All Blacks' 22.

The hosts would score from the resulting five-metre scrum, referee Nika Amashukeli awarding a penalty try under the posts after the All Blacks infringed with the Springboks scrum marching towards the try line. That made the score 12-12 just minutes before halftime, and that's how it would remain going into the break.

Love rejoined the game early in the second half, and he almost kicked a penalty from more than 40m out but pushed his attempt just wide.

The Springboks were dominating at scrum time as they were in the first half, but the All Blacks were hanging in there and scored the next try after wing Leroy Carter regathered a Will Jordan kick before passing back to Jordan, who scored the All Blacks third try of the night.

All Blacks winger Will Jordan scores against the Springboks. Photosport

Love missed the conversion with the score 17-12 to the All Blacks with just over 20 minutes to go.

Their lead was short-lived however as the Springboks hit back almost immediately with midfielder Jesse Kriel storming over after Carter missed a one-on-one tackle.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu added the extras to put South Africa back in front 19-17.

The Springboks' scrum was again dominant, and the hosts were winning consistent penalties at scrum time, making it hard for the All Blacks to build any momentum.

Another scrum penalty led to an attacking lineout for the hosts, and the All Blacks were powerless to stop the ensuing maul as Springboks hooker Malcolm Marx dived over for a try in the 65th minute to extend their lead to 26-17 with the help of another conversion.

Referee Nika Amashukeli talks to Ardie Savea. Photosport

The All Blacks gave away another penalty inside their own half, lock Fabian Holland pinged for an illegal clean out, and South Africa kicked the three points to push out to a 12-point lead (29-17) with just 10 minutes to go.

The crowd by this stage was in full party mode, and the noise inside the 90,000 capacity FNB Stadium was deafening as they began to sing the name of Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus.

The hosts had their tails up and continued to win penalties at the breakdown, the All Blacks running out of time to fight their way back into the game.

The All Blacks needed to be the next to score, but it was South Africa who made all the play with the tourists barely hanging on.

The All Blacks never gave up and they finally cracked the Springboks' defence after the fulltime siren, with replacement front rower Samisoni Taukei'aho scoring a consolation try, but it wasn't enough as the hosts held on for a 29-24 victory and a 2-1 series lead.

The best the All Blacks can now hope for is a drawn series, with game four in the US city of Baltimore next weekend.

World.title: Qantas flight diverted to Christchurch after 'engine issue'
World.content:
A Qantas flight from Queenstown had to be diverted to Christchurch on Saturday afternoon, after it experienced an "engine issue" after takeoff.

The Boeing 737-800 aircraft had just become airborne when the incident occurred.

Witnesses reported hearing banging noises. Video footage on social media appeared to show flames coming from an engine.

Nic Chamberlain was among those in Queenstown who saw flames and heard a series of loud noises.

"It was like just shoots of orange flames shooting out the back.

"You can tell it was coming out of the left engine," he told RNZ.

There was a delay before the loud noises followed, he said.

"This was kind of like rapid succession boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. And then it was loud enough that everyone kind of turned their heads and looked to see what the noise was," he said.

Flight QF122 touched down safely at Christchurch Airport at about 5pm on Saturday. There were no reports of injuries.

RNZ understands about 160 passengers were on board.

A Qantas spokesperson said the incident was under investigation.

"One of our flights to Sydney experienced a suspected engine issue after take-off from Queenstown this afternoon and the aircraft diverted to Christchurch.

"Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely.

"We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support," they said.

Earlier, the Civil Aviation Authority said bird strike caused the incident. It has since amended that statement, saying that it was unable to confirm the cause at this stage.

Hato Hone St John said it was notified of a flight diversion at 4.25pm and multiple ambulance resources responded to Christchurch Airport as a standard procedure.

A spokesperson said St John had not been required to assess or treat anyone, and all ambulance units had since been stood down.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand records show an aircraft emergency was reported at Invercargill Airport at 4.12pm, with Invercargill and Kingswell crews attending.

It is understood the flight was initially expected to divert to Invercargill before continuing to Christchurch.

World.title: Fullback Taine Tuaupiki saves Warriors with hattrick of tries over Sea Eagles
World.content:
Fullback Taine Tuaupiki - who wasn't originally named to play - has saved NZ Warriors' bacon with a hattrick of tries in a desperate 31-30 win over Manly Sea Eagles to keep their NRL minor premiership hopes alive.

The home side needed a late field goal from Chanel Harris-Tavita to snatch victory from their dogged opponents and now await the result between Penrith Panthers and Wests Tigers on Sunday, which will determine the winners of the regular-season crown.

Off to a slow start, the Warriors trailled 12-4 after 20 minutes, but rattled on the next four tries - two to Tuaupiki - to lead 24-12 just after halftime.

Tuaupiki was initially named on the interchange bench as backline cover, but entered the starting line-up when centre Leka Halasima withdrew with an ankle injury 24 hours out.

His inclusion saw Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad shifted to the wing, where he also had a try double in that 20-point run before the Sea Eagles came charging back.

As the match continued, star fullback Tom Trbojevic started to stamp his class on the game, creating chances for those around him.

Manly scored the next three tries and almost had a fourth, which was disallowed for a penalty back on halfway, to grab a 30-24 advantage late in the second half.

Tuaupiki brought the Warriors back on level terms, slicing against the grain to score next to the posts and then converting from in front.

The Warriors had two tries ruled out in the closing minutes, with Harris-Tavita and prop Tanner Stowers-Smith both crossing, and Harris-Tavita also had a field goal attempt charged down.

With the final seconds ticking down, halfback Te Maire Martin received the ball in front of the posts, but was run off his kick. On the next play, Harris-Tavita had more room to operate and duly slotted in the gamewinner.

Victory sees the Warriors set a club record of 18-6 for the season and puts them two points clear at the top of the NRL table.

Penrith can still secure the minor premiership with a three-point win over the 15th-placed Tigers.

World.title: Grain sector 'disappointed' farmers are choosing cheap palm kernel feed over local grain
World.content:
Disappointment is deepening in New Zealand's struggling arable sector over farmers continuing to opt for imported animal feeds over local grain.

New Zealand was one of the largest importers of palm kernel expeller (PKE) in the world, using the byproduct of the palm oil industry as a feed supplement for dairy cattle, largely when pasture was scarce.

Midday rural news for 4 September 2026 Rural News Download MP3 3m

Arable farmers growing feed grain had long fought for greater uptake of their product domestically, but struggled to be competitive against similar imported products on price.

The issue was raised at the industry association Seed and Grain New Zealand (SGNZ) conference in Christchurch this week, where some of the country's top arable and seed companies and government officials explored challenges and opportunities for the legacy sectors.

At the conference, SGNZ vice president Jo Townshend of Midlands Seed in Mid Canterbury raised concerns about the challenges for arable to compete against the usually cheaper imports.

Townshend said New Zealand's arable domestic manufacturing sector lacked government support to help it remain viable and cost competitive.

"It's a huge amount of importing coming into this country, possibly due to free trade agreements or other agreements, that are really putting a ceiling on the ability of arable farmers to support our own domestic economy, including process growers," she said.

"I mean, for $2 billion worth of animal feed coming into the country, for a country that's pretty good at producing it itself, is pretty disappointing."

Aotearoa imported more than 2 million tonnes of the PKE feed product from countries like Indonesia and Malaysia each year, a mostly dry matter product from the fruit of the palm.

When pastures are dry, farmers have a choice of supplementary feeds for dairy herds. Susan Murray RNZ

Environmentalists opposed importing PKE, due to its environmental effects and links to deforesting tropical rainforests.

SGNZ president Edward Luisetti of Canterbury's Luisetti Seeds said arable farmers with irrigation were looking forward to a warmer summer, particularly on the East Coast, if El Niño arrived as forecast.

However, he also expected the drier conditions to drive up farmers' PKE imports this year.

Competitive price point

Farming leader Nathan Guy was a former Horowhenua dairy farmer and agriculture minister, and now is the country's special agricultural trade envoy, flying the flag with government officials to grow New Zealand agriculture exports.

In response to questions from Jo Townshend at the event, Guy said he fed his cattle PKE and found it was an easy supplement to switch on and off.

"A benefit with PK is you can start the cows on it tomorrow. There's no rumen digestion change as there is with some other feeds."

But he said the costs for PKE had increased, and local grain was less price competitive.

"PK's very expensive right now, very expensive with shipping costs," he said.

"But I think right now there's a price point.

"Is there a way of potentially the arable over time becomes more cost competitive?"

He said many farmers, including himself, would get to a point where they would look to grow maize themselves in the face of rising costs.

One farmer who contacted RNZ said PKE was $300 per tonne, versus $500 for grain, and dairy was a business not a national charity.

Fonterra said its cows were 96 percent grass-fed (including silage, hay and forage crops like legumes and brassicas).

The dairy co-op and world's largest exporter of dairy previously told RNZ that PKE made up less than 2 percent on average of its farmer-shareholders' cows' overall diet

Meanwhile, Greenpeace activists staged a protest at an Agrifeeds PKE storage shed at Port Taranaki last year.

Greenpeace activists occupied part of Taranaki's port in April last year, to protest Fonterra's use of palm kernel. Supplied / Greenpeace

Its global project lead for agriculture, Amanda Larsson, said the palm kernel supply chain was "incredibly murky" and made it difficult to guarantee that no rainforests were destroyed in the process.

"We're pretty aligned with the arable farmers on this one," Larsson said.

"I think most New Zealanders would be pretty horrified to hear the dairy industry is connected to rainforest destruction, when there is a homegrown alternative that would actually support New Zealand's own farmers."

Larsson said farmers may need support in transitioning to more diverse and less monocultural farming systems, in the face of climate change.

Delegates at the 2024 Fonterra AGM were greeted by a Greenpeace protest about the use of palm kernel as a stock feed. RNZ / Robin Martin

The Foundation for Arable Research (FAR) [

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/country/575244/arable-sector-launches-new-trademark-to-champion-nz-grain-over-imports launched a landmark NZ Grown Grains certification last year], to help consumers identify products made with local grain and promote local uptake among farmers.

More than 34 producers were now certified, with more being assessed, including grain for animal feed.

World.title: More than half of KiwiSaver hardship applicants directed to other options
World.content:
More than half of would-be applicants for KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals to Simplicity, Milford, SuperLife and NZ Funds are being directed to other ways to deal with their problems instead.

KiwiSaver hardship withdrawal numbers have increased rapidly in recent years. In July 2026, $45.2 million was withdrawn for hardship reasons, up from $43.2m in July 2025.

Some providers have engaged third-party providers to help manage the workload that comes with the applications, such as Debtfix.

Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

In a new report, Debtfix said in the year to March 2026, it received 5964 referrals to it from the KiwiSaver schemes it works with, of people who were seeking money from their KiwiSaver accounts for hardship reasons.

Of those, 2516 went on to be approved for a hardship withdrawal. Another 3450, or 57.9 percent, were supported through other solutions to the problem.

Debtfix said accessing KiwiSaver was not always the most appropriate or sustainable solution.

Alternatives could include applying to creditors for hardship arrangements, negotiating debt repayment plans, no asset procedures or budget and cash flow planning.

Applicants for KiwiSaver withdrawal are meant to have exhausted their other options.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. Supplied

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said people had sometimes not considered the alternatives before putting in an application.

The country's biggest KiwiSaver provider, ANZ, said it saw supporting KiwiSaver members through difficult economic times as part of its role.

"When people reach out to us because they're under financial pressure, our focus is on understanding their circumstances, helping them explore the options available, and providing support through what can often be a very stressful time. We also support members through the hardship withdrawal process itself and can assist them with their application.

"Between December 2025 and July 2026, our KiwiSaver Contact Centre received almost double the number of contacts relating to financial hardship as actual hardship withdrawals. These included enquiries about existing applications, the hardship withdrawal process, and eligibility requirements.

"We would note that because many of our KiwiSaver customers contact us more than once and enquiries cover a wide range of topics, these figures can't be viewed as indicating the proportion of customers who ultimately make a withdrawal."

ANZ's spokesperson said the bank shared the view that KiwiSaver hardship applications should only be made after all reasonable alternatives had been exhausted.

"Applicants need to demonstrate they have explored other reasonable avenues of support, which may include using available savings, cashing in investments or shares, seeking assistance from their bank, or approaching WINZ for support."

Debtfix said people were increasing seeking assistance not because of their own financial decisions, but because they had run out of resources to help them cope with increasing costs.

Loss of employment or reduced work hours were some of the most common reasons people wanted help.

It said there were more people experiencing sustained periods of hardship, rather than isolated financial events.

World.title: Blaze at cafe next to New Zealand's oldest building 'suspicious', FENZ says
World.content:
A café situated just metres from New Zealand's oldest surviving building has been damaged in an overnight blaze, but volunteer firefighters managed to stop the flames spreading to 204-year-old Kemp House at Kerikeri Basin.

Police are investigating the blaze, which started in a storage shed next to Honey House Café around 11.30pm on Friday.

The shed was destroyed while one wall of the café was burned and its water pipes and electric cables were badly damaged.

The two-storey Honey House has the café on the ground level and offices for Heritage New Zealand upstairs.

The business is next to Kemp House, which was built between 1821 and 1822 by missionaries, and was an important focus for early relationships between Māori and Pākehā.

Another heritage building, the Stone Store, which was built not much later - from 1832 to 1836 - is also next door to the cafe.

The fire had been small, and "both Kemp House and Stone Store were thankfully unaffected by the blaze," a Honey House Café spokesperson said.

The Stone Store and Kemp House, seen from Kororipo Pā in 2025. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Kerikeri deputy fire chief Andy Hamberger said the nation owed a debt of gratitude to a Kerikeri man whose vigilance may have saved New Zealand's oldest building.

Hamberger said a man on his way to work about 11.30pm on Friday called 111 when he spotted smoke near Kerikeri Basin.

The first fire truck at the scene found a storage shed next to the Honey House Café - which was immediately behind the 204-year-old Kemp House - was burning fiercely.

The crew called for a second truck as well as backup from Ōkaihau and Paihia.

Hamberger said the shed was razed and the café's exterior, water pipes and electrical cabling were badly damaged.

Kerikeri deputy fire chief Andy Hamberger during an exercise at the Stone Store in February this year. PETER DE GRAAF / RNZ

If firefighters had arrived a few minutes later the flames could have taken hold of the two-storey Honey House and spread from there to nearby Kemp House, which was currently wrapped in plastic for re-roofing.

"It was called in by a chap who was going to work, he spotted the fire," Hamberger said.

"Without him the potential for spread to Kemp House was actually quite scary, to be honest, because they've got it surrounded with plastic sheeting to protect it. Potentially we could have had a fire in that Kemp House as well," he said.

"I don't know him but a big shout out to that guy, because without him being pretty vigilant on his way to work, we could be looking at a major building fire, or a heritage building being lost, or certainly significantly damaged."

John O'Hare, Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga spokesman for Northland, said the entire Kerikeri Mission Station site was closed while police and FENZ carried out their investigations.

It was too early to say with certainty what had caused the fire but initial indications were that it had been deliberately lit.

Fortunately, neither Kemp House nor the Stone Store had been damaged.

"But it was too close for comfort. It was very, very close, and we're just very thankful that that Kemp House didn't catch alight, and incredibly disappointed that somebody would do this. The indicators are that this was a deliberate act, which is appalling," O'Hare said.

The café was likely to be closed for the foreseeable future.

The cause had yet to be confirmed but if police found it had been deliberately lit, as was suspected, that would be "appalling" and "deeply disappointing", he said.

Despite its historic appearance, the Honey House - a former curator's cottage - was only built in 1976.

It was built on the site of a historic barn and took its name from James Kemp Jr's storage shed for beehives, which once stood nearby.

The café opened in 2012 with some of its recipes sourced from historic archives, or made with fruit grown in Kerikeri Mission Station's heritage orchard.

Kemp House was erected in 1821-22 by the London-based Church Missionary Society for the Reverend John Butler, the only ordained minister in the settlement at the time.

It was built by missionary carpenters and Māori sawyers, and later became the home of the Kemp family.

Kemp House is currently wrapped in plastic while it is roof shingles are being replaced, which could have made a fire even more catastrophic.

World.title: The psychiatrist who can now prescribe MDMA
World.content:
Dr Gary Wynn is one of two psychiatrists who have just been approved to administer and prescribe MDMA in New Zealand, to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

In legal terms, MDMA is a Class B high risk drug. It is also known as ecstasy, E, or molly, and is a stimulant and hallucinogen.

It is the first time MDMA assisted treatment has been allowed in Aotearoa.

Dr Wynn talked with Saturday Morning about the research his team will be doing, who could be treated, and what their sessions might look like.

The Psychiatrist Who Can Now Prescribe MDMA Saturday Morning Download MP3 22m

In the 1970s, MDMA's first use was as a medicine known as 'empathy', used by therapists," Wynn says.

"It creates an openness, a connection. An empathy-enhancing compound that sort of reduces the fear centres in the brain, and puts people in this really open space to do some deep work, particularly around traumas that they've experienced in their life."

In the early 1980s MDMA became better known as a party drug, and by the mid-1980s it was made illegal in the United States - which soon became the norm around the world. "And we spent 40-ish years with it being illegal, until Australia in 2023."

Australia's medicines regulator granted permission in 2023 for psychedelics to be used in therapy nationally there, including psilocybin for depression, and MDMA for PTSD.

What could MDMA do clinically?

MDMA's potential "is pretty amazing," Wynn says.

He has done training in Canada and Australia on providing MDMA treatment, and will be working with Dr Tom Paterson for the New Zealand trials.
